paragraphs: This paper proposes a way to simplify neural networks during training so that they generalize better. It adds a complexity penalty to the ordinary error function. The defining idea is that a set of weights is simple when its values can be organized into groups whose members are similar.

The penalty models the distribution of weights as a mixture of Gaussian distributions. Each component supports a cluster of nearby weight values, encouraging a form of soft sharing across the network. The mixture parameters adapt while the network learns, so the preferred groups are themselves learned rather than fully fixed before training begins.

Simulations find this complexity term more effective than the previous terms considered. The result supports similarity among weights as a useful form of network simplicity. It also highlights the role of adaptation in the penalty: the learning process can discover which collections of weights should have related values while continuing to fit the task. Generalization is addressed through the organization of the parameters themselves.
summary.tldr: An adaptive Gaussian-mixture penalty encourages clusters of similar network weights and outperforms earlier complexity penalties in the reported simulations.

title: Adaptive Soft Weight Tying using Gaussian Mixtures

paragraphs: This paper identifies two inhibitory contributions to the visual responses of individual cells in cat striate cortex. One sharpens preferences that are already present across orientation or spatial frequency. The other depends on contrast but is not selective for spatial structure, suggesting a broader influence on how strongly a cell responds.

Presenting contrasts in increasing and decreasing order reveals hysteresis: the response depends on the path by which contrast changes. The authors describe this effect as sensitive, strong, and rapid, suggesting relevance to ordinary vision. They interpret the associated global inhibition as limiting response range and creating spatial selectivity through thresholding.

The local mechanism instead refines the cell's spatial filtering properties. Both forms are characterized as network properties rather than recurrent inhibition, and analysis of spike-burst patterns supports distinct physiological origins. Together, the findings divide inhibitory shaping of receptive fields into broad control of responsiveness and more specific refinement of visual preferences.
summary.tldr: Two distinct inhibitory mechanisms shape cortical visual responses through global thresholding and local refinement of spatial preferences.

title: Dual Inhibitory Mechanisms for Definition of Receptive Field Characteristics in a Cat Striate Cortex

abstract: Intrator (1990) proposed a feature extraction method that is related to recent statistical theory (Huber, 1985; Friedman, 1987), and is based on a biologically motivated model of neuronal plasticity (Bienenstock et al., 1982). This method has been recently applied to feature extraction in the context of recognizing 3D objects from single 2D views (Intrator and Gold, 1991). Here we describe experiments designed to analyze the nature of the extracted features, and their relevance to the theory and psychophysics of object recognition.

paragraphs: Recognizing a three-dimensional object from a single two-dimensional view requires a useful representation of the image. This paper examines features produced by an unsupervised extraction method that had already been applied to that recognition problem. Its focus is on understanding what the learned features represent and how they relate to object recognition.

The underlying method connects statistical ideas about feature extraction with a biologically motivated model of neuronal plasticity. Plasticity concerns how neural responses change through experience. Bringing these perspectives together makes the extracted features relevant to both computational recognition and questions about how biological systems might develop useful representations.

The authors describe experiments designed to investigate the nature of those features and their relevance to recognition theory and psychophysics, the study of relationships between stimuli and perception. The contribution presented here is therefore an analysis of learned representations. It treats the contents of a representation as something to investigate, beyond simply using that representation in a recognition system.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates what an unsupervised feature extractor learns when used to recognize three-dimensional objects from single images.

title: 3D Object Recognition Using Unsupervised Feature Extraction

The algorithm may be ideal for parallel hardware implementations. This paper presents a learning algorithm to train continuous stochastic networks to respond with desired trajectories in the output units to environmental input trajectories. paragraphs: The paper presents a method for teaching a neural network to produce a desired pattern of activity over time in response to a changing input. Both time and neuron activation are continuous. The network is a stochastic version of a Boltzmann machine, so random fluctuations are part of its dynamics.

The key idea is to use the network's intrinsic Brownian noise to calculate learning gradients through entirely local computations. These gradients indicate how learning should change the network to obtain the desired output trajectories. The underlying diffusion networks combine connectionist differential equations with independent additive noise. Local computation makes the method potentially attractive for parallel hardware.

The authors position the algorithm as an extension of earlier stochastic-network learning approaches to continuous trajectories. They identify potential applications in modeling neural processes, controlling artificial movement, and recognizing continuous speech. In the speech example, changing acoustic coefficients would drive a corresponding sequence of phonemic patterns. These are proposed uses of the learning mechanism, whose central contribution is local gradient computation for continuous stochastic behavior.
summary.tldr: A continuous stochastic neural network uses its own Brownian noise to learn output trajectories through local gradient computations.

title: A Local Algorithm to Learn Trajectories with Stochastic Neural Networks

abstract: Sigmoid type belief networks, a class of probabilistic neural net(cid:173) works, provide a natural framework for compactly representing probabilistic information in a variety of unsupervised and super(cid:173) vised learning problems. Often the parameters used in these net(cid:173) works need to be learned from examples. Unfortunately, estimat(cid:173) ing the parameters via exact probabilistic calculations (i.e, the EM-algorithm) is intractable even for networks with fairly small numbers of hidden units. We propose to avoid the infeasibility of the E step by bounding likelihoods instead of computing them ex(cid:173) actly. We introduce extended and complementary representations for these networks and show that the estimation of the network parameters can be made fast (reduced to quadratic optimization) by performing the estimation in either of the alternative domains. The complementary networks can be used for continuous density estimation as well.

paragraphs: Sigmoid belief networks represent probabilistic relationships compactly, but learning their parameters can require expensive calculations over hidden variables. The paper identifies exact expectation-maximization as intractable even when the network has relatively few hidden units. This creates a practical obstacle to using the models for supervised and unsupervised learning.

The authors replace exact likelihood calculations with bounds on those likelihoods. They introduce extended and complementary representations of the networks, then perform parameter estimation in these alternative forms. In either representation, the estimation problem can be reduced to quadratic optimization, providing a tractable route around the expensive expectation step.

The significance is that changing the representation and objective calculation makes learning more manageable while retaining a probabilistic modeling framework. The method directly targets the computation that prevents exact parameter estimation from being practical. The authors also state that complementary networks can estimate continuous probability densities, extending the role of that representation beyond its use in accelerating learning.
summary.tldr: Likelihood bounds and alternative network representations reduce difficult sigmoid belief-network parameter estimation to quadratic optimization.

title: Fast Learning by Bounding Likelihoods in Sigmoid Type Belief Networks

abstract: This paper investigates a number of ensemble methods for improv(cid:173) ing the performance of phoneme classification for use in a speech recognition system. Two ensemble methods are described; boosting and mixtures of experts, both in isolation and in combination. Re(cid:173) sults are presented on two speech recognition databases: an isolated word database and a large vocabulary continuous speech database. These results show that principled ensemble methods such as boost(cid:173) ing and mixtures provide superior performance to more naive en(cid:173) semble methods such as averaging.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how combining classifiers can improve phoneme classification, a component of speech recognition. The central issue is how the individual classifiers are organized and combined. An ensemble can contain several predictors, but the rule connecting their predictions is itself an important part of the method.

The authors examine boosting and mixtures of experts, studying each approach separately and also in combination. They compare these principled ensemble strategies with simpler approaches such as averaging. This setup asks whether a more structured way of building and combining predictors offers benefits beyond the presence of multiple classifiers alone.

Results are reported on two speech databases: one involving isolated words and another involving continuous speech with a large vocabulary. Across the reported comparisons, boosting and mixtures provide better performance than the more naive ensemble methods. The finding supports paying attention to ensemble design when improving phoneme classifiers. It also places the evidence in two distinct speech settings, while keeping the evaluated task focused on phoneme classification.
summary.tldr: Boosting and mixtures of experts improve phoneme classification more effectively than simple ensemble averaging.

title: Ensemble Methods for Phoneme Classification

abstract: We first describe a hierarchical, generative model that can be viewed as a non-linear generalisation of factor analysis and can be implemented in a neural network. The model performs per(cid:173) ceptual inference in a probabilistically consistent manner by using top-down, bottom-up and lateral connections. These connections can be learned using simple rules that require only locally avail(cid:173) able information. We then show how to incorporate lateral con(cid:173) nections into the generative model. The model extracts a sparse, distributed, hierarchical representation of depth from simplified random-dot stereograms and the localised disparity detectors in the first hidden layer form a topographic map. When presented with image patches from natural scenes, the model develops topo(cid:173) graphically organised local feature detectors.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a hierarchical generative model that extends factor analysis to nonlinear relationships and can be implemented as a neural network. Its goal is to infer underlying structure from perceptual input while keeping the inference consistent with the model's probabilities.

Inference uses connections running upward, downward, and laterally through the network. These connections can be learned with simple rules that depend only on information available locally. The authors also explain how lateral connections can be incorporated into the generative model itself. This links the network's communication structure to the statistical account of how observations are produced.

On simplified random-dot stereograms, the model learns a sparse, distributed representation of depth across its hierarchy. Local disparity detectors in its first hidden layer become organized into a topographic map. With natural-scene image patches, it also develops topographically arranged local feature detectors. The results connect probabilistic perceptual learning with the emergence of spatial organization among the network's learned detectors.
summary.tldr: A hierarchical probabilistic neural model learns depth representations and topographic feature maps using locally available information.

title: Hierarchical Non-linear Factor Analysis and Topographic Maps

abstract: Spike timing plasticity (STDP) is a special form of synaptic plasticity where the relative timing of post- and presynaptic activity determines the change of the synaptic weight. On the postsynaptic side, active back- propagating spikes in dendrites seem to play a crucial role in the induc- tion of spike timing dependent plasticity. We argue that postsynaptically the temporal change of the membrane potential determines the weight change. Coming from the presynaptic side induction of STDP is closely related to the activation of NMDA channels. Therefore, we will calculate analytically the change of the synaptic weight by correlating the deriva- tive of the membrane potential with the activity of the NMDA channel. Thus, for this calculation we utilise biophysical variables of the physi- ological cell. The ﬁnal result shows a weight change curve which con- forms with measurements from biology. The positive part of the weight change curve is determined by the NMDA activation. The negative part of the weight change curve is determined by the membrane potential change. Therefore, the weight change curve should change its shape de- pending on the distance from the soma of the postsynaptic cell. We ﬁnd temporally asymmetric weight change close to the soma and temporally symmetric weight change in the distal dendrite.

paragraphs: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity changes a synapse’s strength according to the relative timing of activity on its two sides. This paper develops an analytical account using biophysical variables. It considers NMDA channel activity associated with the presynaptic contribution and changes in postsynaptic membrane voltage, where spikes traveling back through dendrites appear to play an important role.

The proposed calculation correlates NMDA channel activity with the time derivative of membrane potential. In plain language, it combines channel activity with how quickly voltage changes. The resulting curve of synaptic weight changes agrees with biological measurements. In the analysis, NMDA activation determines the positive portion of the curve, while membrane-potential change determines its negative portion.

This division leads to a spatial prediction: the timing rule should change with distance from the cell body. The authors find temporally asymmetric changes near the cell body and symmetric changes in more distant dendrites. The approach therefore connects the shape of a learning rule to local cellular dynamics, rather than treating the timing curve as independent of synaptic location.
summary.tldr: An analytical biophysical model links spike-timing plasticity to NMDA activity and voltage changes, predicting different timing curves along dendrites.

title: Analytical Solution of Spike-timing Dependent Plasticity Based on Synaptic Biophysics

paragraphs: Data may occupy a low-dimensional manifold even when each observation has many coordinates. This paper studies whether a small collection of random linear measurements retains enough information to discover that hidden structure. The manifold is unknown, so dimensionality reduction must work without first constructing a detailed geometric model.

The authors show that intrinsic dimension can be estimated accurately from random projections of sampled points. They also prove that the underlying manifold’s structure can be estimated using only those projected measurements. In both results, the required projection count grows linearly with intrinsic dimension and logarithmically with ambient dimension.

The contribution connects simple linear compression with nonlinear geometric discovery. It suggests that learning the relevant dimension and structure need not begin with full high-dimensional observations when the data satisfy the manifold model. The supplied abstract ends mid-sentence, so the summary relies on its complete statements rather than inferring additional guarantees beyond them.
summary.tldr: A small set of random projections can preserve enough information to estimate intrinsic dimension and manifold structure.

title: Random Projections for Manifold Learning

abstract: Object matching is a fundamental operation in data analysis. It typically requires the definition of a similarity measure between the classes of objects to be matched. Instead, we develop an approach which is able to perform matching by requiring a similarity measure only within each of the classes. This is achieved by maximizing the dependency between matched pairs of observations by means of the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion. This problem can be cast as one of maximizing a quadratic assignment problem with special structure and we present a simple algorithm for finding a locally optimal solution.
originalAbstract: Object matching is a fundamental operation in data analysis. It typically requires the definition of a similarity measure between the classes of objects to be matched. Instead, we develop an approach which is able to perform matching by requiring a similarity measure only within each of the classes. This is achieved by maximizing the dependency between matched pairs of observations by means of the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion. This problem can be cast as one of maximizing a quadratic assignment problem with special structure and we present a simple algorithm for finding a locally optimal solution.

paragraphs: Matching objects across two collections usually requires a way to score the similarity of an object in one collection to an object in the other. The paper changes that requirement. Its approach needs similarity measures only within each collection, allowing the matching problem to be expressed through the structure of the two sets.

The proposed criterion chooses pairings that maximize statistical dependence between the matched observations. It measures that dependence using the Hilbert Schmidt Independence Criterion. In this formulation, within-collection similarities provide the information used to evaluate an arrangement of pairs, so a direct similarity measure across the two object classes is unnecessary.

The resulting optimization is a quadratic assignment problem with special structure. The authors present a simple algorithm that finds a locally optimal solution. That qualification matters: the stated result concerns local optimality, rather than a guarantee of the best possible assignment. The contribution is a different formulation of object matching, together with a practical optimization procedure for using within-set similarities to construct cross-set correspondences.
summary.tldr: Kernelized sorting matches objects using only within-set similarities by seeking a locally optimal pairing that maximizes statistical dependence.

title: Kernelized Sorting

abstract: In this paper we explore the problem of biasing unsupervised models to favor sparsity. We extend the posterior regularization framework [8] to encourage the model to achieve posterior sparsity on the unlabeled training data. We apply this new method to learn ﬁrst-order HMMs for unsupervised part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and show that HMMs learned this way consistently and signiﬁcantly out-performs both EM-trained HMMs, and HMMs with a sparsity-inducing Dirichlet prior trained by variational EM. We evaluate these HMMs on three languages — English, Bulgarian and Portuguese — under four conditions. We ﬁnd that our method always improves performance with respect to both baselines, while variational Bayes actually degrades performance in most cases. We increase accuracy with respect to EM by 2.5%-8.7% absolute and we see improvements even in a semisupervised condition where a limited dictionary is provided.

We apply this new method to learn ﬁrst-order HMMs for unsupervised part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and show that HMMs learned this way consistently and signiﬁcantly out-performs both EM-trained HMMs, and HMMs with a sparsity-inducing Dirichlet prior trained by variational EM. We evaluate these HMMs on three languages — English, Bulgarian and Portuguese — under four conditions. We ﬁnd that our method always improves performance with respect to both baselines, while variational Bayes actually degrades performance in most cases. We increase accuracy with respect to EM by 2.5%-8.7% absolute and we see improvements even in a semisupervised condition where a limited dictionary is provided.

paragraphs: The paper explores where to encourage sparsity in an unsupervised latent-variable model. It extends posterior regularization so that the model favors sparse posterior assignments on unlabeled training examples. The distinction is between encouraging sparse inferred explanations of the data and encouraging sparsity in the model's parameters.

The authors apply the method to first-order hidden Markov models for unsupervised part-of-speech tagging. They compare it with ordinary expectation-maximization training and with a sparsity-inducing Dirichlet prior trained using variational EM. This comparison tests whether imposing sparsity through posterior behavior is more useful for the task than the alternative parameter-focused approach.

Evaluation covers English, Bulgarian, and Portuguese under four conditions. Posterior regularization improves on both baselines throughout the reported evaluation, with absolute accuracy gains of 2.5–8.7 percentage points over EM. Improvements also appear when a limited dictionary supplies some supervision. The variational Bayesian alternative degrades performance in most cases, highlighting that the location of the sparsity preference matters in these experiments.
summary.tldr: Encouraging sparse posterior assignments improves HMM part-of-speech tagging across the reported conditions, outperforming EM and a parameter-sparsity approach.

title: Posterior vs Parameter Sparsity in Latent Variable Models

abstract: Computing two-way and multi-way set similarities is a fundamental problem. This study focuses on estimating 3-way resemblance (Jaccard similarity) using b-bit minwise hashing. While traditional minwise hashing methods store each hashed value using 64 bits, b-bit minwise hashing only stores the lowest b bits (where b>= 2 for 3-way). The extension to 3-way similarity from the prior work on 2-way similarity is technically non-trivial. We develop the precise estimator which is accurate and very complicated; and we recommend a much simplified estimator suitable for sparse data. Our analysis shows that $b$-bit minwise hashing can normally achieve a 10 to 25-fold improvement in the storage space required for a given estimator accuracy of the 3-way resemblance.
originalAbstract: Computing two-way and multi-way set similarities is a fundamental problem. This study focuses on estimating 3-way resemblance (Jaccard similarity) using b-bit minwise hashing. While traditional minwise hashing methods store each hashed value using 64 bits, b-bit minwise hashing only stores the lowest b bits (where b>= 2 for 3-way). The extension to 3-way similarity from the prior work on 2-way similarity is technically non-trivial. We develop the precise estimator which is accurate and very complicated; and we recommend a much simplified estimator suitable for sparse data. Our analysis shows that $b$-bit minwise hashing can normally achieve a 10 to 25-fold improvement in the storage space required for a given estimator accuracy of the 3-way resemblance.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate the resemblance among three sets while storing compact summaries of them. The target is three-way Jaccard similarity, which describes their shared overlap relative to their combined contents. Compact estimates matter because retaining full hashed values can require substantial storage when many set comparisons are needed.

The method uses b-bit minwise hashing. Instead of storing each hashed value in 64 bits, it retains only the lowest b bits, with at least two bits required for the three-way setting considered here. Moving from comparisons of two sets to three is technically demanding. The authors derive a precise but complicated estimator and also recommend a much simpler estimator for sparse data.

Their analysis indicates that the compressed representation can normally reduce storage requirements by a factor of 10 to 25 for a given accuracy in estimating three-way resemblance. This is an accuracy-matched storage comparison, rather than a claim that every choice of b achieves the same benefit. The simplified estimator offers an additional practical option when the sparse-data setting applies.
summary.tldr: The paper extends compact minwise hashing to three-way set similarity, with analysis indicating typical storage savings of 10 to 25 times at matched accuracy.

title: b-Bit Minwise Hashing for Estimating Three-Way Similarities

abstract: Most action potentials in the nervous system take on the form of strong, rapid, and brief voltage deflections known as spikes, in stark contrast to other action potentials, such as in the heart, that are characterized by broad voltage plateaus. We derive the shape of the neuronal action potential from first principles, by postulating that action potential generation is strongly constrained by the brain's need to minimize energy expenditure. For a given height of an action potential, the least energy is consumed when the underlying currents obey the bang-bang principle: the currents giving rise to the spike should be intense, yet short-lived, yielding spikes with sharp onsets and offsets. Energy optimality predicts features in the biophysics that are not per se required for producing the characteristic neuronal action potential: sodium currents should be extraordinarily powerful and inactivate with voltage; both potassium and sodium currents should have kinetics that have a bell-shaped voltage-dependence; and the cooperative action of multiple `gates' should start the flow of current.

paragraphs: Neuronal action potentials commonly appear as brief, sharp voltage spikes, whereas some other action potentials have broad plateaus. This paper asks whether the shape of neuronal spikes can follow from an energy-minimization principle. Its starting assumption is that the brain's need to conserve energy strongly constrains how action potentials are generated.

For a specified spike height, the analysis finds that energy consumption is minimized when the underlying currents follow a bang-bang pattern: they are strong but brief. This produces rapid voltage rises and falls. The result links the visible shape of the spike to an optimization of the currents that generate it.

The same principle predicts additional biophysical features, including very powerful sodium currents that inactivate with voltage, bell-shaped voltage dependence of sodium and potassium kinetics, and cooperative gates that initiate current flow. These properties are not inherently required just to produce a recognizable neuronal spike. Their emergence from energy optimality gives the hypothesis explanatory reach beyond spike shape, while remaining grounded in its stated optimization assumption.
summary.tldr: Assuming energy minimization, the paper derives sharp neuronal spikes and predicts specific properties of their underlying currents.

title: Energetically Optimal Action Potentials

abstract: This paper describes a new approach for computing nonnegative matrix factorizations (NMFs) with linear programming. The key idea is a data-driven model for the factorization, in which the most salient features in the data are used to express the remaining features. More precisely, given a data matrix X, the algorithm identifies a matrix C that satisfies X = CX and some linear constraints. The matrix C selects features, which are then used to compute a low-rank NMF of X. A theoretical analysis demonstrates that this approach has the same type of guarantees as the recent NMF algorithm of Arora et al.~(2012). In contrast with this earlier work, the proposed method has (1) better noise tolerance, (2) extends to more general noise models, and (3) leads to efficient, scalable algorithms. Experiments with synthetic and real datasets provide evidence that the new approach is also superior in practice. An optimized C++ implementation of the new algorithm can factor a multi-Gigabyte matrix in a matter of minutes.

paragraphs: Nonnegative matrix factorization seeks a low-rank representation using nonnegative factors. This paper approaches that task by selecting salient features from the data itself and using them to express the remaining features. The representation is therefore built around a selected portion of the observed data.

For a data matrix X, the algorithm finds a matrix C satisfying X = CX along with additional linear constraints. C identifies the features that will be used to construct the factorization. Casting this selection through linear programming gives the method a concrete optimization framework and connects feature selection to the eventual low-rank representation.

The theoretical analysis provides the same type of guarantees as the earlier algorithm discussed in the abstract, with better noise tolerance and support for more general noise models. Experiments on synthetic and real data provide evidence of practical advantages as well. An optimized C++ implementation factors a multi-gigabyte matrix within minutes, supporting the paper's claim that this approach can lead to efficient, scalable algorithms.
summary.tldr: A linear-programming approach builds nonnegative matrix factorizations from selected data features, with improved noise handling and demonstrated scalability.

title: Factoring nonnegative matrices with linear programs

abstract: Sparse learning models typically combine a smooth loss with a nonsmooth penalty, such as trace norm. Although recent developments in sparse approximation have offered promising solution methods, current approaches either apply only to matrix-norm constrained problems or provide suboptimal convergence rates. In this paper, we propose a boosting method for regularized learning that guarantees $\epsilon$ accuracy within $O(1/\epsilon)$ iterations. Performance is further accelerated by interlacing boosting with fixed-rank local optimization---exploiting a simpler local objective than previous work. The proposed method yields state-of-the-art performance on large-scale problems. We also demonstrate an application to latent multiview learning for which we provide the first efficient weak-oracle.

Performance is further accelerated by interlacing boosting with fixed-rank local optimization---exploiting a simpler local objective than previous work. The proposed method yields state-of-the-art performance on large-scale problems. We also demonstrate an application to latent multiview learning for which we provide the first efficient weak-oracle.

paragraphs: Many sparse learning problems combine a smooth measure of prediction error with a penalty that is not smooth, such as the trace norm. This combination makes optimization challenging. The paper addresses a gap in existing approaches: some apply only when a matrix norm appears as a constraint, while others have weaker convergence rates.

The proposed boosting method handles regularized learning and guarantees accuracy epsilon within O(1/epsilon) iterations. It also alternates boosting steps with local optimization at a fixed rank. These local steps use an objective that is simpler than in previous work, providing an additional way to accelerate training beyond the basic iteration guarantee.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance on large-scale problems and demonstrate the method in latent multiview learning. For that application, they supply what they describe as the first efficient weak oracle. The paper therefore links an optimization guarantee, a practical acceleration strategy, and an application-specific computational ingredient needed to make the approach useful.
summary.tldr: A boosting-based optimizer gives an O(1/epsilon) iteration guarantee for matrix-norm regularization and gains further speed from fixed-rank local optimization.

title: Accelerated Training for Matrix-norm Regularization: A Boosting Approach

abstract: We analyse a plug-in estimator for a large class of integral functionals of one or more continuous probability densities. This class includes important families of entropy, divergence, mutual information, and their conditional versions. For densities on the d-dimensional unit cube [0,1]^d that lie in a beta-Holder smoothness class, we prove our estimator converges at the rate O(n^(1/(beta+d))). Furthermore, we prove that the estimator obeys an exponential concentration inequality about its mean, whereas most previous related results have bounded only expected error of estimators. Finally, we demonstrate our bounds to the case of conditional Renyi mutual information.

paragraphs: Many statistical quantities summarize entire probability densities rather than individual observations. This paper analyzes a plug-in estimator for a broad class of such quantities, including entropy, divergence, mutual information, and conditional versions. The plug-in approach estimates the relevant densities and uses those estimates to calculate the desired integral functional.

The theoretical setting assumes continuous densities on a d-dimensional unit cube that belong to a beta-Hölder smoothness class. Within this setting, the authors establish a convergence result whose stated rate depends on both smoothness and dimension. These assumptions connect the estimator's behavior to the regularity and dimensionality of the underlying distributions.

The paper also proves an exponential concentration inequality around the estimator's mean. This addresses how strongly individual estimates can fluctuate, adding information beyond a bound on average estimation error alone. The authors illustrate the bounds for conditional Rényi mutual information. The contribution is thus a shared theoretical treatment of many density-based quantities, with particular attention to probabilistic control of deviations as well as convergence.
summary.tldr: A plug-in estimator for density-based quantities receives convergence and exponential concentration guarantees under stated support and smoothness assumptions.

title: Exponential Concentration of a Density Functional Estimator

abstract: In many problem settings, parameter vectors are not merely sparse, but dependent in such a way that non-zero coefficients tend to cluster together. We refer to this form of dependency as “region sparsity”. Classical sparse regression methods, such as the lasso and automatic relevance determination (ARD), model parameters as independent a priori, and therefore do not exploit such dependencies. Here we introduce a hierarchical model for smooth, region-sparse weight vectors and tensors in a linear regression setting. Our approach represents a hierarchical extension of the relevance determination framework, where we add a transformed Gaussian process to model the dependencies between the prior variances of regression weights. We combine this with a structured model of the prior variances of Fourier coefficients, which eliminates unnecessary high frequencies. The resulting prior encourages weights to be region-sparse in two different bases simultaneously. We develop efficient approximate inference methods and show substantial improvements over comparable methods (e.g., group lasso and smooth RVM) for both simulated and real datasets from brain imaging.

paragraphs: In some regression problems, nonzero coefficients occur in groups or regions rather than independently. The paper calls this region sparsity. Standard sparse approaches such as lasso and automatic relevance determination do not exploit this dependence in their prior modeling. The authors seek a model that captures both clustered nonzero weights and smooth variation.

Their hierarchical extension of relevance determination uses a transformed Gaussian process to connect the prior variances of regression weights. They combine it with a structured model for the prior variances of Fourier coefficients, suppressing unnecessary high frequencies. Together, these choices encourage region sparsity in two bases and provide a model for smooth weight vectors and tensors in linear regression.

The authors develop efficient approximate inference procedures and evaluate the model on simulated data and real brain imaging datasets. They report substantial improvements over comparable approaches, including group lasso and smooth RVM. These results support explicitly representing dependence among relevant coefficients when the desired regression structure includes both spatial grouping and smoothness.
summary.tldr: Dependent relevance determination models clustered, smooth regression weights through linked prior variances in the original and Fourier representations.

title: Sparse Bayesian structure learning with “dependent relevance determination” priors

abstract: Infinite Hidden Markov Models (iHMM's) are an attractive, nonparametric generalization of the classical Hidden Markov Model which can automatically infer the number of hidden states in the system. However, due to the infinite-dimensional nature of the transition dynamics, performing inference in the iHMM is difficult. In this paper, we present an infinite-state Particle Gibbs (PG) algorithm to resample state trajectories for the iHMM. The proposed algorithm uses an efficient proposal optimized for iHMMs, and leverages ancestor sampling to improve the mixing of the standard PG algorithm. Our algorithm demonstrates significant convergence improvements on synthetic and real world data sets.

In this paper, we present an infinite-state Particle Gibbs (PG) algorithm to resample state trajectories for the iHMM. The proposed algorithm uses an efficient proposal optimized for iHMMs, and leverages ancestor sampling to improve the mixing of the standard PG algorithm. Our algorithm demonstrates significant convergence improvements on synthetic and real world data sets.

paragraphs: Infinite hidden Markov models extend ordinary hidden Markov models by allowing the number of hidden states to be inferred automatically. This flexibility makes them attractive for sequential data whose state structure is unknown. It also creates a computational challenge: the transition dynamics are infinite-dimensional, which makes inference difficult.

The paper introduces a Particle Gibbs algorithm that resamples hidden-state trajectories directly in this infinite-state setting. A trajectory is the sequence of hidden states associated with the observations. The algorithm uses an efficient proposal designed specifically for infinite hidden Markov models, tailoring the sampling procedure to the structure of the inference problem.

The authors also use ancestor sampling to improve mixing relative to standard Particle Gibbs. Better mixing concerns how effectively the sampler moves through possible explanations of the data. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show significant convergence improvements. The contribution therefore targets the practical inference obstacle that accompanies automatic state-number inference, improving the sampling procedure while keeping the infinite-state modeling framework.
summary.tldr: An infinite-state Particle Gibbs sampler uses a tailored proposal and ancestor sampling to improve convergence for infinite hidden Markov models.

title: Particle Gibbs for Infinite Hidden Markov Models

abstract: Example-based explanations are widely used in the effort to improve the interpretability of highly complex distributions. However, prototypes alone are rarely sufficient to represent the gist of the complexity. In order for users to construct better mental models and understand complex data distributions, we also need {\em criticism} to explain what are \textit{not} captured by prototypes. Motivated by the Bayesian model criticism framework, we develop \texttt{MMD-critic} which efficiently learns prototypes and criticism, designed to aid human interpretability. A human subject pilot study shows that the \texttt{MMD-critic} selects prototypes and criticism that are useful to facilitate human understanding and reasoning. We also evaluate the prototypes selected by \texttt{MMD-critic} via a nearest prototype classifier, showing competitive performance compared to baselines.

paragraphs: Representative examples can help people understand a complex dataset, but they may leave important aspects of its distribution unexplained. This paper argues that an explanation should also include criticism: examples that reveal what the selected prototypes fail to capture. The aim is to help users build a more complete mental model of the data.

The authors introduce MMD-critic, an efficient method for selecting both prototypes and criticisms. Its motivation comes from Bayesian model criticism, applied here to the adequacy of an example-based explanation. Prototypes convey representative patterns, while criticisms draw attention to gaps in that representation. Their usefulness comes from these complementary roles.

A pilot study with human participants finds that the selected prototypes and criticisms help understanding and reasoning. The authors also evaluate the prototypes through a nearest-prototype classifier, reporting competitive performance against baselines. These evaluations address different aspects of the method: whether the examples assist people and whether the prototypes provide a useful representation for classification.
summary.tldr: MMD-critic pairs representative examples with criticisms that expose their gaps, helping human understanding in a pilot study.

title: Examples are not enough, learn to criticize! Criticism for Interpretability

abstract: We propose a geometric algorithm for topic learning and inference that is built on the convex geometry of topics arising from the Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) model and its nonparametric extensions. To this end we study the optimization of a geometric loss function, which is a surrogate to the LDA's likelihood. Our method involves a fast optimization based weighted clustering procedure augmented with geometric corrections, which overcomes the computational and statistical inefficiencies encountered by other techniques based on Gibbs sampling and variational inference, while achieving the accuracy comparable to that of a Gibbs sampler. The topic estimates produced by our method are shown to be statistically consistent under some conditions. The algorithm is evaluated with extensive experiments on simulated and real data.

paragraphs: This paper approaches topic learning through the geometry underlying Latent Dirichlet Allocation and its nonparametric extensions. Instead of directly optimizing the LDA likelihood, it studies a geometric loss that serves as a substitute objective. This makes the geometric structure of topics the basis for both learning and inference.

The resulting algorithm combines an efficient weighted-clustering procedure with geometric corrections. Clustering provides the main optimization step, while the corrections incorporate the topic model's geometry. The authors present this combination as a way to overcome computational and statistical inefficiencies associated with techniques based on Gibbs sampling and variational inference, while retaining accuracy comparable to a Gibbs sampler.

The paper also establishes statistical consistency of its topic estimates under specified conditions. That is a conditional theoretical result, complementing the practical motivation for faster inference. Extensive experiments on simulated and real data evaluate the method. Together, the contributions show how replacing a likelihood with a geometrically motivated surrogate can produce an efficient topic-learning procedure with both accuracy evidence and a consistency guarantee.
summary.tldr: Geometric Dirichlet Means combines weighted clustering and geometric corrections for efficient topic inference with conditional statistical consistency.

title: Geometric Dirichlet Means Algorithm for topic inference

abstract: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent orconvolutional neural networks in an encoder and decoder configuration. The best performing such models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attentionm echanisms. We propose a novel, simple network architecture based solely onan attention mechanism, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely.Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superiorin quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less timeto train. Our single model with 165 million parameters, achieves 27.5 BLEU onEnglish-to-German translation, improving over the existing best ensemble result by over 1 BLEU. On English-to-French translation, we outperform the previoussingle state-of-the-art with model by 0.7 BLEU, achieving a BLEU score of 41.1.

paragraphs: Sequence-transduction systems commonly used recurrent or convolutional encoders and decoders, often with attention connecting them. This paper proposes an architecture built solely around attention, removing recurrence and convolutions from the model. The motivation is to improve translation while allowing more computation to proceed in parallel.

The authors evaluate the architecture on two machine-translation tasks and report better quality with substantially less training time. Their supplied abstract describes a single model with 165 million parameters achieving 27.5 BLEU on English-to-German translation, more than 1 BLEU above the previous best ensemble result.

For English-to-French translation, the abstract reports 41.1 BLEU, exceeding the previous best single-model result by 0.7 BLEU. These are the figures stated in this source abstract. The evidence concerns the two translation tasks, and the abstract does not provide a detailed architectural breakdown or establish performance across all sequence-learning applications.
summary.tldr: An attention-only sequence architecture improves translation quality while allowing more parallel computation.

title: Attention is All you Need

abstract: Learning to communicate through interaction, rather than relying on explicit supervision, is often considered a prerequisite for developing a general AI. We study a setting where two agents engage in playing a referential game and, from scratch, develop a communication protocol necessary to succeed in this game. Unlike previous work, we require that messages they exchange, both at train and test time, are in the form of a language (i.e. sequences of discrete symbols). We compare a reinforcement learning approach and one using a differentiable relaxation (straight-through Gumbel-softmax estimator) and observe that the latter is much faster to converge and it results in more effective protocols. Interestingly, we also observe that the protocol we induce by optimizing the communication success exhibits a degree of compositionality and variability (i.e. the same information can be phrased in different ways), both properties characteristic of natural languages. As the ultimate goal is to ensure that communication is accomplished in natural language, we also perform experiments where we inject prior information about natural language into our model and study properties of the resulting protocol.

paragraphs: This paper studies how two agents can learn to communicate through a referential game without explicit supervision of their messages. Success requires developing a shared communication protocol from scratch. Messages must consist of sequences of discrete symbols during both training and testing, making the communication channel language-like in its form.

The authors compare reinforcement learning with a training approach based on a differentiable relaxation, using a straight-through Gumbel-softmax estimator. In their experiments, the relaxation converges much faster and produces more effective protocols. This comparison concerns how the agents learn to use discrete messages to coordinate successfully.

Optimizing communication success also produces protocols with some compositionality and variability: messages exhibit reusable structure, and the same information can be expressed in different ways. These are partial similarities to natural language, rather than a claim that the agents independently acquire a human language. The authors additionally inject prior information about natural language and examine the resulting protocols, connecting the game setting to their longer-term aim of natural-language communication.
summary.tldr: Agents learn discrete-symbol communication through a game, with differentiable relaxation yielding faster learning and partially language-like protocols.

title: Emergence of Language with Multi-agent Games: Learning to Communicate with Sequences of Symbols

abstract: We investigate the efficiency of k-means in terms of both statistical and computational requirements. More precisely, we study a Nystr\"om approach to kernel k-means. We analyze the statistical properties of the proposed method and show that it achieves the same accuracy of exact kernel k-means with only a fraction of computations. Indeed, we prove under basic assumptions that sampling $\sqrt{n}$ Nystr\"om landmarks allows to greatly reduce computational costs without incurring in any loss of accuracy. To the best of our knowledge this is the first result showing in this kind for unsupervised learning.

Indeed, we prove under basic assumptions that sampling $\sqrt{n}$ Nystr\"om landmarks allows to greatly reduce computational costs without incurring in any loss of accuracy. To the best of our knowledge this is the first result showing in this kind for unsupervised learning.

paragraphs: This paper examines whether kernel k-means can become substantially cheaper without losing statistical accuracy. Its proposed approach uses a Nyström approximation, based on a sampled set of landmarks. The central question is how large that landmark set needs to be for the approximate method to preserve the accuracy of exact kernel k-means.

The authors prove that, under their stated basic assumptions, sampling √n landmarks is sufficient to greatly reduce computation without an accuracy loss. The result gives a specific relationship between the sample size and the number of landmarks needed. Its significance is that the computational shortcut comes with a statistical analysis, rather than only a demonstration that the approximation runs faster.

The guarantee concerns matching the accuracy of exact kernel k-means under the analysis’s assumptions. It does not require describing the approximate and exact procedures as producing identical cluster assignments. By treating statistical and computational requirements together, the paper shows that reducing the cost of this unsupervised learning method need not inherently weaken its stated accuracy guarantee.
summary.tldr: Under basic assumptions, kernel k-means with √n Nyström landmarks matches exact kernel k-means accuracy while greatly reducing computation.

title: Statistical and Computational Trade-Offs in Kernel K-Means

abstract: Stochastic convex optimization algorithms are the most popular way to train machine learning models on large-scale data. Scaling up the training process of these models is crucial, but the most popular algorithm, Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD), is a serial method that is surprisingly hard to parallelize. In this paper, we propose an efficient distributed stochastic optimization method by combining adaptivity with variance reduction techniques. Our analysis yields a linear speedup in the number of machines, constant memory footprint, and only a logarithmic number of communication rounds. Critically, our approach is a black-box reduction that parallelizes any serial online learning algorithm, streamlining prior analysis and allowing us to leverage the significant progress that has been made in designing adaptive algorithms. In particular, we achieve optimal convergence rates without any prior knowledge of smoothness parameters, yielding a more robust algorithm that reduces the need for hyperparameter tuning. We implement our algorithm in the Spark distributed framework and exhibit dramatic performance gains on large-scale logistic regression problems.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradient descent is effective for large-scale training, but its sequential updates make distributing work across machines difficult. This paper develops a distributed method for stochastic convex optimization by combining adaptive learning with variance reduction. The aim is to gain parallel speed without requiring extensive communication or prior tuning information.

The approach is a black-box reduction that can parallelize a serial online learning algorithm. This makes existing advances in adaptive online learning available within the distributed framework. The analysis establishes linear speedup with the number of machines, a constant memory footprint, and a logarithmic number of communication rounds. It also gives optimal convergence rates without advance knowledge of smoothness parameters.

Avoiding the need to supply those parameters reduces one source of hyperparameter tuning. The authors implement the method in Spark and report substantial performance gains on large-scale logistic regression problems. The contribution combines theoretical scaling guarantees in the studied optimization setting with an implementation showing practical benefits, linking distributed computation to adaptable serial learning procedures through a reusable reduction.
summary.tldr: A black-box distributed optimization framework combines adaptivity and variance reduction to achieve strong scaling guarantees with less parameter tuning.

title: Distributed Stochastic Optimization via Adaptive SGD

abstract: Learning the minimum/maximum mean among a finite set of distributions is a fundamental sub-problem in planning, game tree search and reinforcement learning. We formalize this learning task as the problem of sequentially testing how the minimum mean among a finite set of distributions compares to a given threshold. We develop refined non-asymptotic lower bounds, which show that optimality mandates very different sampling behavior for a low vs high true minimum. We show that Thompson Sampling and the intuitive Lower Confidence Bounds policy each nail only one of these cases. We develop a novel approach that we call Murphy Sampling. Even though it entertains exclusively low true minima, we prove that MS is optimal for both possibilities. We then design advanced self-normalized deviation inequalities, fueling more aggressive stopping rules. We complement our theoretical guarantees by experiments showing that MS works best in practice.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to determine whether the smallest mean among a finite collection of distributions lies above or below a threshold. Samples are gathered sequentially, so the method must decide which distribution to observe next and when enough evidence has accumulated. This question arises as a subproblem in planning, game-tree search, and reinforcement learning.

Refined finite-sample lower bounds show that optimal sampling behavior differs substantially depending on whether the true minimum is low or high. Thompson Sampling and a Lower Confidence Bounds policy each handle only one of these cases optimally. The authors introduce Murphy Sampling, which considers exclusively low-minimum possibilities yet is proved optimal for both outcomes.

The paper also develops self-normalized deviation inequalities that support more aggressive stopping rules. These rules concern when the accumulated observations justify ending the test, complementing the choice of what to sample. Experiments show Murphy Sampling performing best in the tested comparisons. The contribution combines an explanation of the task’s asymmetric demands with a method that addresses both sides.
summary.tldr: Murphy Sampling optimally tests whether a collection’s lowest mean crosses a threshold, handling two cases that challenge standard sampling policies differently.

title: Sequential Test for the Lowest Mean: From Thompson to Murphy Sampling

abstract: Entropy estimation is one of the prototypical problems in distribution property testing. To consistently estimate the Shannon entropy of a distribution on $S$ elements with independent samples, the optimal sample complexity scales sublinearly with $S$ as $\Theta(\frac{S}{\log S})$ as shown by Valiant and Valiant \cite{Valiant--Valiant2011}. Extending the theory and algorithms for entropy estimation to dependent data, this paper considers the problem of estimating the entropy rate of a stationary reversible Markov chain with $S$ states from a sample path of $n$ observations. We show that \begin{itemize} \item Provided the Markov chain mixes not too slowly, \textit{i.e.}, the relaxation time is at most $O(\frac{S}{\ln^3 S})$, consistent estimation is achievable when $n \gg \frac{S^2}{\log S}$. \item Provided the Markov chain has some slight dependency, \textit{i.e.}, the relaxation time is at least $1+\Omega(\frac{\ln^2 S}{\sqrt{S}})$, consistent estimation is impossible when $n \lesssim \frac{S^2}{\log S}$. \end{itemize} Under both assumptions, the optimal estimation accuracy is shown to be $\Theta(\frac{S^2}{n \log S})$. In comparison, the empirical entropy rate requires at least $\Omega(S^2)$ samples to be consistent, even when the Markov chain is memoryless. In addition to synthetic experiments, we also apply the estimators that achieve the optimal sample complexity to estimate the entropy rate of the English language in the Penn Treebank and the Google One Billion Words corpora, which provides a natural benchmark for language modeling and relates it directly to the widely used perplexity measure.
originalAbstract: Entropy estimation is one of the prototypical problems in distribution property testing. To consistently estimate the Shannon entropy of a distribution on $S$ elements with independent samples, the optimal sample complexity scales sublinearly with $S$ as $\Theta(\frac{S}{\log S})$ as shown by Valiant and Valiant \cite{Valiant--Valiant2011}. Extending the theory and algorithms for entropy estimation to dependent data, this paper considers the problem of estimating the entropy rate of a stationary reversible Markov chain with $S$ states from a sample path of $n$ observations. We show that \begin{itemize} \item Provided the Markov chain mixes not too slowly, \textit{i.e.}, the relaxation time is at most $O(\frac{S}{\ln^3 S})$, consistent estimation is achievable when $n \gg \frac{S^2}{\log S}$. \item Provided the Markov chain has some slight dependency, \textit{i.e.}, the relaxation time is at least $1+\Omega(\frac{\ln^2 S}{\sqrt{S}})$, consistent estimation is impossible when $n \lesssim \frac{S^2}{\log S}$. \end{itemize} Under both assumptions, the optimal estimation accuracy is shown to be $\Theta(\frac{S^2}{n \log S})$. In comparison, the empirical entropy rate requires at least $\Omega(S^2)$ samples to be consistent, even when the Markov chain is memoryless. In addition to synthetic experiments, we also apply the estimators that achieve the optimal sample complexity to estimate the entropy rate of the English language in the Penn Treebank and the Google One Billion Words corpora, which provides a natural benchmark for language modeling and relates it directly to the widely used perplexity measure.

This paper studies estimating it from a single observed path of a stationary, reversible Markov chain with S states. The central question is how much data is needed when the state space is large and observations are dependent.

The authors prove that consistent estimation is achievable with n much larger than S²/log S when relaxation time is at most O(S/ln³ S). They also establish an impossibility result at sample sizes on the order of S²/log S or smaller when relaxation time is at least 1 + Ω(ln² S/√S). Under both conditions, optimal estimation accuracy scales as Θ(S²/(n log S)).

The empirical entropy-rate estimator requires at least order S² samples for consistency, even for memoryless chains. The proposed optimal estimators therefore improve sample requirements in the stated regime. Alongside synthetic experiments, the authors apply them to English-language corpora, linking entropy-rate estimation to perplexity and a benchmark for language modeling.
summary.tldr: Under stated mixing and dependence conditions, Markov-chain entropy rates can be estimated optimally with sample requirements scaling as S²/log S.

title: Entropy Rate Estimation for Markov Chains with Large State Space

abstract: To better understand the representations in visual cortex, we need to generate better predictions of neural activity in awake animals presented with their ecological input: natural video. Despite recent advances in models for static images, models for predicting responses to natural video are scarce and standard linear-nonlinear models perform poorly. We developed a new deep recurrent network architecture that predicts inferred spiking activity of thousands of mouse V1 neurons simultaneously recorded with two-photon microscopy, while accounting for confounding factors such as the animal's gaze position and brain state changes related to running state and pupil dilation. Powerful system identification models provide an opportunity to gain insight into cortical functions through in silico experiments that can subsequently be tested in the brain. However, in many cases this approach requires that the model is able to generalize to stimulus statistics that it was not trained on, such as band-limited noise and other parameterized stimuli. We investigated these domain transfer properties in our model and find that our model trained on natural images is able to correctly predict the orientation tuning of neurons in responses to artificial noise stimuli. Finally, we show that we can fully generalize from movies to noise and maintain high predictive performance on both stimulus domains by fine-tuning only the final layer's weights on a network otherwise trained on natural movies. The converse, however, is not true.

That asymmetry is a stated finding and matters when choosing training stimuli for models intended to support experiments across stimulus types.
summary.tldr: A recurrent cortical-response model transfers from natural movies to noise through final-layer fine-tuning, but the reverse transfer does not hold.

title: Stimulus domain transfer in recurrent models for large scale cortical population prediction on video

abstract: We study the problem of fair classification within the versatile framework of Dwork et al. [ITCS '12], which assumes the existence of a metric that measures similarity between pairs of individuals. Unlike earlier work, we do not assume that the entire metric is known to the learning algorithm; instead, the learner can query this arbitrary metric a bounded number of times. We propose a new notion of fairness called metric multifairness and show how to achieve this notion in our setting. Metric multifairness is parameterized by a similarity metric d on pairs of individuals to classify and a rich collection C of (possibly overlapping) "comparison sets" over pairs of individuals. At a high level, metric multifairness guarantees that similar subpopulations are treated similarly , as long as these subpopulations are identified within the class C.

paragraphs: This paper studies fair classification when a metric describes how similar two individuals are. The motivating principle is that similar people should receive similar treatment. The learner is assumed to have access to such a metric, but it does not know all pairwise similarities and can query the metric only a bounded number of times.

The authors introduce metric multifairness to express fairness under this restricted access. The definition combines the similarity metric with a rich collection of comparison sets, each describing pairs of individuals. These sets may overlap, allowing the fairness requirement to cover multiple intersecting ways of comparing populations.

The paper shows how to achieve this notion in the stated setting. Its guarantee concerns similar subpopulations represented within the chosen collection of comparison sets. That qualification determines which comparisons the guarantee covers. The contribution is therefore a way to connect limited access to similarity information with a fairness requirement that can encompass many explicitly represented subpopulation comparisons.
summary.tldr: Metric multifairness guarantees similar treatment for represented similar subpopulations using only bounded access to an individual-similarity metric.

title: Fairness Through Computationally-Bounded Awareness

abstract: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is a widely deployed method to sample from high-dimensional distributions in Statistics and Machine learning. HMC is known to run very efficiently in practice and its popular second-order ``leapfrog" implementation has long been conjectured to run in $d^{1/4}$ gradient evaluations. Here we show that this conjecture is true when sampling from strongly log-concave target distributions that satisfy a weak third-order regularity property associated with the input data. Our regularity condition is weaker than the Lipschitz Hessian property and allows us to show faster convergence bounds for a much larger class of distributions than would be possible with the usual Lipschitz Hessian constant alone. Important distributions that satisfy our regularity condition include posterior distributions used in Bayesian logistic regression for which the data satisfies an ``incoherence" property. Our result compares favorably with the best available bounds for the class of strongly log-concave distributions, which grow like $d^{{1}/{2}}$ gradient evaluations with the dimension. Moreover, our simulations on synthetic data suggest that, when our regularity condition is satisfied, leapfrog HMC performs better than its competitors -- both in terms of accuracy and in terms of the number of gradient evaluations it requires.

This paper addresses a conjecture about how that efficiency scales with dimension d: that the required number of gradient evaluations has a d^(1/4) dependence. The authors prove this dependence for a specified class of target distributions.

summary.tldr: Leapfrog HMC achieves the conjectured d^(1/4) gradient-evaluation dependence for strongly log-concave distributions satisfying a stated regularity condition.

title: Dimensionally Tight Bounds for Second-Order Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

abstract: We present a neurosymbolic framework for the lifelong learning of algorithmic tasks that mix perception and procedural reasoning. Reusing high-level concepts across domains and learning complex procedures are key challenges in lifelong learning. We show that a program synthesis approach that combines gradient descent with combinatorial search over programs can be a more effective response to these challenges than purely neural methods. Our framework, called HOUDINI, represents neural networks as strongly typed, differentiable functional programs that use symbolic higher-order combinators to compose a library of neural functions. Our learning algorithm consists of: (1) a symbolic program synthesizer that performs a type-directed search over parameterized programs, and decides on the library functions to reuse, and the architectures to combine them, while learning a sequence of tasks; and (2) a neural module that trains these programs using stochastic gradient descent. We evaluate HOUDINI on three benchmarks that combine perception with the algorithmic tasks of counting, summing, and shortest-path computation. Our experiments show that HOUDINI transfers high-level concepts more effectively than traditional transfer learning and progressive neural networks, and that the typed representation of networks signiﬁcantly accelerates the search.

paragraphs: HOUDINI addresses learning a sequence of tasks that require both perception and procedural reasoning. The central challenge is to reuse high-level concepts while constructing more complex procedures. The framework approaches this through program synthesis, combining a search over program structures with gradient-based training of their neural components.

Neural networks are represented as strongly typed, differentiable functional programs. Symbolic higher-order combinators assemble functions from a library into larger programs. A type-directed synthesizer chooses which library functions to reuse and how to compose them for each task, while a neural module trains the resulting parameterized program using stochastic gradient descent. The types help guide the structural search.

The evaluation uses three benchmarks combining perception with counting, summing, and shortest-path computation. In these experiments, HOUDINI transfers high-level concepts more effectively than traditional transfer learning and progressive neural networks. The typed representation also substantially speeds up program search. Together, these findings support explicitly searching for reusable procedures as a practical approach to the evaluated lifelong learning tasks.
summary.tldr: HOUDINI combines typed program synthesis and neural training to reuse concepts across tasks involving perception and procedural reasoning.

title: HOUDINI: Lifelong Learning as Program Synthesis

abstract: Modern applications of machine learning (ML) deal with increasingly heterogeneous datasets comprised of data collected from overlapping latent subpopulations. As a result, traditional models trained over large datasets may fail to recognize highly predictive localized effects in favour of weakly predictive global patterns. This is a problem because localized effects are critical to developing individualized policies and treatment plans in applications ranging from precision medicine to advertising. To address this challenge, we propose to estimate sample-specific models that tailor inference and prediction at the individual level. In contrast to classical ML models that estimate a single, complex model (or only a few complex models), our approach produces a model personalized to each sample. These sample-specific models can be studied to understand subgroup dynamics that go beyond coarse-grained class labels. Crucially, our approach does not assume that relationships between samples (e.g. a similarity network) are known a priori. Instead, we use unmodeled covariates to learn a latent distance metric over the samples. We apply this approach to financial, biomedical, and electoral data as well as simulated data and show that sample-specific models provide fine-grained interpretations of complicated phenomena without sacrificing predictive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art models such as deep neural networks.

paragraphs: A dataset can contain overlapping groups whose predictive relationships differ substantially. A model trained across everyone may emphasize weak global patterns while missing strong local effects. This paper addresses that problem by learning a personalized model for every sample, aiming to support predictions and interpretations at the individual level.

The approach does not require a predefined network of similarities between samples. Instead, it uses covariates outside the modeled relationships to learn a latent distance metric over the samples. These findings indicate that, in the studied applications, personalization can reveal localized relationships while retaining strong prediction, rather than making interpretation depend on a single model shared by all samples.
summary.tldr: Sample-specific regression models reveal localized predictive relationships while matching strong predictive models in the evaluated datasets.

title: Learning Sample-Specific Models with Low-Rank Personalized Regression

abstract: In this paper, from a theoretical perspective, we study how powerful graph neural networks (GNNs) can be for learning approximation algorithms for combinatorial problems. To this end, we first establish a new class of GNNs that can solve a strictly wider variety of problems than existing GNNs. Then, we bridge the gap between GNN theory and the theory of distributed local algorithms. We theoretically demonstrate that the most powerful GNN can learn approximation algorithms for the minimum dominating set problem and the minimum vertex cover problem with some approximation ratios with the aid of the theory of distributed local algorithms. We also show that most of the existing GNNs such as GIN, GAT, GCN, and GraphSAGE cannot perform better than with these ratios. This paper is the first to elucidate approximation ratios of GNNs for combinatorial problems. Furthermore, we prove that adding coloring or weak-coloring to each node feature improves these approximation ratios. This indicates that preprocessing and feature engineering theoretically strengthen model capabilities.

paragraphs: The paper asks how good graph neural networks can theoretically be at finding approximate solutions to combinatorial problems. An approximation ratio describes how a solution compares with the best possible one. This shifts attention from whether a network performs well on examples to what quality of solution its architecture can support.

The authors introduce a class of graph neural networks that can solve a strictly broader collection of problems than existing architectures. They then connect these networks to distributed local algorithms. That connection supplies tools for establishing achievable approximation ratios for minimum dominating set and minimum vertex cover, along with limits that apply to widely used architectures such as GIN, GAT, GCN, and GraphSAGE.

A further result shows that supplying node coloring or weak-coloring information improves the approximation ratios. Consequently, the capabilities being analyzed depend on both the network and its input features. The contribution gives a theoretical reason for preprocessing: appropriately structured node information can strengthen the solution guarantees available to a graph neural network.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes approximation guarantees and limits for graph neural networks and proves that node-coloring features can improve those guarantees.

title: Approximation Ratios of Graph Neural Networks for Combinatorial Problems

abstract: Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) aims to enhance the generalization capability of a certain model from a source domain to a target domain. UDA is of particular significance since no extra effort is devoted to annotating target domain samples. However, the different data distributions in the two domains, or \emph{domain shift/discrepancy}, inevitably compromise the UDA performance. Although there has been a progress in matching the marginal distributions between two domains, the classifier favors the source domain features and makes incorrect predictions on the target domain due to category-agnostic feature alignment. In this paper, we propose a novel category anchor-guided (CAG) UDA model for semantic segmentation, which explicitly enforces category-aware feature alignment to learn shared discriminative features and classifiers simultaneously. First, the category-wise centroids of the source domain features are used as guided anchors to identify the active features in the target domain and also assign them pseudo-labels. Then, we leverage an anchor-based pixel-level distance loss and a discriminative loss to drive the intra-category features closer and the inter-category features further apart, respectively. Finally, we devise a stagewise training mechanism to reduce the error accumulation and adapt the proposed model progressively. Experiments on both the GTA5$\rightarrow $Cityscapes and SYNTHIA$\rightarrow $Cityscapes scenarios demonstrate the superiority of our CAG-UDA model over the state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/RogerZhangzz/CAG\_UDA}.

title: Category Anchor-Guided Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Semantic Segmentation

abstract: The performance of policy gradient methods is sensitive to hyperparameter settings that must be tuned for any new application. Widely used grid search methods for tuning hyperparameters are sample inefficient and computationally expensive. More advanced methods like Population Based Training that learn optimal schedules for hyperparameters instead of fixed settings can yield better results, but are also sample inefficient and computationally expensive. In this paper, we propose Hyperparameter Optimisation on the Fly (HOOF), a gradient-free algorithm that requires no more than one training run to automatically adapt the hyperparameter that affect the policy update directly through the gradient. The main idea is to use existing trajectories sampled by the policy gradient method to optimise a one-step improvement objective, yielding a sample and computationally efficient algorithm that is easy to implement. Our experimental results across multiple domains and algorithms show that using HOOF to learn these hyperparameter schedules leads to faster learning with improved performance.
