paragraphs: Policy-gradient reinforcement learning can be highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices. Searching over those choices with separate training runs consumes both computation and interaction samples. Even methods that learn changing hyperparameter schedules can be expensive. This paper proposes Hyperparameter Optimisation on the Fly, or HOOF, to adapt relevant hyperparameters within a single training run.

HOOF reuses trajectories already collected by the policy-gradient algorithm. It uses them to optimize an objective measuring one-step improvement, adapting hyperparameters that directly influence the gradient-based policy update. The hyperparameter optimization itself is gradient-free. Reusing existing experience is central to the claimed sample and computational efficiency, since tuning does not require a collection of independent training runs.

Experiments across multiple domains and policy-gradient algorithms show faster learning and improved performance when HOOF learns these schedules. The result supports changing update-related hyperparameters during training using evidence already produced by the learner. Its stated scope concerns hyperparameters affecting the policy update directly through the gradient, rather than every possible choice involved in building a reinforcement-learning system.
summary.tldr: HOOF reuses collected trajectories to tune policy-update hyperparameters during one training run, improving learning in the reported experiments.

title: Fast Efficient Hyperparameter Tuning for Policy Gradient Methods

abstract: We propose a novel memory cell for recurrent neural networks that dynamically maintains information across long windows of time using relatively few resources. The Legendre Memory Unit~(LMU) is mathematically derived to orthogonalize its continuous-time history -- doing so by solving $d$ coupled ordinary differential equations~(ODEs), whose phase space linearly maps onto sliding windows of time via the Legendre polynomials up to degree $d - 1$. Backpropagation across LMUs outperforms equivalently-sized LSTMs on a chaotic time-series prediction task, improves memory capacity by two orders of magnitude, and significantly reduces training and inference times. LMUs can efficiently handle temporal dependencies spanning $100\text{,}000$ time-steps, converge rapidly, and use few internal state-variables to learn complex functions spanning long windows of time -- exceeding state-of-the-art performance among RNNs on permuted sequential MNIST. These results are due to the network's disposition to learn scale-invariant features independently of step size. Backpropagation through the ODE solver allows each layer to adapt its internal time-step, enabling the network to learn task-relevant time-scales. We demonstrate that LMU memory cells can be implemented using $m$ recurrently-connected Poisson spiking neurons, $\mathcal{O}( m )$ time and memory, with error scaling as $\mathcal{O}( d / \sqrt{m} )$. We discuss implementations of LMUs on analog and digital neuromorphic hardware.

title: Legendre Memory Units: Continuous-Time Representation in Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: This paper extends robust principal component analysis (RPCA) to nonlinear manifolds. Suppose that the observed data matrix is the sum of a sparse component and a component drawn from some low dimensional manifold. Is it possible to separate them by using similar ideas as RPCA? Is there any benefit in treating the manifold as a whole as opposed to treating each local region independently? We answer these two questions affirmatively by proposing and analyzing an optimization framework that separates the sparse component from the manifold under noisy data. Theoretical error bounds are provided when the tangent spaces of the manifold satisfy certain incoherence conditions. We also provide a near optimal choice of the tuning parameters for the proposed optimization formulation with the help of a new curvature estimation method. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated on both synthetic and real datasets.

We answer these two questions affirmatively by proposing and analyzing an optimization framework that separates the sparse component from the manifold under noisy data. Theoretical error bounds are provided when the tangent spaces of the manifold satisfy certain incoherence conditions. We also provide a near optimal choice of the tuning parameters for the proposed optimization formulation with the help of a new curvature estimation method. The efficacy of our method is demonstrated on both synthetic and real datasets.

It assumes an observed matrix contains a component drawn from a low-dimensional manifold together with a sparse component. The goal is to separate those components even when the data are noisy, allowing the underlying structure to curve rather than treating it as purely linear.

The proposed optimization framework treats the manifold as a whole. The authors report benefits over handling each local region independently and provide theoretical error bounds when the manifold's tangent spaces satisfy specified incoherence conditions. These conditions are part of the guarantee, so the separation result is tied to properties of the underlying manifold.

The work also addresses how to set the optimization's tuning parameters. A new method for estimating curvature supports a near-optimal parameter choice, connecting the manifold's geometry to the formulation's settings. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Together, the framework, conditional error analysis, and parameter-selection method develop a nonlinear extension of robust component separation.
summary.tldr: A nonlinear robust PCA framework separates sparse corruption from manifold-structured data, with conditional error bounds and curvature-based parameter selection.

title: Manifold denoising by Nonlinear Robust Principal Component Analysis

abstract: Variance reduction has emerged in recent years as a strong competitor to stochastic gradient descent in non-convex problems, providing the first algorithms to improve upon the converge rate of stochastic gradient descent for finding first-order critical points. However, variance reduction techniques typically require carefully tuned learning rates and willingness to use excessively large "mega-batches" in order to achieve their improved results. We present a new algorithm, STORM, that does not require any batches and makes use of adaptive learning rates, enabling simpler implementation and less hyperparameter tuning. Our technique for removing the batches uses a variant of momentum to achieve variance reduction in non-convex optimization. On smooth losses $F$, STORM finds a point $x$ with $\mathbb{E}[\|\nabla F(x)\|]\le O(1/\sqrt{T}+\sigma^{1/3}/T^{1/3})$ in $T$ iterations with $\sigma^2$ variance in the gradients, matching the best-known rate but without requiring knowledge of $\sigma$.

paragraphs: Stochastic gradients introduce noise into optimization, and variance-reduction methods can improve convergence for nonconvex problems. However, obtaining their stronger guarantees often involves carefully chosen learning rates and very large batches. This paper introduces STORM to retain a strong convergence rate while removing those batching requirements and reducing the need for hyperparameter tuning.

STORM uses a variant of momentum to reduce gradient variance and chooses learning rates adaptively. The algorithm requires no batches and does not need advance knowledge of the gradient-noise variance. Its target is a first-order critical point, assessed through the size of the gradient, so the guarantee concerns approaching stationarity in a nonconvex objective.

For smooth losses, after T iterations the expected gradient norm is bounded by O(1/√T + σ^(1/3)/T^(1/3)), where σ² is the gradient variance. This matches the best-known rate stated in the paper. The significance is that STORM reaches that rate without knowing σ or relying on large batches, making the theoretical improvement compatible with a simpler optimization procedure.
summary.tldr: STORM uses adaptive learning rates and momentum-based variance reduction to match a best-known nonconvex convergence rate without batches or known noise variance.

title: Momentum-Based Variance Reduction in Non-Convex SGD

abstract: Computing the permanent of a non-negative matrix is a core problem with practical applications ranging from target tracking to statistical thermodynamics. However, this problem is also #P-complete, which leaves little hope for finding an exact solution that can be computed efficiently. While the problem admits a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme, this method has seen little use because it is both inefficient in practice and difficult to implement. We present ADAPART, a simple and efficient method for exact sampling of permutations, each associated with a weight as determined by a matrix. ADAPART uses an adaptive, iterative partitioning strategy over permutations to convert any upper bounding method for the permanent into one that satisfies a desirable `nesting' property over the partition used. These samples are then used to construct tight bounds on the permanent which hold with a high probability. Empirically, ADAPART provides significant speedups (sometimes exceeding 50x) over prior work. We also empirically observe polynomial scaling in some cases. In the context of multi-target tracking, ADAPART allows us to use the optimal proposal distribution during particle filtering, leading to orders of magnitude fewer samples and improved tracking performance.

Although a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme exists, the abstract describes it as impractical and difficult to implement. This paper introduces ADAPART to make sampling and approximation more usable.

ADAPART samples permutations exactly according to weights defined by a matrix. It repeatedly adapts a partition of the permutation space, turning an upper-bounding method for the permanent into one with the required nesting property across that partition. The resulting samples support tight bounds on the permanent that hold with high probability. Exactness applies to the sampling procedure; the permanent itself is bounded probabilistically.

summary.tldr: ADAPART uses adaptive partitions to sample weighted permutations exactly and build high-probability permanent bounds, with substantial empirical speedups.

title: Approximating the Permanent by Sampling from Adaptive Partitions

abstract: The universal approximation theorem states that any regular function can be approximated closely using a single hidden layer neural network. Some recent work has shown that, for some special functions, the number of nodes in such an approximation could be exponentially reduced with multi-layer neural networks. In this work, we extend this idea to a rich class of functions, namely the discriminant functions that arise in optimal Bayesian classification of Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) in $\mathds{R}^n$. We show that such functions can be approximated with arbitrary precision using $O(n)$ nodes in a neural network with two hidden layers (deep neural network), while in contrast, a neural network with a single hidden layer (shallow neural network) would require at least $O(\exp(n))$ nodes or exponentially large coefficients. Given the universality of the Gaussian distribution in the feature spaces of data, e.g., in speech, image and text, our results shed light on the observed efficiency of deep neural networks in practical classification problems.

paragraphs: A neural network's ability to approximate a function does not by itself establish how large that network must be. This paper studies that distinction for discriminant functions used in optimal Bayesian classification of Gaussian mixture models. These functions provide a substantial class of classification problems in which to compare shallow and deeper network representations.

The authors show that a network with two hidden layers can approximate these functions to arbitrary precision using a number of nodes that scales linearly with the input dimension. Their contrasting result for a single hidden layer requires exponentially many nodes or exponentially large coefficients. The second alternative matters: the comparison concerns both network size and the scale of its coefficients.

The result gives a mathematical account of how an additional hidden layer can make certain classification functions much more economical to represent. Because Gaussian distributions are relevant to feature representations in speech, images, and text, the authors connect the analysis to the practical efficiency of deep classifiers. The theorem concerns approximation of the studied function class; its explanatory relevance to practical learning follows from that representational advantage.
summary.tldr: For Gaussian-mixture classification functions, two hidden layers offer a strong representational efficiency advantage over one hidden layer.

title: Efficient Deep Approximation of GMMs

abstract: Imitation learning trains policies to map from input observations to the actions that an expert would choose. In this setting, distribution shift frequently exacerbates the effect of misattributing expert actions to nuisance correlates among the observed variables. We observe that a common instance of this causal confusion occurs in partially observed settings when expert actions are strongly correlated over time: the imitator learns to cheat by predicting the expert's previous action, rather than the next action. To combat this "copycat problem", we propose an adversarial approach to learn a feature representation that removes excess information about the previous expert action nuisance correlate, while retaining the information necessary to predict the next action. In our experiments, our approach improves performance significantly across a variety of partially observed imitation learning tasks.

paragraphs: Behavioral cloning learns to predict an expert's actions from observations. When the available observations reveal only part of the situation, a policy may use observation histories to guide its decisions. The paper identifies a misleading shortcut in this setting: if expert actions are strongly correlated over time, predicting the previous action can resemble predicting the next one.

This copycat behavior is a form of causal confusion. The imitator associates its target with a convenient correlate instead of learning the information needed for the upcoming decision. Distribution shift can amplify the resulting errors. The authors address the problem by learning a representation that suppresses excess information about the expert's previous action.

The representation is trained adversarially while preserving information needed to predict the next action. The aim is selective removal of a nuisance correlate, rather than indiscriminately discarding historical information. Experiments show significant performance improvements across several partially observed imitation-learning tasks. The findings demonstrate that controlling what a policy's representation reveals about previous actions can help counter this particular imitation shortcut.
summary.tldr: An adversarially learned representation reduces an imitation policy's tendency to copy previous expert actions, improving performance on partially observed tasks.

title: Fighting Copycat Agents in Behavioral Cloning from Observation Histories

abstract: Bregman divergences generalize measures such as the squared Euclidean distance and the KL divergence, and arise throughout many areas of machine learning. In this paper, we focus on the problem of approximating an arbitrary Bregman divergence from supervision, and we provide a well-principled approach to analyzing such approximations. We develop a formulation and algorithm for learning arbitrary Bregman divergences based on approximating their underlying convex generating function via a piecewise linear function. We provide theoretical approximation bounds using our parameterization and show that the generalization error $O_p(m^{-1/2})$ for metric learning using our framework matches the known generalization error in the strictly less general Mahalanobis metric learning setting. We further demonstrate empirically that our method performs well in comparison to existing metric learning methods, particularly for clustering and ranking problems.

paragraphs: Bregman divergences form a broad family of comparison measures that includes squared Euclidean distance and KL divergence. This paper asks how to learn an approximation to an arbitrary member of that family from supervision. The aim is to learn the comparison rule itself, giving metric learning access to a wider class of relationships.

The method works through the convex function that generates a Bregman divergence. It approximates that generating function with a piecewise linear function and develops a corresponding learning formulation and algorithm. This provides a structured way to learn divergences, along with theoretical bounds describing the quality of approximations available through the parameterization.

The authors also establish a generalization-error rate of O_p(m^(-1/2)) for metric learning in their framework. This matches the known rate for the less general Mahalanobis metric-learning setting. Empirical comparisons show good performance against existing metric-learning methods, particularly in clustering and ranking, supporting the usefulness of the broader family as well as its theoretical analysis.
summary.tldr: Learning a piecewise linear convex generator enables supervised approximation of Bregman divergences with approximation and generalization guarantees.

title: Learning to Approximate a Bregman Divergence

abstract: Fair representation learning provides an effective way of enforcing fairness constraints without compromising utility for downstream users. A desirable family of such fairness constraints, each requiring similar treatment for similar individuals, is known as individual fairness. In this work, we introduce the first method that enables data consumers to obtain certificates of individual fairness for existing and new data points. The key idea is to map similar individuals to close latent representations and leverage this latent proximity to certify individual fairness. That is, our method enables the data producer to learn and certify a representation where for a data point all similar individuals are at l-infinity distance at most epsilon, thus allowing data consumers to certify individual fairness by proving epsilon-robustness of their classifier. Our experimental evaluation on five real-world datasets and several fairness constraints demonstrates the expressivity and scalability of our approach.

paragraphs: Individual fairness requires similar individuals to receive similar treatment. This paper develops a representation-learning method that lets downstream data users obtain certificates of that property for both existing and new data points. The approach divides the task between learning a suitable representation and verifying the behavior of the classifier that uses it.

The data producer learns a latent representation in which every individual considered similar to a given point lies within an epsilon-sized neighborhood of that point. The distance is measured with the l-infinity norm, which bounds the largest difference along any coordinate. The producer can certify this proximity property rather than relying only on observed closeness among examples.

The data consumer then proves that its classifier is epsilon-robust in the representation space. Together, the proximity certificate and classifier robustness establish individual fairness under the specified similarity constraint. Experiments on five real-world datasets and several fairness constraints demonstrate the method's expressivity and scalability. The contribution is a concrete connection between representation geometry and downstream fairness certification.
summary.tldr: Certified proximity between similar individuals lets downstream users establish individual fairness by verifying classifier robustness in the learned representation.

title: Learning Certified Individually Fair Representations

abstract: Developing learning methods which do not discriminate subgroups in the population is a central goal of algorithmic fairness. One way to reach this goal is by modifying the data representation in order to meet certain fairness constraints. In this work we measure fairness according to demographic parity. This requires the probability of the possible model decisions to be independent of the sensitive information. We argue that the goal of imposing demographic parity can be substantially facilitated within a multitask learning setting. We present a method for learning a shared fair representation across multiple tasks, by means of different new constraints based on MMD and Sinkhorn Divergences. We derive learning bounds establishing that the learned representation transfers well to novel tasks. We present experiments on three real world datasets, showing that the proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches by a significant margin.

paragraphs: This paper studies fairness through the representation that a learning system builds from its data. It uses demographic parity as the fairness criterion: probabilities of model decisions should be independent of sensitive information. The authors argue that learning across multiple tasks can make it easier to impose this requirement on a shared representation.

Their method introduces constraints based on MMD and Sinkhorn divergences to learn that representation jointly across tasks. These quantities provide ways to compare distributions, supplying mathematical tools for the fairness constraints. The shared representation is intended to support multiple prediction problems while meeting the selected demographic-parity objective.

The authors derive learning bounds supporting transfer of the learned representation to previously unseen tasks. They also evaluate the method on three real-world datasets and report a significant advantage over the state-of-the-art approaches considered. The contribution links fairness and transfer: knowledge shared across tasks can help shape a representation that remains useful beyond the tasks used to learn it. The fairness claim is specifically framed around demographic parity.
summary.tldr: Distribution-based constraints learn a shared representation that supports demographic parity and comes with transfer bounds for new tasks.

title: Exploiting MMD and Sinkhorn Divergences for Fair and Transferable Representation Learning

abstract: We study the problem of learning Ising models in a setting where some of the samples from the underlying distribution can be arbitrarily corrupted. In such a setup, we aim to design statistically optimal estimators in a high-dimensional scaling in which the number of nodes p, the number of edges k and the maximal node degree d are allowed to increase to infinity as a function of the sample size n. Our analysis is based on exploiting moments of the underlying distribution, coupled with novel reductions to univariate estimation. Our proposed estimators achieve an optimal dimension independent dependence on the fraction of corrupted data in the contaminated setting, while also simultaneously achieving high-probability error guarantees with optimal sample-complexity. We corroborate our theoretical results by simulations.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning Ising models when some observed samples may be corrupted arbitrarily. The goal is to estimate the underlying model reliably despite that contamination. The analysis allows the model to grow with the amount of data: the numbers of nodes and edges, and the maximum node degree, can all increase with sample size.

The proposed estimators exploit moments of the underlying distribution and reduce parts of the problem to estimation of a single variable. These reductions connect a high-dimensional robust learning problem to simpler estimation tasks. The resulting analysis tracks both the effect of corrupted observations and the amount of data needed for accurate estimation.

The estimators achieve optimal dependence on the corrupted fraction that does not worsen with dimension. They simultaneously provide high-probability error guarantees with optimal sample complexity. Dimension independence applies specifically to the contamination dependence; the abstract does not characterize every part of the estimation problem that way. Simulations corroborate the theory, supporting the proposed approach to learning growing Ising models from contaminated samples.
summary.tldr: Moment-based estimators learn contaminated Ising models with optimal, dimension-independent contamination dependence and optimal sample complexity.

title: On Learning Ising Models under Huber's Contamination Model

abstract: We consider the problem of online learning with non-convex losses. In terms of feedback, we assume that the learner observes – or otherwise constructs – an inexact model for the loss function encountered at each stage, and we propose a mixed-strategy learning policy based on dual averaging. In this general context, we derive a series of tight regret minimization guarantees, both for the learner’s static (external) regret, as well as the regret incurred against the best dynamic policy in hindsight. Subsequently, we apply this general template to the case where the learner only has access to the actual loss incurred at each stage of the process. This is achieved by means of a kernel-based estimator which generates an inexact model for each round’s loss function using only the learner’s realized losses as input.

paragraphs: Online learning requires repeated decisions as losses are encountered over time. This paper considers nonconvex losses and imperfect feedback: at each stage, the learner observes or constructs only an approximate model of the current loss function. The central question is how effectively learning can proceed when neither a simple loss shape nor an exact loss model is available.

The authors propose a mixed-strategy policy based on dual averaging. They derive tight regret guarantees against two comparators: the best fixed decision in hindsight and the best dynamic policy in hindsight. These comparisons assess different goals, since a fixed comparator uses one choice throughout while a dynamic comparator can change its decisions over time.

The framework also covers a more restricted feedback setting in which the learner sees only the loss of the action it actually took. A kernel-based estimator turns these realized losses into approximate models for each round. This connects the general analysis to limited-feedback learning by showing how the inexact models assumed by the policy can be constructed from observed outcomes.
summary.tldr: A dual-averaging policy provides regret guarantees for online nonconvex learning using approximate loss models, including models built from realized losses alone.

title: Online Non-Convex Optimization with Imperfect Feedback

abstract: We develop a general approach to distill symbolic representations of a learned deep model by introducing strong inductive biases. We focus on Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). The technique works as follows: we first encourage sparse latent representations when we train a GNN in a supervised setting, then we apply symbolic regression to components of the learned model to extract explicit physical relations. We find the correct known equations, including force laws and Hamiltonians, can be extracted from the neural network. We then apply our method to a non-trivial cosmology example—a detailed dark matter simulation—and discover a new analytic formula which can predict the concentration of dark matter from the mass distribution of nearby cosmic structures. The symbolic expressions extracted from the GNN using our technique also generalized to out-of-distribution-data better than the GNN itself. Our approach offers alternative directions for interpreting neural networks and discovering novel physical principles from the representations they learn.

paragraphs: This paper develops a route from a trained neural network to explicit mathematical expressions. It focuses on graph neural networks and deliberately shapes their learned representations to make symbolic extraction more feasible. The goal is to obtain relations that can be inspected directly and potentially reveal physical structure in the data.

The process first trains a graph neural network with supervision while encouraging sparse latent representations. Symbolic regression then searches for expressions describing components of the learned model. In the examples studied, this procedure extracts correct known equations, including force laws and Hamiltonians, showing that useful physical relations can be recovered from the network's internal representations.

These findings connect interpretability with scientific discovery and improved generalization in the examined settings.
summary.tldr: Sparse graph-network representations enable symbolic regression to recover physical equations and discover a predictive formula from a dark matter simulation.

title: Discovering Symbolic Models from Deep Learning with Inductive Biases

abstract: When observed decisions depend only on observed features, off-policy policy evaluation (OPE) methods for sequential decision problems can estimate the performance of evaluation policies before deploying them. However, this assumption is frequently violated due to unobserved confounders, unrecorded variables that impact both the decisions and their outcomes. We assess robustness of OPE methods under unobserved confounding by developing worst-case bounds on the performance of an evaluation policy. When unobserved confounders can affect every decision in an episode, we demonstrate that even small amounts of per-decision confounding can heavily bias OPE methods. Fortunately, in a number of important settings found in healthcare, policy-making, and technology, unobserved confounders may directly affect only one of the many decisions made, and influence future decisions/rewards only through the directly affected decision. Under this less pessimistic model of one-decision confounding, we propose an efficient loss-minimization-based procedure for computing worst-case bounds, and prove its statistical consistency. On simulated healthcare examples---management of sepsis and interventions for autistic children---where this is a reasonable model, we demonstrate that our method invalidates non-robust results and provides meaningful certificates of robustness, allowing reliable selection of policies under unobserved confounding.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a new decision policy would perform using data collected under another policy. Such estimates can become biased when unrecorded variables influence both past decisions and their outcomes. This paper develops worst-case performance bounds to assess how robust policy evaluations remain under this hidden confounding.

The authors show that even small amounts of confounding at every decision can produce substantial bias over an episode. They then study a narrower model: hidden confounders directly affect only one decision, with later effects passing through that decision. Under this assumption, they develop an efficient procedure based on loss minimization to compute worst-case bounds and prove its statistical consistency.

Simulated healthcare examples involve sepsis management and interventions for autistic children, where the authors consider the one-decision model reasonable. The method both rejects conclusions from non-robust evaluations and provides meaningful robustness certificates. These results show how the bounds can support policy selection while making the assumed structure of hidden confounding central to the evaluation.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds policy performance under hidden confounding, with an efficient consistent method when confounding directly affects only one decision.

title: Off-policy Policy Evaluation For Sequential Decisions Under Unobserved Confounding

abstract: In this paper, we propose a unified analysis of variants of distributed SGD with arbitrary compressions and delayed updates. Our framework is general enough to cover different variants of quantized SGD, Error-Compensated SGD (EC-SGD), and SGD with delayed updates (D-SGD). Via single theorem, we derive the complexity results for all the methods that fit our framework. For the existing methods, this theorem gives the best-known complexity results. Moreover, using our general scheme, we develop new variants of SGD that combine variance reduction or arbitrary sampling with error feedback and quantization and derive the convergence rates for these methods beating the state-of-the-art results. In order to illustrate the strength of our framework, we develop 16 new methods that fit this. In particular, we propose the first method called EC-SGD-DIANA that is based on error-feedback for biased compression operator and quantization of gradient differences and prove the convergence guarantees showing that EC-SGD-DIANA converges to the exact optimum asymptotically in expectation with constant learning rate for both convex and strongly convex objectives when workers compute full gradients of their loss functions. Moreover, for the case when the loss function of the worker has the form of finite sum, we modified the method and got a new one called EC-LSVRG-DIANA which is the first distributed stochastic method with error feedback and variance reduction that converges to the exact optimum asymptotically in expectation with constant learning rate.

Via single theorem, we derive the complexity results for all the methods that fit our framework. For the existing methods, this theorem gives the best-known complexity results. Moreover, using our general scheme, we develop new variants of SGD that combine variance reduction or arbitrary sampling with error feedback and quantization and derive the convergence rates for these methods beating the state-of-the-art results. In order to illustrate the strength of our framework, we develop 16 new methods that fit this. In particular, we propose the first method called EC-SGD-DIANA that is based on error-feedback for biased compression operator and quantization of gradient differences and prove the convergence guarantees showing that EC-SGD-DIANA converges to the exact optimum asymptotically in expectation with constant learning rate for both convex and strongly convex objectives when workers compute full gradients of their loss functions. Moreover, for the case when the loss function of the worker has the form of finite sum, we modified the method and got a new one called EC-LSVRG-DIANA which is the first distributed stochastic method with error feedback and variance reduction that converges to the exact optimum asymptotically in expectation with constant learning rate.

paragraphs: Distributed stochastic gradient descent can use compressed messages or delayed updates, creating several related optimization problems. This paper develops a unified analysis covering quantized, error-compensated, and delayed-update variants. A single theorem supplies complexity results for methods within the framework, matching the best-known results for existing methods covered by the analysis.

The framework also generates new methods combining error feedback and quantization with variance reduction or arbitrary sampling. The authors present sixteen new variants and derive improved convergence rates. One method, EC-SGD-DIANA, combines error feedback for biased compression with quantization of gradient differences, connecting two ways of managing information lost or transmitted during distributed updates.

When workers compute full gradients, EC-SGD-DIANA approaches the exact optimum asymptotically in expectation with a constant learning rate for convex and strongly convex objectives. For worker losses expressed as finite sums, the authors introduce EC-LSVRG-DIANA, a stochastic method combining error feedback and variance reduction with the same stated type of exact asymptotic convergence. These qualifications distinguish the guarantees from claims of exact finite-time optimization.
summary.tldr: A unified analysis yields new compressed distributed SGD methods, including constant-learning-rate methods with exact asymptotic convergence in expectation under stated conditions.

title: Linearly Converging Error Compensated SGD

abstract: Motivated by the connection between sampling and optimization, we study a mirror descent analogue of Langevin dynamics and analyze three different discretization schemes, giving nonasymptotic convergence rate under functional inequalities such as Log-Sobolev in the corresponding metric. Compared to the Euclidean setting, the result reveals intricate relationship between the underlying geometry and the target distribution and suggests that care might need to be taken in order for the discretized algorithm to achieve vanishing bias with diminishing stepsize for sampling from potentials under weaker smoothness/convexity regularity conditions.

paragraphs: This paper studies a connection between optimization and sampling. It considers a version of Langevin dynamics analogous to mirror descent, allowing the sampling process to reflect an underlying geometry beyond the usual Euclidean setting. The central question is how that geometric choice affects convergence toward the target distribution.

The authors analyze three discretization schemes, which turn the continuous dynamics into algorithms that proceed in finite steps. They establish nonasymptotic convergence rates under functional inequalities, including a Log-Sobolev inequality expressed in the corresponding metric. These rates describe convergence after a finite amount of computation within the stated mathematical conditions.

The results reveal a close interaction between the geometry and the distribution being sampled. In particular, under weaker smoothness or convexity conditions on the potential, shrinking the step size may require additional care to ensure that discretization bias vanishes. The analysis therefore highlights both convergence guarantees and the importance of choosing a discretization compatible with the geometry and regularity of the sampling problem.
summary.tldr: An analysis of three mirror-Langevin discretizations shows how sampling convergence and vanishing bias depend on geometry and regularity conditions.

title: Mirror Langevin Monte Carlo: the Case Under Isoperimetry

abstract: Machine learning models that are developed to be invariant under certain types of data transformations have shown improved generalization in practice. However, a principled understanding of why invariance benefits generalization is limited. Given a dataset, there is often no principled way to select "suitable" data transformations under which model invariance guarantees better generalization. This paper studies the generalization benefit of model invariance by introducing the sample cover induced by transformations, i.e., a representative subset of a dataset that can approximately recover the whole dataset using transformations. For any data transformations, we provide refined generalization bounds for invariant models based on the sample cover. We also characterize the "suitability" of a set of data transformations by the sample covering number induced by transformations, i.e., the smallest size of its induced sample covers. We show that we may tighten the generalization bounds for "suitable" transformations that have a small sample covering number. In addition, our proposed sample covering number can be empirically evaluated and thus provides a guidance for selecting transformations to develop model invariance for better generalization. In experiments on multiple datasets, we evaluate sample covering numbers for some commonly used transformations and show that the smaller sample covering number for a set of transformations (e.g., the 3D-view transformation) indicates a smaller gap between the test and training error for invariant models, which verifies our propositions.

paragraphs: Making a model invariant to a transformation means requiring its prediction to remain unchanged under that transformation. Such invariance often helps in practice, but choosing suitable transformations lacks a clear general rule. This paper studies suitability through the relationship between the transformations and the particular dataset.

The authors introduce a sample cover: a representative subset whose transformed examples can approximately recover the whole dataset. The sample covering number is the smallest size of such a subset. They derive generalization bounds for invariant models using this quantity and show that transformations with a small covering number may yield tighter bounds.

Across multiple datasets, the authors find that smaller covering numbers for tested transformations, including changes in 3D view, indicate smaller gaps between training and test error. The result connects the usefulness of invariance to how efficiently transformations represent the data, rather than treating every transformation as equally beneficial.
summary.tldr: Transformation-induced sample covers connect model invariance to generalization bounds and offer empirical guidance for choosing transformations.

title: Understanding the Generalization Benefit of Model Invariance from a Data Perspective

abstract: Generalised linear models for multi-class classification problems are one of the fundamental building blocks of modern machine learning tasks. In this manuscript, we characterise the learning of a mixture of $K$ Gaussians with generic means and covariances via empirical risk minimisation (ERM) with any convex loss and regularisation. In particular, we prove exact asymptotics characterising the ERM estimator in high-dimensions, extending several previous results about Gaussian mixture classification in the literature. We exemplify our result in two tasks of interest in statistical learning: a) classification for a mixture with sparse means, where we study the efficiency of $\ell_1$ penalty with respect to $\ell_2$; b) max-margin multi-class classification, where we characterise the phase transition on the existence of the multi-class logistic maximum likelihood estimator for $K>2$. Finally, we discuss how our theory can be applied beyond the scope of synthetic data, showing that in different cases Gaussian mixtures capture closely the learning curve of classification tasks in real data sets.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes multiclass learning when data come from a mixture of Gaussian distributions. It considers generalized linear models trained through empirical risk minimization with convex loss and regularization. The mixture components can have generic means and covariances, giving the analysis scope beyond more restricted Gaussian mixture settings.

The main result gives exact asymptotic characterizations of the learned estimator in high dimensions. The authors apply it to two concrete questions. For mixtures with sparse means, they study the efficiency of an l1 penalty relative to an l2 penalty. For multiclass max-margin classification, they characterize a phase transition governing whether the logistic maximum likelihood estimator exists when there are more than two classes.

These applications show how the general theory can address both regularization choices and changes in the mathematical behavior of an estimator. The paper also examines relevance beyond synthetic Gaussian data: in several cases, Gaussian mixture models closely capture the learning curves observed on real classification datasets. That empirical correspondence supports the theory's usefulness in those cases without making the Gaussian model universal.
summary.tldr: Exact high-dimensional asymptotics describe convex empirical risk minimization for Gaussian mixture classification and illuminate regularization and estimator-existence transitions.

title: Learning Gaussian Mixtures with Generalized Linear Models: Precise Asymptotics in High-dimensions

abstract: Learning auxiliary tasks, such as multiple predictions about the world, can provide many benefits to reinforcement learning systems. A variety of off-policy learning algorithms have been developed to learn such predictions, but as yet there is little work on how to adapt the behavior to gather useful data for those off-policy predictions. In this work, we investigate a reinforcement learning system designed to learn a collection of auxiliary tasks, with a behavior policy learning to take actions to improve those auxiliary predictions. We highlight the inherent non-stationarity in this continual auxiliary task learning problem, for both prediction learners and the behavior learner. We develop an algorithm based on successor features that facilitates tracking under non-stationary rewards, and prove the separation into learning successor features and rewards provides convergence rate improvements. We conduct an in-depth study into the resulting multi-prediction learning system.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems can benefit from learning auxiliary predictions about their environment. Existing off-policy algorithms can learn such predictions from collected experience, but they leave another question: how should the agent act to gather experience that improves those predictions? This paper makes that data-collection behavior part of the learning problem.

The proposed system learns a collection of auxiliary tasks while also learning a behavior policy whose actions aim to improve them. This creates non-stationarity on both sides. The prediction learners operate within an evolving system, and the behavior learner must adapt as the usefulness of different experiences changes during learning.

The authors develop an algorithm based on successor features to support tracking when rewards change. Its structure separates learning successor features from learning rewards, and they prove that this separation improves convergence rates. An in-depth study examines the resulting system of multiple predictions and learned behavior. The contribution links auxiliary learning with active experience collection, treating both as interacting parts of a continual learning process.
summary.tldr: A successor-feature approach learns both auxiliary predictions and behavior that gathers useful experience, with convergence-rate benefits from separating features and rewards.

title: Continual Auxiliary Task Learning

abstract: Risk assessment instrument (RAI) datasets, particularly ProPublica’s COMPAS dataset, are commonly used in algorithmic fairness papers due to benchmarking practices of comparing algorithms on datasets used in prior work. In many cases, this data is used as a benchmark to demonstrate good performance without ac-counting for the complexities of criminal justice (CJ) processes. However, we show that pretrial RAI datasets can contain numerous measurement biases and errors, and due to disparities in discretion and deployment, algorithmic fairness applied to RAI datasets is limited in making claims about real-world outcomes.These reasons make the datasets a poor fit for benchmarking under assumptions of ground truth and real-world impact. Furthermore, conventional practices of simply replicating previous data experiments may implicitly inherit or edify normative positions without explicitly interrogating value-laden assumptions. Without con-text of how interdisciplinary fields have engaged in CJ research and context of how RAIs operate upstream and downstream, algorithmic fairness practices are misaligned for meaningful contribution in the context of CJ, and would benefit from transparent engagement with normative considerations and values related to fairness, justice, and equality. These factors prompt questions about whether benchmarks for intrinsically socio-technical systems like the CJ system can exist in a beneficial and ethical way.

paragraphs: This paper examines the use of criminal justice risk assessment datasets, especially ProPublica’s COMPAS dataset, as algorithmic fairness benchmarks. Reusing familiar datasets makes comparison with earlier studies convenient. The authors argue that this practice can overlook the processes that produced the records and the ways risk assessment tools influence decisions before and after prediction.

They show that pretrial risk assessment datasets can contain measurement errors and biases. Differences in discretion and deployment further limit what fairness results on these datasets can establish about real-world outcomes. Treating recorded outcomes as ground truth, or benchmark improvements as evidence of practical impact, therefore rests on assumptions that require scrutiny.

The critique also concerns values: repeating earlier experiments can carry forward normative positions without explicitly examining them. The authors call for engagement with criminal justice research and transparent discussion of fairness, justice, and equality. They raise the broader question of whether benchmarks for such deeply social and technical systems can be designed and used in beneficial, ethical ways.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that measurement problems, deployment context, and implicit values limit what criminal justice fairness benchmarks can establish about real-world outcomes.

title: It's COMPASlicated: The Messy Relationship between RAI Datasets and Algorithmic Fairness Benchmarks

abstract: In this paper, we study dataset distillation (DD), from a novel perspective and introduce a \emph{dataset factorization} approach, termed \emph{HaBa}, which is a plug-and-play strategy portable to any existing DD baseline. Unlike conventional DD approaches that aim to produce distilled and representative samples, \emph{HaBa} explores decomposing a dataset into two components: data \emph{Ha}llucination networks and \emph{Ba}ses, where the latter is fed into the former to reconstruct image samples. The flexible combinations between bases and hallucination networks, therefore, equip the distilled data with exponential informativeness gain, which largely increase the representation capability of distilled datasets. To furthermore increase the data efficiency of compression results, we further introduce a pair of adversarial contrastive \xw{constraints} on the resultant hallucination networks and bases, which increase the diversity of generated images and inject more discriminant information into the factorization. Extensive comparisons and experiments demonstrate that our method can yield significant improvement on downstream classification tasks compared with previous state of the arts, while reducing the total number of compressed parameters by up to 65\%. Moreover, distilled datasets by our approach also achieve \textasciitilde10\% higher accuracy than baseline methods in cross-architecture generalization. Our code is available \href{https://github.com/Huage001/DatasetFactorization}{here}.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation compresses training information into a small representation that can support later learning. This paper proposes HaBa, which represents distilled data through two reusable components: bases and image-producing networks called hallucination networks. Feeding bases into those networks reconstructs training images.

The approach shifts attention from storing representative images individually to learning components that can be combined flexibly. These combinations increase the representational capacity of the compressed dataset. HaBa is presented as a plug-and-play strategy for existing distillation methods. The authors also introduce paired adversarial contrastive constraints designed to increase generated-image diversity and strengthen information useful for distinguishing classes.

Experiments report substantial improvements in downstream classification compared with previous methods while reducing compressed parameter counts by up to 65%. The distilled data also achieve approximately 10% higher accuracy than baselines in cross-architecture generalization. These results support factorization as a way to make compressed training information more useful, including when the architecture consuming the distilled data differs from the one involved in producing it.
summary.tldr: HaBa factorizes distilled datasets into reusable bases and image-generating networks, improving reported classification performance with fewer compressed parameters.

title: Dataset Distillation via Factorization

abstract: Large sparsely-activated models have obtained excellent performance in multiple domains.However, such models are typically trained on a single modality at a time.We present the Language-Image MoE, LIMoE, a sparse mixture of experts model capable of multimodal learning.LIMoE accepts both images and text simultaneously, while being trained using a contrastive loss.MoEs are a natural fit for a multimodal backbone, since expert layers can learn an appropriate partitioning of modalities.However, new challenges arise; in particular, training stability and balanced expert utilization, for which we propose an entropy-based regularization scheme.Across multiple scales, we demonstrate performance improvement over dense models of equivalent computational cost.LIMoE-L/16 trained comparably to CLIP-L/14 achieves 77.9% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy (vs. 76.2%), and when further scaled to H/14 (with additional data) it achieves 83.8%, approaching state-of-the-art methods which use custom per-modality backbones and pre-training schemes.We analyse the quantitative and qualitative behavior of LIMoE, and demonstrate phenomena such as differing treatment of the modalities and the emergence of modality-specific experts.

paragraphs: LIMoE is a sparse mixture-of-experts model that learns from images and text together using a contrastive objective. Its expert layers provide a way for one multimodal backbone to develop different processing behavior for different inputs. The paper explores whether this design can deliver stronger performance at a comparable computational cost.

Training introduces challenges involving stability and balanced use of the experts. The authors propose entropy-based regularization to address them. Their analysis finds different treatment of the two modalities and the emergence of experts specialized for individual modalities, showing how distinct processing can arise within the shared model.

Across several scales, LIMoE improves on dense models with equivalent computational costs. A version trained comparably to CLIP-L/14 reaches 77.9% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy, compared with 76.2%. A larger version trained with additional data reaches 83.8%, approaching leading methods that use separate modality-specific backbones and pretraining schemes. The additional data is part of that scaling result. Together, the findings support sparse expert models as a practical architecture for joint image–text learning.
summary.tldr: LIMoE uses a shared sparse expert model for images and text, improving on dense models at equivalent computational cost.

title: Multimodal Contrastive Learning with LIMoE: the Language-Image Mixture of Experts

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs), which propagate the node features through the edges and learn how to transform the aggregated features under label supervision, have achieved great success in supervised feature extraction for both node-level and graph-level classification tasks. However, GNNs typically treat the graph structure as given and ignore how the edges are formed. This paper introduces a graph generative process to model how the observed edges are generated by aggregating the node interactions over a set of overlapping node communities, each of which contributes to the edges via a logical OR mechanism. Based on this generative model, we partition each edge into the summation of multiple community-specific weighted edges and use them to define community-specific GNNs. A variational inference framework is proposed to jointly learn a GNN-based inference network that partitions the edges into different communities, these community-specific GNNs, and a GNN-based predictor that combines community-specific GNNs for the end classification task. Extensive evaluations on real-world graph datasets have verified the effectiveness of the proposed method in learning discriminative representations for both node-level and graph-level classification tasks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks usually learn from the connections they receive without modeling why those connections exist. This paper makes edge formation part of representation learning. It describes a graph as arising from interactions within overlapping communities of nodes, so a node can participate in several communities that contribute to the observed connections.

The generative model combines community contributions through a logical OR: a connection can arise through any contributing community. The method then splits each observed edge into weighted contributions associated with different communities. These contributions define separate community-specific graph neural networks, allowing the model to process different patterns of interaction through different networks.

A variational inference framework learns the edge partition, the community-specific networks, and a predictor that combines their outputs for classification together. Evaluations on real-world graphs support the method's effectiveness for both node and whole-graph classification. The central contribution is to connect an explanation of how edges arise with the supervised task of learning features that distinguish classes.
summary.tldr: The model partitions graph edges into overlapping community contributions and learns community-specific networks jointly for classification.

title: A Variational Edge Partition Model for Supervised Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Capitalizing on the recent advances in image generation models, existing controllable face image synthesis methods are able to generate high-fidelity images with some levels of controllability, e.g., controlling the shapes, expressions, textures, and poses of the generated face images. However, these methods focus on 2D image generative models, which are prone to producing inconsistent face images under large expression and pose changes. In this paper, we propose a new NeRF-based conditional 3D face synthesis framework, which enables 3D controllability over the generated face images by imposing explicit 3D conditions from 3D face priors. At its core is a conditional Generative Occupancy Field (cGOF) that effectively enforces the shape of the generated face to commit to a given 3D Morphable Model (3DMM) mesh. To achieve accurate control over fine-grained 3D face shapes of the synthesized image, we additionally incorporate a 3D landmark loss as well as a volume warping loss into our synthesis algorithm. Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, which is able to generate high-fidelity face images and shows more precise 3D controllability than state-of-the-art 2D-based controllable face synthesis methods.

paragraphs: Generating a realistic face image and controlling its three-dimensional shape are related but distinct challenges. Existing controllable image generators can change attributes such as expression or pose, yet their outputs may become inconsistent under large changes. This paper introduces explicit three-dimensional conditions to make those controls more precise.

The framework combines a NeRF-based generator with a conditional Generative Occupancy Field, or cGOF. Its central role is to make the generated face geometry conform to a mesh supplied by a 3D Morphable Model. The synthesis process also includes losses based on three-dimensional landmarks and volume warping, adding constraints intended to improve control over fine details of facial shape.

Experiments show that the method produces high-fidelity face images and offers more precise three-dimensional control than the compared state-of-the-art methods based on two-dimensional generation. The contribution is therefore both a geometry-conditioned synthesis framework and evidence that explicitly enforcing a face shape can strengthen control while retaining visual quality.
summary.tldr: A geometry-conditioned face generator produces high-quality images with more precise 3D control than the compared 2D-based methods.

title: Controllable 3D Face Synthesis with Conditional Generative Occupancy Fields

abstract: In this work, we study how to efficiently obtain perfect samples from a discrete distribution $\mathcal{D}$ given access only to pairwise comparisons of elements of its support. Specifically, we assume access to samples $(x, S)$, where $S$ is drawn from a distribution over sets $\mathcal{Q}$ (indicating the elements being compared), and $x$ is drawn from the conditional distribution $\mathcal{D}_S$ (indicating the winner of the comparison) and aim to output a clean sample $y$ distributed according to $\mathcal{D}$. We mainly focus on the case of pairwise comparisons where all sets $S$ have size 2. We design a Markov chain whose stationary distribution coincides with $\mathcal{D}$ and give an algorithm to obtain exact samples using the technique of Coupling from the Past. However, the sample complexity of this algorithm depends on the structure of the distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and can be even exponential in the support of $\mathcal{D}$ in many natural scenarios. Our main contribution is to provide an efficient exact sampling algorithm whose complexity does not depend on the structure of $\mathcal{D}$. To this end, we give a parametric Markov chain that mixes significantly faster given a good approximation to the stationary distribution. We can obtain such an approximation using an efficient learning from pairwise comparisons algorithm (Shah et al., JMLR 17, 2016). Our technique for speeding up sampling from a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is approximately known is simple, general and possibly of independent interest.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to draw an exact sample from an unknown discrete distribution when only comparison outcomes are available. Each observation supplies a compared set and a winner drawn from the target distribution conditioned on that set. The main focus is pairwise comparisons, where each observed set contains two elements.

The authors first construct a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is the desired target and use Coupling from the Past to obtain exact samples. However, this route can require exponentially many observations in natural cases because its cost depends on the target distribution's structure. Exactness alone therefore does not ensure an efficient sampling procedure.

The main contribution removes that structural dependence from the sampling complexity. An efficient comparison-learning algorithm supplies a good approximation to the target distribution, which is then used to speed up a parameterized Markov chain. Crucially, the final samples remain exact even though the acceleration uses an approximation. The authors also suggest that this general technique for accelerating chains with approximately known stationary distributions may have independent value.
summary.tldr: An approximate distribution learned from pairwise comparisons accelerates a Markov-chain procedure that still produces exact samples.

title: Perfect Sampling from Pairwise Comparisons

abstract: A goal of artificial intelligence is to construct an agent that can solve a wide variety of tasks. Recent progress in text-guided image synthesis has yielded models with an impressive ability to generate complex novel images, exhibiting combinatorial generalization across domains. Motivated by this success, we investigate whether such tools can be used to construct more general-purpose agents. Specifically, we cast the sequential decision making problem as a text-conditioned video generation problem, where, given a text-encoded specification of a desired goal, a planner synthesizes a set of future frames depicting its planned actions in the future, after which control actions are extracted from the generated video. By leveraging text as the underlying goal specification, we are able to naturally and combinatorially generalize to novel goals. The proposed policy-as-video formulation can further represent environments with different state and action spaces in a unified space of images, which, for example, enables learning and generalization across a variety of robot manipulation tasks. Finally, by leveraging pretrained language embeddings and widely available videos from the internet, the approach enables knowledge transfer through predicting highly realistic video plans for real robots.

The paper uses this formulation to support learning and generalization across robot manipulation tasks.

summary.tldr: The paper turns text-specified goals into video plans and extracts control actions, creating a shared visual formulation for varied robot tasks.

title: Learning Universal Policies via Text-Guided Video Generation

abstract: Monocular 3D detection of vehicle and infrastructure sides are two important topics in autonomous driving. Due to diverse sensor installations and focal lengths, researchers are faced with the challenge of constructing algorithms for the two topics based on different prior knowledge. In this paper, by taking into account the diversity of pitch angles and focal lengths, we propose a unified optimization target named normalized depth, which realizes the unification of 3D detection problems for the two sides. Furthermore, to enhance the accuracy of monocular 3D detection, 3D normalized cube depth of obstacle is developed to promote the learning of depth information. We posit that the richness of depth clues is a pivotal factor impacting the detection performance on both the vehicle and infrastructure sides. A richer set of depth clues facilitates the model to learn better spatial knowledge, and the 3D normalized cube depth offers sufficient depth clues. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Without introducing any extra information, our method, named MonoUNI, achieves state-of-the-art performance on five widely used monocular 3D detection benchmarks, including Rope3D and DAIR-V2X-I for the infrastructure side, KITTI and Waymo for the vehicle side, and nuScenes for the cross-dataset evaluation.

These results support a unified approach built around a shared depth target and richer depth supervision, rather than treating the two camera-placement settings as separate detection problems.
summary.tldr: MonoUNI unifies vehicle- and infrastructure-side monocular 3D detection through normalized depth and richer obstacle-depth representations.

title: MonoUNI: A Unified Vehicle and Infrastructure-side Monocular 3D Object Detection Network with Sufficient Depth Clues

abstract: Continual learning (CL) aims to incrementally learn different tasks (such as classification) in a non-stationary data stream without forgetting old ones. Most CL works focus on tackling catastrophic forgetting under a learning-from-scratch paradigm. However, with the increasing prominence of foundation models, pre-trained models equipped with informative representations have become available for various downstream requirements. Several CL methods based on pre-trained models have been explored, either utilizing pre-extracted features directly (which makes bridging distribution gaps challenging) or incorporating adaptors (which may be subject to forgetting). In this paper, we propose a concise and effective approach for CL with pre-trained models. Given that forgetting occurs during parameter updating, we contemplate an alternative approach that exploits training-free random projectors and class-prototype accumulation, which thus bypasses the issue. Specifically, we inject a frozen Random Projection layer with nonlinear activation between the pre-trained model's feature representations and output head, which captures interactions between features with expanded dimensionality, providing enhanced linear separability for class-prototype-based CL. We also demonstrate the importance of decorrelating the class-prototypes to reduce the distribution disparity when using pre-trained representations. These techniques prove to be effective and circumvent the problem of forgetting for both class- and domain-incremental continual learning. Compared to previous methods applied to pre-trained ViT-B/16 models, we reduce final error rates by between 20% and 62% on seven class-incremental benchmark datasets, despite not using any rehearsal memory. We conclude that the full potential of pre-trained models for simple, effective, and fast continual learning has not hitherto been fully tapped. Code is available at https://github.com/RanPAC/RanPAC.

title: RanPAC: Random Projections and Pre-trained Models for Continual Learning

abstract: Given the rich visual information available in each glance, humans can internally direct their visual attention to enhance goal-relevant information---a capacity often absent in standard vision models. Here we introduce cognitively and biologically-inspired long-range modulatory pathways to enable `cognitive steering’ in vision models. First, we show that models equipped with these feedback pathways naturally show improved image recognition, adversarial robustness, and increased brain alignment, relative to baseline models. Further, these feedback projections from the final layer of the vision backbone provide a meaningful steering interface, where goals can be specified as vectors in the output space. We show that there are effective ways to steer the model that dramatically improve recognition of categories in composite images of multiple categories, succeeding where baseline feed-forward models without flexible steering fail. And, our multiplicative modulatory motif prevents rampant hallucination of the top-down goal category, dissociating what the model is looking for, from what it is looking at. Thus, these long-range modulatory pathways enable new behavioral capacities for goal-directed visual encoding, offering a flexible communication interface between cognitive and visual systems.

paragraphs: People can inspect the same scene with different goals, directing attention toward information that matters for the current task. Standard vision models often lack this flexibility. The paper adds long-range feedback connections inspired by cognitive and biological mechanisms, allowing a model's visual processing to respond to an internally specified goal.

The feedback originates in the final layer of the visual backbone. Goals are expressed as vectors in its output space, providing an interface for steering how the network processes an image. The connections modulate activity multiplicatively. The authors report that this design avoids rampant hallucination of the requested category, helping separate a search goal from the actual visual evidence.

Steering also substantially improves category recognition in composite images containing multiple categories, where the feed-forward baselines struggle. These results support feedback as a useful mechanism for goal-directed vision and as an interface through which cognitive goals can influence visual representations.
summary.tldr: Long-range feedback connections let vision models respond to goals while improving recognition and limiting goal-driven hallucination.

title: Cognitive Steering in Deep Neural Networks via Long-Range Modulatory Feedback Connections

abstract: Obtaining accurate solutions to the Schrödinger equation is the key challenge in computational quantum chemistry. Deep-learning-based Variational Monte Carlo (DL-VMC) has recently outperformed conventional approaches in terms of accuracy, but only at large computational cost.Whereas in many domains models are trained once and subsequently applied for inference, accurate DL-VMC so far requires a full optimization for every new problem instance, consuming thousands of GPUhs even for small molecules.We instead propose a DL-VMC model which has been pre-trained using self-supervised wavefunction optimization on a large and chemically diverse set of molecules. Applying this model to new molecules without any optimization, yields wavefunctions and absolute energies that outperform established methods such as CCSD(T)-2Z.To obtain accurate relative energies, only few fine-tuning steps of this base model are required.We accomplish this with a fully end-to-end machine-learned model, consisting of an improved geometry embedding architecture and an existing SE(3)-equivariant model to represent molecular orbitals. Combining this architecture with continuous sampling of geometries, we improve zero-shot accuracy by two orders of magnitude compared to the state of the art.We extensively evaluate the accuracy, scalability and limitations of our base model on a wide variety of test systems.

paragraphs: Deep-learning-based variational Monte Carlo can produce highly accurate quantum-chemistry calculations, but optimizing a new model for every molecule is expensive. This paper proposes reusing a neural wavefunction model pretrained through self-supervised optimization on a large, chemically diverse collection of molecules. The aim is to transfer that work to new molecular problems.

The model combines an improved geometry embedding with an existing SE(3)-equivariant architecture for molecular orbitals. Training also continuously samples geometries. Together, these choices improve zero-shot accuracy by two orders of magnitude relative to the state of the art reported by the authors, making pretrained predictions substantially more useful before molecule-specific optimization.

On new molecules, the model produces wavefunctions and absolute energies without further optimization that outperform established methods such as CCSD(T)-2Z. Accurate relative energies still require a few fine-tuning steps. That distinction separates immediate reuse from the additional adaptation needed for energy differences. The authors evaluate accuracy, scalability, and limitations across varied test systems, supporting pretraining as a way to reduce repeated optimization costs.
summary.tldr: Pretrained neural wavefunctions deliver strong zero-shot molecular predictions, while a few fine-tuning steps provide accurate relative energies.

title: Variational Monte Carlo on a Budget — Fine-tuning pre-trained Neural Wavefunctions

abstract: Weight Average (WA) is an active research topic due to its simplicity in ensembling deep networks and the effectiveness in promoting generalization. Existing weight average approaches, however, are often carried out along only one training trajectory in a post-hoc manner (i.e., the weights are averaged after the entire training process is finished), which significantly degrades the diversity between networks and thus impairs the effectiveness. In this paper, inspired by weight average, we propose Lookaround, a straightforward yet effective SGD-based optimizer leading to flatter minima with better generalization. Specifically, Lookaround iterates two steps during the whole training period: the around step and the average step. In each iteration, 1) the around step starts from a common point and trains multiple networks simultaneously, each on transformed data by a different data augmentation, and 2) the average step averages these trained networks to get the averaged network, which serves as the starting point for the next iteration. The around step improves the functionality diversity while the average step guarantees the weight locality of these networks during the whole training, which is essential for WA to work. We theoretically explain the superiority of Lookaround by convergence analysis, and make extensive experiments to evaluate Lookaround on popular benchmarks including CIFAR and ImageNet with both CNNs and ViTs, demonstrating clear superiority over state-of-the-arts. Our code is available at https://github.com/Ardcy/Lookaround.
