paragraphs: Averaging neural network weights can improve generalization, but the paper identifies a weakness in approaches that average points along one training trajectory only after training ends. Those networks may lack enough functional diversity for averaging to deliver its full benefit. Lookaround builds diversification and averaging into the optimization process itself.

Each iteration begins from a shared set of weights and trains several networks using different data augmentations. This is the around step. The average step then combines their weights, and that average becomes the common starting point for the next iteration. The two steps aim to maintain both diversity in what the networks do and proximity in their weights.

The authors argue that this combination is essential for effective weight averaging and leads to flatter minima with better generalization. They provide convergence analysis and experiments on benchmarks including CIFAR and ImageNet, using both convolutional networks and Vision Transformers. The reported improvements over competing methods support repeated exploration and recombination during training as an effective optimization strategy.
summary.tldr: Lookaround repeatedly trains networks from shared weights with different augmentations, then averages them to promote diversity, flatter minima, and better generalization.

title: Lookaround Optimizer: $k$ steps around, 1 step average

abstract: Antibodies have become an important class of therapeutic agents to treat human diseases.To accelerate therapeutic antibody discovery, computational methods, especially machine learning, have attracted considerable interest for predicting specific interactions between antibody candidates and target antigens such as viruses and bacteria.However, the publicly available datasets in existing works have notable limitations, such as small sizes and the lack of non-binding samples and exact amino acid sequences.To overcome these limitations, we have developed AVIDa-hIL6, a large-scale dataset for predicting antigen-antibody interactions in the variable domain of heavy chain of heavy chain antibodies (VHHs), produced from an alpaca immunized with the human interleukin-6 (IL-6) protein, as antigens.By leveraging the simple structure of VHHs, which facilitates identification of full-length amino acid sequences by DNA sequencing technology, AVIDa-hIL6 contains 573,891 antigen-VHH pairs with amino acid sequences.All the antigen-VHH pairs have reliable labels for binding or non-binding, as generated by a novel labeling method.Furthermore, via introduction of artificial mutations, AVIDa-hIL6 contains 30 different mutants in addition to wild-type IL-6 protein.This characteristic provides opportunities to develop machine learning models for predicting changes in antibody binding by antigen mutations.We report experimental benchmark results on AVIDa-hIL6 by using machine learning models.The results indicate that the existing models have potential, but further research is needed to generalize them to predict effective antibodies against unknown mutants.The dataset is available at https://avida-hil6.cognanous.com.

paragraphs: Predicting whether an antibody binds a target requires examples that describe both the interacting molecules and the outcome. Existing public datasets can be small or lack non-binding examples and exact amino acid sequences. AVIDa-hIL6 addresses these gaps using VHH antibody domains obtained from an alpaca immunized with the human IL-6 protein.

The dataset contains 573,891 antigen–VHH pairs, with amino acid sequences and binding or non-binding labels produced by a new labeling method. The relatively simple structure of VHHs enables identification of full-length sequences through DNA sequencing. Including both outcomes gives learning methods examples of unsuccessful interactions as well as successful ones.

Alongside the original IL-6 protein, the dataset includes 30 artificially mutated variants. This supports studying how antigen changes affect antibody binding. Benchmark experiments indicate promise in existing machine-learning models, but also show that further work is needed to predict effective antibodies against previously unknown mutants. The resource makes that generalization problem an explicit target for evaluation.
summary.tldr: AVIDa-hIL6 provides 573,891 labeled antigen–VHH pairs for studying antibody binding and generalization to mutated IL-6 targets.

title: AVIDa-hIL6: A Large-Scale VHH Dataset Produced from an Immunized Alpaca for Predicting Antigen-Antibody Interactions

abstract: The advent of large language models (LLMs) and their adoption by the legal community has given rise to the question: what types of legal reasoning can LLMs perform? To enable greater study of this question, we present LegalBench: a collaboratively constructed legal reasoning benchmark consisting of 162 tasks covering six different types of legal reasoning. LegalBench was built through an interdisciplinary process, in which we collected tasks designed and hand-crafted by legal professionals. Because these subject matter experts took a leading role in construction, tasks either measure legal reasoning capabilities that are practically useful, or measure reasoning skills that lawyers find interesting. To enable cross-disciplinary conversations about LLMs in the law, we additionally show how popular legal frameworks for describing legal reasoning—which distinguish between its many forms—correspond to LegalBench tasks, thus giving lawyers and LLM developers a common vocabulary. This paper describes LegalBench, presents an empirical evaluation of 20 open-source and commercial LLMs, and illustrates the types of research explorations LegalBench enables.

This organization makes it possible to investigate distinct reasoning capabilities through a collection of tasks grounded in the interests and practices of legal professionals.

The benchmark was built through interdisciplinary collaboration, with legal experts taking a leading role in designing and handcrafting tasks. The resulting tasks assess capabilities that are practically useful or reasoning skills that lawyers consider interesting. The paper also connects the tasks to established legal frameworks for describing different forms of reasoning, creating a shared vocabulary for lawyers and model developers.

The contribution combines an evaluation resource with a way to discuss its results across disciplines. Its task structure and expert involvement help make studies of model behavior more closely connected to recognizable legal reasoning activities.
summary.tldr: LegalBench offers 162 expert-designed tasks across six forms of legal reasoning and evaluates 20 language models.

title: LegalBench: A Collaboratively Built Benchmark for Measuring Legal Reasoning in Large Language Models

abstract: Partial client participation has been widely adopted in Federated Learning (FL) to reduce the communication burden efficiently. However, an inadequate client sampling scheme can lead to the selection of unrepresentative subsets, resulting in significant variance in model updates and slowed convergence. Existing sampling methods are either biased or can be further optimized for faster convergence.In this paper, we present DELTA, an unbiased sampling scheme designed to alleviate these issues. DELTA characterizes the effects of client diversity and local variance, and samples representative clients with valuable information for global model updates. In addition, DELTA is a proven optimal unbiased sampling scheme that minimizes variance caused by partial client participation and outperforms other unbiased sampling schemes in terms of convergence. Furthermore, to address full-client gradient dependence, we provide a practical version of DELTA depending on the available clients' information, and also analyze its convergence. Our results are validated through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: Federated learning often involves only a subset of clients in each update to reduce communication. If that subset is unrepresentative, the resulting updates can vary substantially and convergence can slow. DELTA addresses the choice of participants by seeking informative, representative client samples while maintaining an unbiased sampling scheme.

The method characterizes how differences between clients and local variance affect updates to the global model. Those quantities guide which clients are sampled. The authors prove that DELTA is optimal among unbiased sampling schemes for minimizing the variance caused by partial participation, and establish better convergence than other unbiased schemes. The optimality claim is tied to that variance objective and comparison class.

A practical obstacle is that the original scheme depends on gradients from all clients. The paper therefore supplies a version using information from available clients and analyzes its convergence as well. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets validate the results. Together, the theoretical and practical versions connect principled participant selection with the information actually available during federated training.
summary.tldr: DELTA improves federated client selection through unbiased variance-minimizing sampling and a practical version that uses available-client information.

title: DELTA: Diverse Client Sampling for Fasting Federated Learning

abstract: *Molecular dynamics* (MD) simulation is a widely used technique to simulate molecular systems, most commonly at the all-atom resolution where equations of motion are integrated with timesteps on the order of femtoseconds ($1\textrm{fs}=10^{-15}\textrm{s}$). MD is often used to compute equilibrium properties, which requires sampling from an equilibrium distribution such as the Boltzmann distribution. However, many important processes, such as binding and folding, occur over timescales of milliseconds or beyond, and cannot be efficiently sampled with conventional MD.Furthermore, new MD simulations need to be performed for each molecular system studied.We present *Timewarp*, an enhanced sampling method which uses a normalising flow as a proposal distribution in a Markov chain Monte Carlo method targeting the Boltzmann distribution. The flow is trained offline on MD trajectories and learns to make large steps in time, simulating the molecular dynamics of $10^{5} - 10^{6} \textrm{fs}$.Crucially, Timewarp is *transferable* between molecular systems: once trained, we show that it generalises to unseen small peptides (2-4 amino acids) at all-atom resolution, exploring their metastable states and providing wall-clock acceleration of sampling compared to standard MD.Our method constitutes an important step towards general, transferable algorithms for accelerating MD.

The flow is trained offline on MD trajectories and learns to make large steps in time, simulating the molecular dynamics of $10^{5} - 10^{6} \textrm{fs}$.Crucially, Timewarp is *transferable* between molecular systems: once trained, we show that it generalises to unseen small peptides (2-4 amino acids) at all-atom resolution, exploring their metastable states and providing wall-clock acceleration of sampling compared to standard MD.Our method constitutes an important step towards general, transferable algorithms for accelerating MD.

This timescale gap makes equilibrium sampling expensive. Timewarp aims to accelerate exploration by learning larger moves from existing molecular dynamics trajectories.

The method trains a normalizing flow offline to propose changes corresponding to 100,000 to 1,000,000 femtoseconds of molecular dynamics. Those proposals are used within a Markov chain Monte Carlo method targeting the Boltzmann distribution. The learned model thus supplies large candidate steps inside a sampling procedure directed at the desired equilibrium distribution.

A central result is transfer between molecular systems. After training, Timewarp generalizes to previously unseen small peptides containing two to four amino acids at all-atom resolution. It explores their metastable states and accelerates sampling in wall-clock time compared with standard molecular dynamics. These findings support transferable learned proposals as a route toward faster molecular sampling, with the demonstrated transfer specifically covering the small peptides studied.
summary.tldr: Timewarp learns large molecular sampling proposals and transfers them to unseen small peptides, accelerating equilibrium sampling compared with standard molecular dynamics.

title: Timewarp: Transferable Acceleration of Molecular Dynamics by Learning Time-Coarsened Dynamics

abstract: We consider a novel dynamic pricing and learning setting where in addition to setting prices of products in sequential rounds, the seller also ex-ante commits to ‘advertising schemes’. That is, in the beginning of each round the seller can decide what kind of signal they will provide to the buyer about the product’s quality upon realization. Using the popular Bayesian persuasion framework to model the effect of these signals on the buyers’ valuation and purchase responses, we formulate the problem of finding an optimal design of the advertising scheme along with a pricing scheme that maximizes the seller’s expected revenue. Without any apriori knowledge of the buyers’ demand function, our goal is to design an online algorithm that can use past purchase responses to adaptively learn the optimal pricing and advertising strategy. We study the regret of the algorithm when compared to the optimal clairvoyant price and advertisingscheme. Our main result is a computationally efficient online algorithm that achieves an $O(T^{2/3}(m \log T )^{1/3})$ regret bound when the valuation function is linear in the product quality. Here $m$ is the cardinality of the discrete product quality domain and $T$ is the time horizon. This result requires some natural monotonicity and Lipschitz assumptions on the valuation function, but no Lipschitz or smoothness assumption on the buyers’ demand function. For constant $m$, our result matches the regret lower bound for dynamic pricing within logarithmic factors, which is a special case of our problem. We also obtain several improved results for the widely considered special case of additive valuations, including an $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ regret bound independent of $m$ when $m\le T^{1/3}$.

title: Dynamic Pricing and Learning with Bayesian Persuasion

abstract: Prompt-based continual learning is an emerging direction in leveraging pre-trained knowledge for downstream continual learning, and has almost reached the performance pinnacle under supervised pre-training. However, our empirical research reveals that the current strategies fall short of their full potential under the more realistic self-supervised pre-training, which is essential for handling vast quantities of unlabeled data in practice. This is largely due to the difficulty of task-specific knowledge being incorporated into instructed representations via prompt parameters and predicted by uninstructed representations at test time. To overcome the exposed sub-optimality, we conduct a theoretical analysis of the continual learning objective in the context of pre-training, and decompose it into hierarchical components: within-task prediction, task-identity inference, and task-adaptive prediction. Following these empirical and theoretical insights, we propose Hierarchical Decomposition (HiDe-)Prompt, an innovative approach that explicitly optimizes the hierarchical components with an ensemble of task-specific prompts and statistics of both uninstructed and instructed representations, further with the coordination of a contrastive regularization strategy. Our extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of HiDe-Prompt and its robustness to pre-training paradigms in continual learning (e.g., up to 15.01% and 9.61% lead on Split CIFAR-100 and Split ImageNet-R, respectively).

paragraphs: Prompt-based continual learning adapts pretrained knowledge to tasks encountered over time. The paper finds that existing strategies perform less effectively under self-supervised pretraining than their success with supervised pretraining might suggest. It attributes much of this gap to difficulties incorporating task-specific knowledge through prompts and using representations without that prompting to make decisions at test time.

The authors analyze the learning objective and separate it into three components: prediction within a task, inference of task identity, and prediction adapted to the task. Their HiDe-Prompt method explicitly optimizes these components. It combines an ensemble of task-specific prompts with statistics of representations both with and without prompt instruction, coordinated through contrastive regularization.

Experiments report superior continual-learning performance and robustness across pretraining paradigms. The stated leads reach up to 15.01% on Split CIFAR-100 and 9.61% on Split ImageNet-R. The contribution is a diagnosis and a corresponding training design: separating several responsibilities hidden inside prompt-based learning helps address the shortcomings observed with self-supervised pretraining.
summary.tldr: HiDe-Prompt explicitly separates task inference and prediction objectives to improve continual learning across supervised and self-supervised pretraining.

title: Hierarchical Decomposition of Prompt-Based Continual Learning: Rethinking Obscured Sub-optimality

abstract: We consider the problem of best arm identification in the multi-armed bandit model, under fixed confidence. Given a confidence input $\delta$, the goal is to identify the arm with the highest mean reward with a probability of at least $1 - \delta$, while minimizing the number of arm pulls. While the literature provides solutions to this problem under the assumption of independent arms distributions, we propose a more flexible scenario where arms can be dependent and rewards can be sampled simultaneously. This framework allows the learner to estimate the covariance among the arms distributions, enabling a more efficient identification of the best arm. The relaxed setting we propose is relevant in various applications, such as clinical trials, where similarities between patients or drugs suggest underlying correlations in the outcomes. We introduce new algorithms that adapt to the unknown covariance of the arms and demonstrate through theoretical guarantees that substantial improvement can be achieved over the standard setting. Additionally, we provide new lower bounds for the relaxed setting and present numerical simulations that support their theoretical findings.

paragraphs: Best-arm identification asks which available option has the highest average reward while using as few observations as possible. In the fixed-confidence setting studied here, the learner receives an error tolerance, delta, and must identify the best option with probability at least one minus delta. The paper broadens the usual setting by allowing rewards from different options to be dependent.

The key additional capability is simultaneous sampling of rewards. This lets the learner estimate covariance: information about how the outcomes of different options vary together. The proposed algorithms adapt to this initially unknown dependence structure. Rather than treating every option's observations as unrelated, they use relationships among outcomes to make identification more efficient.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees showing that substantial improvements over the standard setting can be achieved. They also derive lower bounds for the relaxed setting and present numerical simulations supporting the theory. The contribution is therefore both algorithmic and foundational: it explains how correlated observations can help and establishes constraints on what identification procedures can accomplish.
summary.tldr: Algorithms that learn correlations among simultaneously sampled rewards can identify the best option more efficiently at a specified confidence level.

title: Covariance-adaptive best arm identification

abstract: Training certifiably robust neural networks remains a notoriously hard problem.While adversarial training optimizes under-approximations of the worst-case loss, which leads to insufficient regularization for certification, sound certified training methods, optimize loose over-approximations, leading to over-regularization and poor (standard) accuracy.In this work, we propose TAPS, an (unsound) certified training method that combines IBP and PGD training to optimize more precise, although not necessarily sound, worst-case loss approximations, reducing over-regularization and increasing certified and standard accuracies.Empirically, TAPS achieves a new state-of-the-art in many settings, e.g., reaching a certified accuracy of $22$% on TinyImageNet for $\ell_\infty$-perturbations with radius $\epsilon=1/255$. We make our implementation and networks public at https://github.com/eth-sri/taps.
originalAbstract: Training certifiably robust neural networks remains a notoriously hard problem.While adversarial training optimizes under-approximations of the worst-case loss, which leads to insufficient regularization for certification, sound certified training methods, optimize loose over-approximations, leading to over-regularization and poor (standard) accuracy.In this work, we propose TAPS, an (unsound) certified training method that combines IBP and PGD training to optimize more precise, although not necessarily sound, worst-case loss approximations, reducing over-regularization and increasing certified and standard accuracies.Empirically, TAPS achieves a new state-of-the-art in many settings, e.g., reaching a certified accuracy of $22$% on TinyImageNet for $\ell_\infty$-perturbations with radius $\epsilon=1/255$. We make our implementation and networks public at https://github.com/eth-sri/taps.

paragraphs: Training a robust classifier requires accounting for harmful input perturbations, but estimating the worst possible loss is difficult. Adversarial training uses estimates that can fall below the true worst case, providing insufficient regularization for certification. Sound certified training uses upper bounds, but loose bounds can impose excessive regularization and reduce accuracy on ordinary inputs.

TAPS combines interval bound propagation, or IBP, with projected gradient descent, or PGD, training. The goal is to obtain more precise estimates of worst-case loss and reduce the excessive conservatism of certified training. Crucially, these training estimates are not necessarily sound: the method does not guarantee that its optimization objective always bounds the true worst-case loss.

Despite that qualification, the authors report improvements in both standard and certified accuracy, with state-of-the-art empirical results in many settings. One example reaches 22% certified accuracy on TinyImageNet for perturbations bounded by an infinity-norm radius of 1/255. The result shows that an unsound training approximation can still help produce networks with stronger measured certified performance.
summary.tldr: TAPS combines IBP and PGD training using tighter but potentially unsound loss estimates, empirically improving both ordinary and certified accuracy.

title: Connecting Certified and Adversarial Training

abstract: Occupancy functions play an instrumental role in reinforcement learning (RL) for guiding exploration, handling distribution shift, and optimizing general objectives beyond the expected return. Yet, computationally efficient policy optimization methods that use (only) occupancy functions are virtually non-existent. In this paper, we establish the theoretical foundations of model-free policy gradient (PG) methods that compute the gradient through the occupancy for both online and offline RL, without modeling value functions. Our algorithms reduce gradient estimation to squared-loss regression and are computationally oracle-efficient. We characterize the sample complexities of both local and global convergence, accounting for both finite-sample estimation error and the roles of exploration (online) and data coverage (offline). Occupancy-based PG naturally handles arbitrary offline data distributions, and, with one-line algorithmic changes, can be adapted to optimize any differentiable objective functional.

paragraphs: Occupancy functions describe how a policy distributes its visits through an environment. They are useful for exploration, distribution shift, and objectives beyond expected reward. This paper develops a theoretical foundation for policy-gradient methods that compute updates through occupancy functions without learning value functions, covering both online interaction and learning from offline data.

The algorithms turn gradient estimation into squared-loss regression. Their computational efficiency is expressed in an oracle sense: the optimization procedure can use a regression-solving component. The analysis characterizes the sample requirements for local and global convergence while accounting for errors caused by estimating quantities from finite data.

The guarantees also account for exploration in online learning and coverage in offline datasets. Although the formulation accommodates arbitrary offline data distributions, the role of coverage remains part of the convergence analysis. The authors further show that small algorithmic changes allow optimization of any differentiable objective functional. This makes occupancy a common basis for policy optimization across objectives, rather than restricting the method to the usual expected-return formulation.
summary.tldr: Occupancy-based policy gradients support online and offline optimization without value functions, with convergence analyses and flexible differentiable objectives.

title: Occupancy-based Policy Gradient: Estimation, Convergence, and Optimality

abstract: We consider the problem of hypothesis testing for discrete distributions. In the standard model, where we have sample access to an underlying distribution $p$, extensive research has established optimal bounds for uniformity testing, identity testing (goodness of fit), and closeness testing (equivalence or two-sample testing). We explore these problems in a setting where a predicted data distribution, possibly derived from historical data or predictive machine learning models, is available. We demonstrate that such a predictor can indeed reduce the number of samples required for all three property testing tasks. The reduction in sample complexity depends directly on the predictor’s quality, measured by its total variation distance from $p$. A key advantage of our algorithms is their adaptability to the precision of the prediction. Specifically, our algorithms can self-adjust their sample complexity based on the accuracy of the available prediction, operating without any prior knowledge of the estimation’s accuracy (i.e. they are consistent). Additionally, we never use more samples than the standard approaches require, even if the predictions provide no meaningful information (i.e. they are also robust). We provide lower bounds to indicate that the improvements in sample complexity achieved by our algorithms are information-theoretically optimal. Furthermore, experimental results show that the performance of our algorithms on real data significantly exceeds our worst-case guarantees for sample complexity, demonstrating the practicality of our approach.

paragraphs: Testing a discrete distribution usually relies on drawing samples to determine whether it is uniform, matches a specified distribution, or agrees with another sampled distribution. This paper studies how those tasks change when a predicted distribution is also available, perhaps from historical data or a predictive model.

The proposed algorithms use that prediction to reduce sample requirements, with the improvement depending on its total variation distance from the true distribution. They adapt to prediction quality without needing its accuracy in advance. They also retain the standard sample guarantees when predictions are uninformative, so poor advice does not increase the sample requirement beyond standard approaches.

The combined result makes predictive information useful without requiring blind trust in it: accurate predictions can save samples, while the methods preserve established guarantees when predictions offer little help.
summary.tldr: Prediction-assisted distribution tests adaptively save samples while preserving standard sample guarantees when predictions are poor.

title: Optimal Algorithms for Augmented Testing of Discrete Distributions

abstract: Learning from preference feedback has emerged as an essential step for improving the generation quality and performance of modern language models (LMs). Despite its widespread use, the way preference-based learning is applied varies wildly, with differing data, learning algorithms, and evaluations used, making disentangling the impact of each aspect difficult. In this work, we identify four core aspects of preference-based learning: preference data, learning algorithm, reward model, and policy training prompts, systematically investigate the impact of these components on downstream model performance, and suggest a recipe for strong learning for preference feedback. Our findings indicate that all aspects are important for performance, with better preference data leading to the largest improvements, followed by the choice of learning algorithm, the use of improved reward models, and finally the use of additional unlabeled prompts for policy training. Notably, PPO outperforms DPO by up to 2.5% in math and 1.2% in general domains. High-quality preference data leads to improvements of up to 8% in instruction following and truthfulness. Despite significant gains of up to 5% in mathematical evaluation when scaling up reward models, we surprisingly observe marginal improvements in other categories.

paragraphs: Preference-based language-model training varies in its data, algorithms, and evaluation, making it hard to identify which choices drive improvements. This paper systematically separates four components: preference data, the learning algorithm, the reward model, and prompts used for policy training. The goal is to turn those comparisons into a stronger training recipe.

In the reported study, preference-data quality produces the largest improvements, followed by algorithm choice, improved reward models, and additional unlabeled policy-training prompts. PPO exceeds DPO by up to 2.5% in mathematical tasks and 1.2% in general domains. Higher-quality preference data produces gains of up to 8% in instruction following and truthfulness, highlighting the importance of the feedback itself.

Scaling reward models yields gains of up to 5% in mathematical evaluation but only marginal improvements in other categories. This variation shows why a single overall account of better preference training can hide task-specific effects. The findings support attention to every component while giving data quality the strongest priority within the authors' evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A systematic preference-training study finds the largest gains from better data, with additional benefits from algorithm choice and task-dependent reward-model improvements.

title: Unpacking DPO and PPO: Disentangling Best Practices for Learning from Preference Feedback

abstract: Text-to-image diffusion generative models can generate high quality images at the cost of tedious prompt engineering. Controllability can be improved by introducing layout conditioning, however existing methods lack layout editing ability and fine-grained control over object attributes. The concept of multi-layer generation holds great potential to address these limitations, however generating image instances concurrently to scene composition limits control over fine-grained object attributes, relative positioning in 3D space and scene manipulation abilities. In this work, we propose a novel multi-stage generation paradigm that is designed for fine-grained control, flexibility and interactivity. To ensure control over instance attributes, we devise a novel training paradigm to adapt a diffusion model to generate isolated scene components as RGBA images with transparency information. To build complex images, we employ these pre-generated instances and introduce a multi-layer composite generation process that smoothly assembles components in realistic scenes. Our experiments show that our RGBA diffusion model is capable of generating diverse and high quality instances with precise control over object attributes. Through multi-layer composition, we demonstrate that our approach allows to build and manipulate images from highly complex prompts with fine-grained control over object appearance and location, granting a higher degree of control than competing methods.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of controlling individual objects in text-to-image generation. High-quality output can require extensive prompt adjustment, and layout conditioning still leaves limits on editing and detailed object attributes. The proposed approach divides generation into stages so that object appearance can be established before those objects are assembled into a complete scene.

A new training procedure adapts a diffusion model to produce isolated scene components as RGBA images, which include transparency information. These separately generated instances then become inputs to a multilayer composition process. The composition stage smoothly assembles them into realistic images, supporting control over both the components themselves and how they are placed together.

Experiments show diverse, high-quality instances with precise attribute control. The authors also demonstrate building and manipulating scenes from highly complex prompts, with detailed control over object appearance and location. They report greater control than competing methods. The significance of the staged design is that generating an object and arranging a scene become separately controllable steps, supporting the flexibility and interactivity that motivated the work.
summary.tldr: Generating transparent object images before multilayer composition enables finer control over scene appearance, placement, and editing.

title: Generating compositional scenes via Text-to-image RGBA Instance Generation

abstract: Language models (LMs) are bound to their tokenizer, which maps raw text to a sequence of vocabulary items (tokens). This restricts their flexibility: for example, LMs trained primarily on English may still perform well in other natural and programming languages, but have vastly decreased efficiency due to their English-centric tokenizer. To mitigate this, we should be able to swap the original LM tokenizer with an arbitrary one, on the fly, without degrading performance. Hence, in this work we define a new problem: Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer (ZeTT). The challenge at the core of ZeTT is finding embeddings for the tokens in the vocabulary of the new tokenizer. Since prior heuristics for initializing embeddings often perform at chance level in a ZeTT setting, we propose a new solution: we train a hypernetwork taking a tokenizer as input and predicting the corresponding embeddings. We empirically demonstrate that the hypernetwork generalizes to new tokenizers both with encoder (e.g., XLM-R) and decoder LLMs (e.g., Mistral-7B). Our method comes close to the original models' performance in cross-lingual and coding tasks while markedly reducing the length of the tokenized sequence. We also find that the remaining gap can be quickly closed by continued training on less than 1B tokens. Finally, we show that a ZeTT hypernetwork trained for a base (L)LM can also be applied to fine-tuned variants without extra training. Overall, our results make substantial strides toward detaching LMs from their tokenizer.

paragraphs: A language model's tokenizer determines how text is split into vocabulary items. A tokenizer suited to English can produce inefficiently long sequences for other languages or code, even when the model can handle those tasks. Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer asks how to replace that tokenizer without first retraining the model for the replacement.

The main challenge is assigning useful embeddings to the new vocabulary. The authors train a hypernetwork that takes a tokenizer as input and predicts its embeddings. Experiments show that this network generalizes to unfamiliar tokenizers for both encoder and decoder models, including XLM-R and Mistral-7B.

The transferred models approach their original performance on cross-lingual and coding tasks while substantially shortening token sequences. The remaining performance gap can be closed quickly through continued training on fewer than one billion tokens, so the initial zero-shot result is close rather than identical. A hypernetwork trained for a base model also transfers to its fine-tuned variants without extra training, supporting more flexible reuse of tokenizer adaptation.
summary.tldr: A hypernetwork predicts embeddings for new tokenizers, enabling near-original model performance with shorter sequences before additional adaptation training.

title: Zero-Shot Tokenizer Transfer

abstract: Recent approaches have shown promises distilling expensive diffusion models into efficient one-step generators.Amongst them, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) produces one-step generators that match their teacher in distribution, i.e., the distillation process does not enforce a one-to-one correspondence with the sampling trajectories of their teachers.However, to ensure stable training in practice, DMD requires an additional regression loss computed using a large set of noise--image pairs, generated by the teacher with many steps of a deterministic sampler.This is not only computationally expensive for large-scale text-to-image synthesis, but it also limits the student's quality, tying it too closely to the teacher's original sampling paths.We introduce DMD2, a set of techniques that lift this limitation and improve DMD training.First, we eliminate the regression loss and the need for expensive dataset construction.We show that the resulting instability is due to the "fake" critic not estimating the distribution of generated samples with sufficient accuracy and propose a two time-scale update rule as a remedy.Second, we integrate a GAN loss into the distillation procedure, discriminating between generated samples and real images.This lets us train the student model on real data, thus mitigating the imperfect "real" score estimation from the teacher model, and thereby enhancing quality.Third, we introduce a new training procedure that enables multi-step sampling in the student, andaddresses the training--inference input mismatch of previous work, by simulating inference-time generator samples during training. Taken together, our improvements set new benchmarks in one-step image generation, with FID scores of 1.28 on ImageNet-64×64 and 8.35 on zero-shot COCO 2014, surpassing the original teacher despite a 500X reduction in inference cost.Further, we show our approach can generate megapixel images by distilling SDXL, demonstrating exceptional visual quality among few-step methods, and surpassing the teacher. We release our code and pretrained models.
originalAbstract: Recent approaches have shown promises distilling expensive diffusion models into efficient one-step generators.Amongst them, Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) produces one-step generators that match their teacher in distribution, i.e., the distillation process does not enforce a one-to-one correspondence with the sampling trajectories of their teachers.However, to ensure stable training in practice, DMD requires an additional regression loss computed using a large set of noise--image pairs, generated by the teacher with many steps of a deterministic sampler.This is not only computationally expensive for large-scale text-to-image synthesis, but it also limits the student's quality, tying it too closely to the teacher's original sampling paths.We introduce DMD2, a set of techniques that lift this limitation and improve DMD training.First, we eliminate the regression loss and the need for expensive dataset construction.We show that the resulting instability is due to the "fake" critic not estimating the distribution of generated samples with sufficient accuracy and propose a two time-scale update rule as a remedy.Second, we integrate a GAN loss into the distillation procedure, discriminating between generated samples and real images.This lets us train the student model on real data, thus mitigating the imperfect "real" score estimation from the teacher model, and thereby enhancing quality.Third, we introduce a new training procedure that enables multi-step sampling in the student, andaddresses the training--inference input mismatch of previous work, by simulating inference-time generator samples during training. We release our code and pretrained models.

paragraphs: Distribution Matching Distillation compresses a diffusion model into a fast generator by matching output distributions. However, its original training procedure also uses regression on expensive teacher-generated noise–image pairs. DMD2 removes that requirement, addressing both the cost of constructing those pairs and the restriction imposed by closely following the teacher's sampling paths.

Removing regression destabilizes training because the fake critic estimates the generated distribution insufficiently accurately. DMD2 addresses this with a two-time-scale update rule. It also adds a GAN loss comparing generated images with real data, reducing dependence on imperfect teacher score estimates. For multi-step students, it simulates inference-time generator samples during training to address mismatched training and inference inputs.

Together, these changes achieve reported one-step FID scores of 1.28 on ImageNet-64×64 and 8.35 on zero-shot COCO 2014, surpassing the teacher with a 500-fold reduction in inference cost. The results show that distribution matching, real-data training, and better training dynamics can jointly improve speed and quality.
summary.tldr: DMD2 improves fast image generation by removing costly regression targets, stabilizing distribution matching, and adding real-data adversarial training.

title: Improved Distribution Matching Distillation for Fast Image Synthesis

abstract: Tensor multiplication with learned weight matrices is the fundamental building block in deep learning models. These matrices can often be sparsified, decomposed, quantized, or subjected to random parameter sharing without losing accuracy, suggesting the possibility of more efficient transforms. Although many variants of weight matrices exist, unstructured ones are incompatible with modern hardware, slowing inference and training. On the other hand, structured variants often limit expressivity or fail to deliver the promised latency benefits. We present Sketch Structured Transform (SS1), an expressive and GPU-friendly operator that accelerates inference. SS1 leverages parameter sharing in a random yet structured manner to reduce computation while retraining the rich expressive nature of parameter sharing. We confirm empirically that SS1 offers better quality-efficiency tradeoffs than competing variants. Interestingly SS1 can be combined with Quantization to achieve gains unattainable by either method alone, a finding we justify via theoretical analysis. The analysis may be of independent interest.Moreover, existing pre-trained models can be projected onto SS1 and finetuned for efficient deployment. Surprisingly, these projected models can perform reasonably well even without finetuning. Our experiments highlight various applications of the SS1:(a) Training GPT2 and DLRM models from scratch for faster inference. (b) Finetuning projected BERT models for 1.31× faster inference while maintaining GLUE scores. (c) Proof of concept with Llama-3-8b, showing 1.11× faster wall clock inference using projected SS1 layers without finetuning. We open source our code :https://github.com/apd10/Sketch-Structured-Linear/

Irregular structure can fit hardware poorly, while rigid structure can restrict what a model represents. Sketch Structured Transform, or SS1, addresses this tradeoff with parameter sharing that is random yet organized for efficient GPU execution.

The authors report better quality-efficiency tradeoffs than competing matrix variants. They also show that SS1 can work alongside quantization to obtain benefits unavailable from either method alone, supported by theoretical analysis. Existing pretrained models can be projected into the SS1 form and fine-tuned, and some projected models retain reasonable performance even without fine-tuning.

Fine-tuned projected BERT models achieve 1.31 times faster inference while maintaining GLUE scores. A Llama-3-8b proof of concept achieves 1.11 times faster wall-clock inference without fine-tuning. These examples demonstrate practical latency gains across several uses of the proposed operator.
summary.tldr: SS1 uses structured random parameter sharing to accelerate neural-network inference and can complement quantization or adapt pretrained models.

title: SS1: Accelerating Inference with Fast and Expressive Sketch Structured Transform

abstract: Submodular functions, crucial for various applications, often lack practical learning methods for their acquisition. Seemingly unrelated, learning a scaling from oracles offering graded pairwise preferences (GPC) is underexplored, despite a rich history in psychometrics. In this paper, we introduce deep submodular peripteral networks (DSPNs), a novel parametric family of submodular functions, and methods for their training using a GPC-based strategy to connect and then tackle both of the above challenges. We introduce newly devised GPC-style ``peripteral'' loss which leverages numerically graded relationships between pairs of objects (sets in our case). Unlike traditional contrastive learning, or RHLF preference ranking, our method utilizes graded comparisons, extracting more nuanced information than just binary-outcome comparisons, and contrasts sets of any size (not just two). We also define a novel suite of automatic sampling strategies for training, including active-learning inspired submodular feedback. We demonstrate DSPNs' efficacy in learning submodularity from a costly target submodular function and demonstrate its superiority both for experimental design and online streaming applications.

paragraphs: Submodular functions are useful for scoring sets, but acquiring them through practical learning methods remains a challenge. This paper connects that problem with learning from graded pairwise preferences: feedback that says how strongly one object is preferred to another, rather than supplying only a binary preference.

The authors introduce deep submodular peripteral networks, a parameterized family of submodular functions, together with a training strategy based on graded comparisons. Their peripteral loss uses numerical relationships between pairs of sets. Those sets may contain any number of elements, so the comparisons are not restricted to sets of two items. The numerical grades provide information beyond which set wins a comparison.

The framework also includes automatic ways to select training examples, including a strategy inspired by active learning that uses submodular feedback. Experiments demonstrate learning from a costly target submodular function and report superior performance in experimental-design and online-streaming applications. The contribution brings together a structured function family, a loss that uses preference strength, and sampling procedures for choosing useful comparisons during training.
summary.tldr: Deep submodular peripteral networks learn set-scoring functions from numerically graded preferences, using a specialized loss and automatic sampling strategies.

title: Deep Submodular Peripteral Networks

abstract: Embeddings play a pivotal role across various disciplines, offering compact representations of complex data structures. Randomized methods like Johnson-Lindenstrauss (JL) provide state-of-the-art and essentially unimprovable theoretical guarantees for achieving such representations. These guarantees are worst-case and in particular, neither the analysis, ${\textit{nor the algorithm}}$, takes into account any potential structural information of the data. The natural question is: must we randomize? Could we instead use an optimization-based approach, working directly with the data? A first answer is no: as we show, the distance-preserving objective of JL has a non-convex landscape over the space of projection matrices, with many bad stationary points. But this is not the final answer. We present a novel method motivated by diffusion models, that circumvents this fundamental challenge: rather than performing optimization directly over the space of projection matrices, we use optimization over the larger space of $\textit{random solution samplers}$, gradually reducing the variance of the sampler. We show that by moving through this larger space, our objective converges to a deterministic (zero variance) solution, avoiding bad stationary points. This method can also be seen as an optimization-based derandomization approach, and is an idea and method that we believe can be applied to many other problems.

paragraphs: Johnson–Lindenstrauss embeddings provide compact representations with strong guarantees for preserving distances. Standard randomized methods offer essentially unimprovable worst-case guarantees, but neither their algorithms nor their analyses exploit possible structure in a particular dataset. This paper asks whether optimization directly informed by the data can provide another route.

The authors first establish an obstacle: optimizing the distance-preservation objective directly over projection matrices produces a nonconvex landscape with many bad stationary points. Their proposed method changes the space being optimized. Inspired by diffusion models, it optimizes over random solution samplers rather than individual projection matrices and gradually reduces the sampler’s variance.

The paper shows that optimization through this larger space converges to a deterministic solution with zero variance while avoiding bad stationary points. Randomness therefore serves as part of the route to a final deterministic embedding. The authors interpret the method as optimization-based derandomization and suggest that the idea could extend to other problems. That broader applicability is presented as a possibility, while the stated result concerns the embedding objective studied here.
summary.tldr: Optimizing over random solution samplers and shrinking their variance yields deterministic embeddings while avoiding bad stationary points.

title: Optimization Can Learn Johnson Lindenstrauss Embeddings

abstract: Time Series Classification (TSC) encompasses two settings: classifying entire sequences or classifying segmented subsequences. The raw time series for segmented TSC usually contain Multiple classes with Varying Duration of each class (MVD). Therefore, the characteristics of MVD pose unique challenges for segmented TSC, yet have been largely overlooked by existing works. Specifically, there exists a natural temporal dependency between consecutive instances (segments) to be classified within MVD. However, mainstream TSC models rely on the assumption of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), focusing on independently modeling each segment. Additionally, annotators with varying expertise may provide inconsistent boundary labels, leading to unstable performance of noise-free TSC models. To address these challenges, we first formally demonstrate that valuable contextual information enhances the discriminative power of classification instances. Leveraging the contextual priors of MVD at both the data and label levels, we propose a novel consistency learning framework Con4m, which effectively utilizes contextual information more conducive to discriminating consecutive segments in segmented TSC tasks, while harmonizing inconsistent boundary labels for training. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets validate the effectiveness of Con4m in handling segmented TSC tasks on MVD. The source code is available at https://github.com/MrNobodyCali/Con4m.

paragraphs: Con4m addresses classification of consecutive segments within time series that contain several classes lasting for different durations. In this setting, neighboring segments have temporal dependencies that can help identify their classes. Treating every segment as an independent example overlooks that context and leaves useful information outside the classification process.

The paper also addresses disagreement about where one class ends and another begins. Annotators with different expertise can assign inconsistent boundary labels, which can destabilize models designed around clean labels. The authors first formally establish that valuable context can improve the ability to distinguish classes, then build a consistency-learning framework around that insight.

Con4m uses contextual prior information at both the data and label levels. It draws on relationships among consecutive segments while harmonizing inconsistent boundary labels during training. Experiments across multiple datasets support its effectiveness for this segmented classification setting. The findings connect two aspects of the same temporal structure: context can help interpret a segment, and it can also help handle ambiguity in the labels near class transitions.
summary.tldr: Con4m uses temporal context and label consistency to improve classification of neighboring time-series segments with uncertain boundaries.

title: Con4m: Context-aware Consistency Learning Framework for Segmented Time Series Classification

abstract: In the rapidly evolving field of Large Language Models (LLMs), ensuring safety is a crucial and widely discussed topic. However, existing works often overlooks the geo-diversity of cultural and legal standards across the world. To reveal the chal5 lenges posed by geo-diverse safety standards, we introduce SafeWorld, a novel benchmark specifically designed to evaluate LLMs’ ability to generate responses that are not only helpful but also culturally sensitive and legally compliant across diverse global contexts. SafeWorld encompasses 2,775 test user queries, each grounded in high-quality, human-verified cultural norms and legal policies from 50 countries and 493 regions/races. On top of it, we propose a multi-dimensional automatic safety evaluation framework that assesses the contextual appropriateness, accuracy, and comprehensiveness of responses. Our evaluations reveal that current LLMs struggle to meet these criteria effectively. To enhance LLMs’ alignment with geo-diverse safety standards, we synthesize helpful preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) alignment. The preference pair construction aims to encourage LLMs to behave appropriately and provide precise references to relevant cultural norms and policies when necessary. Our trained SafeWorldLM outperforms all competing models, including GPT-4o on all the three evaluation dimensions by a large margin. Global human evaluators also note a nearly 20% higher winning rate in helpfulness and harmfulness evaluation.

Its benchmark contains 2,775 test queries grounded in human-verified material covering 50 countries and 493 regions or races.

These findings support the value of geographically informed training and evaluation within the studied setting, with both automated criteria and human judgments used to assess the resulting responses.
summary.tldr: SafeWorld benchmarks geographically varied safety standards and trains a preference-aligned model that improves contextual response quality in its evaluations.

title: SafeWorld: Geo-Diverse Safety Alignment

abstract: Stereo matching algorithms that leverage end-to-end convolutional neural networks have recently demonstrated notable advancements in performance. However, a common issue is their susceptibility to domain shifts, hindering their ability in generalizing to diverse, unseen realistic domains. We argue that existing stereo matching networks overlook the importance of extracting semantically and structurally meaningful features. To address this gap, we propose an effective hierarchical object-aware dual-level contrastive learning (HODC) framework for domain generalized stereo matching. Our framework guides the model in extracting features that support semantically and structurally driven matching by segmenting objects at different scales and enhances correspondence between intra- and inter-scale regions from the left feature map to the right using dual-level contrastive loss. HODC can be integrated with existing stereo matching models in the training stage, requiring no modifications to the architecture. Remarkably, using only synthetic datasets for training, HODC achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance with various existing stereo matching network architectures, across multiple realistic datasets.

paragraphs: Stereo matching identifies corresponding content in left and right images. Although convolutional networks have improved this task, their performance can suffer when deployment images differ from training data. This paper argues that stronger attention to meaningful objects and their structure can help models generalize to unfamiliar visual domains.

The HODC framework segments objects at multiple scales and uses contrastive learning to guide feature extraction. Its dual-level loss strengthens correspondence between left and right feature regions both within a scale and across scales. The objective is to make matching depend more on semantic and structural information represented at these different levels.

HODC is applied during training and can be integrated into existing stereo networks without architectural changes. Using only synthetic training datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art generalization across multiple realistic datasets and several existing network architectures. This combination matters because it links improved transfer to a reusable training framework, with experimental evidence that the benefit is not confined to a single stereo architecture.
summary.tldr: HODC uses object-aware contrastive training across spatial scales to improve stereo matching on unseen domains without changing network architectures.

title: Hierarchical Object-Aware Dual-Level Contrastive Learning for Domain Generalized Stereo Matching

abstract: Situation awareness is essential for understanding and reasoning about 3D scenes in embodied AI agents. However, existing datasets and benchmarks for situated understanding suffer from severe limitations in data modality, scope, diversity, and scale. To address these limitations, we propose Multi-modal Situated Question Answering (MSQA), a large-scale multi-modal situated reasoning dataset, scalably collected leveraging 3D scene graphs and vision-language models (VLMs) across a diverse range of real-world 3D scenes. MSQA includes 251K situated questionanswering pairs across 9 distinct question categories, covering complex scenarios and object modalities within 3D scenes. We introduce a novel interleaved multimodal input setting in our benchmark to provide both texts, images, and point clouds for situation and question description, aiming to resolve ambiguity in describing situations with single-modality inputs (e.g., texts). Additionally, we devise the Multi-modal Next-step Navigation (MSNN) benchmark to evaluate models’ grounding of actions and transitions between situations. Comprehensive evaluations on reasoning and navigation tasks highlight the limitations of existing vision-language models and underscore the importance of handling multi-modal interleaved inputs and situation modeling. Experiments on data scaling and crossdomain transfer further demonstrate the effectiveness of leveraging MSQA as a pre-training dataset for developing more powerful situated reasoning models, contributing to advancements in 3D scene understanding for embodied AI.

paragraphs: An embodied agent must reason about a scene in relation to its current situation. Existing datasets provide limited coverage of the modalities, scenarios, and scale needed to evaluate that ability. This paper introduces MSQA, a situated question-answering dataset containing 251,000 question-answer pairs across nine categories and diverse real-world three-dimensional scenes.

The collection process uses 3D scene graphs and vision-language models. The benchmark interleaves text, images, and point clouds when describing situations and questions, aiming to reduce ambiguity that can arise from a single input modality. A second benchmark, MSNN, evaluates next-step navigation, focusing on how models connect actions with transitions between situations.

Evaluations of reasoning and navigation expose limitations in existing vision-language models and emphasize the importance of explicitly modeling situations and handling mixed input formats. Experiments on data scaling and transfer across domains also support MSQA’s usefulness as pretraining data. The work therefore provides both a broader evaluation of situated understanding and evidence that its dataset can help train more capable models.
summary.tldr: MSQA and MSNN evaluate situated 3D reasoning and navigation with interleaved text, images, and point clouds.

title: Multi-modal Situated Reasoning in 3D Scenes

abstract: Bioart's hybrid nature—spanning art, science, technology, ethics, and politics—defies traditional single-axis categorization. I present BioArtlas, analyzing 81 bioart works across thirteen curated dimensions using novel axis-aware representations that preserve semantic distinctions while enabling cross-dimensional comparison. Our codebook-based approach groups related concepts into unified clusters, addressing polysemy in cultural terminology. Comprehensive evaluation of up to 800 representation–space–algorithm combinations identifies Agglomerative clustering at k=15 on 4D UMAP as optimal (silhouette 0.664 ± 0.008, trustworthiness/continuity 0.805/0.812). The approach reveals four organizational patterns: artist-specific methodological cohesion, technique-based segmentation, temporal artistic evolution, and trans-temporal conceptual affinities. By separating analytical optimization from public communication, I provide rigorous analysis and accessible exploration through an interactive web interface (https://www.bioartlas.com) with the dataset publicly available (https://github.com/joonhyungbae/BioArtlas).

Bioart combines artistic, scientific, technological, ethical, and political concerns, making a single organizing category inadequate. The project represents these dimensions in a way that preserves their different meanings while allowing works to be compared across them.

A codebook groups related concepts and addresses cultural terms that can carry multiple meanings. The author evaluates up to 800 combinations of representations, spaces, and clustering algorithms. Among these, agglomerative clustering with 15 groups in a four-dimensional UMAP representation performs best, with a reported silhouette score of 0.664 ± 0.008 and trustworthiness and continuity scores of 0.805 and 0.812.

The resulting groups reveal shared methods within artists’ practices, divisions associated with techniques, changes over time, and conceptual connections across periods. These patterns provide several complementary ways to navigate the collection. BioArtlas separates the computational choices used for analysis from public presentation, offering an interactive website for exploration and a publicly available dataset.
summary.tldr: BioArtlas clusters 81 bioart works across thirteen dimensions, revealing relationships involving artists, techniques, historical change, and cross-period concepts.

title: BioArtlas: Computational Clustering of Multi-Dimensional Complexity in Bioart

abstract: The influence function (IF) of a statistical functional is the Riesz representer of its derivative, also known as its first variation and Fisher-Rao gradient. It is a key object for numerical optimization over probability measures, semiparametric efficiency theory, standard constructions of efficient estimators, and an arsenal of inference methods for these estimators. Yet, deriving the IF analytically is often an obstruction for practitioners. To automate this task, we develop a novel spectral representation of the IF that lends itself to a low-rank functional estimator in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (rkHs). Our estimator (i) does not require analytic derivations by the user, (ii) relies on kernel Principal Component Analysis and numerical pathwise derivatives along these components. We present the derivation of the representation and prove consistency of the low-rank rkHs estimator.

paragraphs: An influence function describes how a statistical quantity changes as its underlying probability distribution is perturbed. It is important for optimizing over distributions, constructing efficient estimators, and carrying out statistical inference. Obtaining it often requires a difficult analytical derivation, which can obstruct the use of those methods.

This paper develops a spectral representation that makes influence-function estimation more automatic. The method uses kernel principal component analysis to identify components and then calculates numerical pathwise derivatives along them. These ingredients produce a low-rank estimator in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, allowing the calculation to proceed without a user-supplied analytical influence function.

The authors derive the representation and prove consistency of the proposed estimator. The contribution therefore includes both a computational construction and a theoretical justification for its convergence. Its practical significance lies in turning an otherwise manual derivation into a procedure built around kernel components and numerical derivatives, while preserving a formal connection to the influence function being estimated.
summary.tldr: A kernel spectral representation enables influence-function estimation without manual analytical derivation and comes with a consistency proof.

title: Kernel von Mises Formula of the Influence Function

abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) trained on internet-scale data achieve remarkable zero-shot detection performance on common objects like car, truck, and pedestrian. However, state-of-the-art models still struggle to generalize to out-of-distribution classes, tasks and imaging modalities not typically found in their pre-training. Rather than simply re-training VLMs on more visual data, we argue that one should align VLMs to new concepts with annotation instructions containing a few visual examples and rich textual descriptions. To this end, we introduce Roboflow100-VL, a large-scale collection of 100 multi-modal object detection datasets with diverse concepts not commonly found in VLM pre-training. We evaluate state-of-the-art models on our benchmark in zero-shot, few-shot, semi-supervised, and fully-supervised settings, allowing for comparison across data regimes. Notably, we find that VLMs like GroundingDINO and Qwen2.5-VL achieve less than 2% zero-shot accuracy on challenging medical imaging datasets within Roboflow100-VL, demonstrating the need for few-shot concept alignment. Lastly, we discuss our recent CVPR 2025 Foundational FSOD competition and share insights from the community. Notably, the winning team significantly outperforms our baseline by 17 mAP! Our code and dataset are available on GitHub and Roboflow.

paragraphs: Strong detection of familiar objects does not ensure that a vision-language model understands specialized concepts or unfamiliar imaging formats. Roboflow100-VL investigates this gap through 100 multimodal object detection datasets containing diverse concepts uncommon in pretraining. The benchmark makes adaptation to unfamiliar domains a central evaluation target.

Models are tested under zero-shot, few-shot, semi-supervised, and fully supervised conditions. Comparing these settings helps reveal how access to examples and annotations changes performance. The authors argue for concept alignment through annotation instructions that combine a few visual examples with detailed textual descriptions, giving models richer guidance about what a new detection task means.

The results expose a substantial challenge: GroundingDINO and Qwen2.5-VL achieve under 2% zero-shot accuracy on challenging medical imaging datasets within the collection. This finding is specific to those difficult datasets. The paper also discusses a few-shot detection competition whose winning system exceeds the authors’ baseline by 17 mAP. Together, the benchmark and competition results show both weak unaided transfer in demanding settings and room for substantial improvement through adaptation.
summary.tldr: Roboflow100-VL evaluates detection across unfamiliar domains and reveals major zero-shot weaknesses alongside opportunities for few-shot concept alignment.

title: Roboflow100-VL: A Multi-Domain Object Detection Benchmark for Vision-Language Models

abstract: Globally interpretable models are a promising approach for trustworthy AI in safety-critical domains. Alongside global explanations, detailed local explanations are a crucial complement to effectively support human experts during inference. This work proposes the Calibrated Hierarchical QPM (CHiQPM) which offers uniquely comprehensive global and local interpretability, paving the way for human-AI complementarity. CHiQPM achieves superior global interpretability by contrastively explaining the majority of classes and offers novel hierarchical explanations that are more similar to how humans reason and can be traversed to offer a built-in interpretable Conformal prediction (CP) method. Our comprehensive evaluation shows that CHiQPM achieves state-of-the-art accuracy as a point predictor, maintaining 99% accuracy of non-interpretable models. This demonstrates a substantial improvement, where interpretability is incorporated without sacrificing overall accuracy. Furthermore, its calibrated set prediction is competitively efficient to other CP methods, while providing interpretable predictions of coherent sets along its hierarchical explanation.

paragraphs: An interpretable classifier should explain its overall decision structure and individual predictions. CHiQPM combines global contrastive explanations with a hierarchy that users can traverse, aiming to make both the model’s classes and its uncertainty easier to understand.

The hierarchy supports an interpretable conformal-prediction procedure that returns coherent sets along the explanation structure. This extends the model beyond a single class label, while retaining local and global interpretability within the same system.

The evaluation reports state-of-the-art point prediction while retaining 99% of the accuracy of noninterpretable models. That means relative accuracy retention, not necessarily a 99% classification accuracy. Calibrated set predictions are competitively efficient against other conformal methods. The abstract does not give dataset-level results or user-study evidence, so improved human-AI collaboration is a proposed benefit rather than a directly quantified outcome here.
summary.tldr: CHiQPM combines hierarchical explanations with calibrated prediction sets while retaining high point accuracy.

title: CHiQPM: Calibrated Hierarchical Interpretable Image Classification

abstract: In concept erasure, a model is modified to selectively prevent it from generating a target concept. Despite the rapid development of new methods, it remains unclear how thoroughly these approaches remove the target concept from the model. We begin by proposing two conceptual models for the erasure mechanism in diffusion models: (i) interfering with the model’s internal guidance processes, and (ii) reducing the unconditional likelihood of generating the target concept, potentially removing it entirely. To assess whether a concept has been truly erased from the model, we introduce a comprehensive suite of independent probing techniques: supplying visual context, modifying the diffusion trajectory, applying classifier guidance, and analyzing the model's alternative generations that emerge in place of the erased concept. Our results shed light on the value of exploring concept erasure robustness outside of adversarial text inputs, and emphasize the importance of comprehensive evaluations for erasure in diffusion models.

paragraphs: Concept erasure modifies a diffusion model to stop it from generating a chosen concept. The paper asks how thoroughly such changes remove the concept from the model. It distinguishes two possible mechanisms: disrupting the model's internal guidance and lowering the concept's unconditional generation likelihood, potentially removing it entirely.

That distinction motivates several independent ways to probe an edited model. The authors supply visual context, alter the diffusion trajectory, apply classifier guidance, and inspect alternative generations produced in place of the targeted concept. Together, these probes examine the model through several routes that extend beyond attempts to recover a concept using adversarial text prompts.

The reported findings emphasize the value of this broader evaluation when assessing erasure robustness. A method's response to text inputs is only one aspect of the proposed assessment; visual information and changes to generation dynamics provide additional tests. The contribution is a conceptual framework for thinking about erasure mechanisms alongside a suite of probes for investigating whether suppression is robust across different interventions.
summary.tldr: The paper distinguishes possible concept-erasure mechanisms and introduces diverse probes to evaluate robustness beyond adversarial text prompts.

title: When Are Concepts Erased From Diffusion Models?

abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding, the ability to map natural language instructions to specific actions on graphical user interfaces, remains a critical bottleneck in computer use agent development. Current benchmarks oversimplify grounding tasks as short referring expressions, failing to capture the complexity of real-world interactions that require software commonsense, layout understanding, and fine-grained manipulation capabilities. To address these limitations, we introduce OSWorld-G, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 564 finely annotated samples across diverse task types including text matching, element recognition, layout understanding, and precise manipulation. Additionally, we synthesize and release the largest computer use grounding dataset Jedi, which contains 4 million examples through multi-perspective decoupling of tasks. Our multi-scale models trained on Jedi demonstrate its effectiveness by outperforming existing approaches on ScreenSpot-v2, ScreenSpot-Pro, and our OSWorld-G. Furthermore, we demonstrate that improved grounding with Jedi directly enhances agentic capabilities of general foundation models on complex computer tasks with state-of-the-art performance, improving from 23% to 51% on OSWorld. Through detailed ablation studies, we identify key factors contributing to grounding performance and verify that combining specialized data for different interface elements enables compositional generalization to novel interfaces. All benchmark, data, checkpoints, and code are open-sourced and available at https://osworld-grounding.github.io.

paragraphs: Computer-use grounding connects a natural-language instruction to the relevant interface action. This paper argues that short referring expressions underrepresent the demands of real software use, which also involves understanding layouts, recognizing elements, and manipulating them precisely. It introduces OSWorld-G, a benchmark of 564 carefully annotated samples spanning these different task types.

The authors also create Jedi, a dataset containing four million grounding examples synthesized through task decomposition from multiple perspectives. Models of several sizes trained on Jedi outperform existing approaches on ScreenSpot-v2, ScreenSpot-Pro, and OSWorld-G. This links the data-generation strategy to improved performance across multiple grounding evaluations.

The study then examines whether better grounding improves complete computer tasks. It reports an increase from 23% to 51% on OSWorld, reaching state-of-the-art performance in the evaluated setup. Ablations identify factors affecting grounding and show that combining specialized data for different interface elements supports compositional generalization to unfamiliar interfaces. The contribution therefore spans both locating actions and improving broader agent behavior.
summary.tldr: A richer interface-grounding benchmark and four-million-example synthetic dataset improve both grounding models and complete computer-use task performance.

title: Scaling Computer-Use Grounding via User Interface Decomposition and Synthesis

abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) achieve competitive performance across a wide range of natural language processing tasks through zero-shot or few-shot prompting. However, domain-specific tasks often still require fine-tuning, which is frequently hindered by data scarcity, i.e., collecting sufficient domain-specific data remains a practical challenge. A widely adopted solution is to generate synthetic data using LLMs by augmenting a small set of available domain-specific examples. In this work, we first identify fundamental limitations of such approach in terms of both data diversity and quality, particularly when relying on only a handful of domain-specific examples. We then propose our method, PANGEA, which leverages large-scale, publicly available general-purpose data---entirely unrelated to the target domain---to generate more diverse and higher-quality synthetic data. Our extensive experiments on domain-specific benchmarks, including GSM8K, MedQA, and FinQA, as well as a custom domain-specific language task, validate the effectiveness of our approach.
