paragraphs: Quantization helps make neural networks practical on embedded devices, but it can degrade their performance. This paper exploits a freedom in many networks: an output channel in one layer can be scaled if the corresponding weights in the next layer are scaled inversely. These coordinated changes preserve the network’s function.

That freedom produces multiple weight factorizations for the same underlying computation. The authors develop a simple method for choosing factorizations that reduce the damage introduced by quantization. The key observation is that functionally equivalent weight arrangements can behave differently once their numerical representation is quantized, making the factorization itself useful to optimize.

The authors report improvements across a wide variety of networks and state-of-the-art quantization degradation results for MobileNets. These findings show that changing the weight representation can improve quantization outcomes without changing the function before quantization. They also identify pruning, regularization, and interpretability as possible application areas for the factorization idea, while their reported focus is quantization.
summary.tldr: Function-preserving rescaling across neighboring layers reduces quantization degradation, with reported improvements across networks and state-of-the-art results for MobileNets.

title: Same, Same But Different: Recovering Neural Network Quantization Error Through Weight Factorization

abstract: Our work focuses on stochastic gradient methods for optimizing a smooth non-convex loss function with a non-smooth non-convex regularizer. Research on this class of problem is quite limited, and until recently no non-asymptotic convergence results have been reported. We present two simple stochastic gradient algorithms, for finite-sum and general stochastic optimization problems, which have superior convergence complexities compared to the current state-of-the-art. We also compare our algorithms’ performance in practice for empirical risk minimization.
originalAbstract: Our work focuses on stochastic gradient methods for optimizing a smooth non-convex loss function with a non-smooth non-convex regularizer. Research on this class of problem is quite limited, and until recently no non-asymptotic convergence results have been reported. We present two simple stochastic gradient algorithms, for finite-sum and general stochastic optimization problems, which have superior convergence complexities compared to the current state-of-the-art. We also compare our algorithms’ performance in practice for empirical risk minimization.

paragraphs: The paper studies objectives that combine a smooth, nonconvex loss with a regularizer that is both nonsmooth and nonconvex. This combination makes the optimization problem different from one with a smooth loss alone. The authors focus on stochastic gradient methods for this setting, where finite-time convergence results had been relatively limited.

They introduce two simple algorithms covering finite-sum optimization and general stochastic optimization. In a finite-sum problem, the objective is assembled from a collection of terms; the general stochastic setting accommodates optimization through random information more broadly. Addressing both forms makes the contribution relevant to two distinct formulations of the regularized learning problem.

The main stated finding is improved convergence complexity compared with the current state of the art for this problem class. The authors also compare the algorithms empirically on empirical risk minimization. The theoretical contribution concerns how efficiently the methods meet their convergence criteria, while the practical comparisons examine their behavior when optimizing learning objectives.
summary.tldr: Two stochastic gradient algorithms improve convergence complexity for smooth nonconvex losses combined with nonsmooth nonconvex regularizers.

title: Simple Stochastic Gradient Methods for Non-Smooth Non-Convex Regularized Optimization

abstract: Adversarial or test time robustness measures the susceptibility of a classifier to perturbations to the test input. While there has been a flurry of recent work on designing defenses against such perturbations, the theory of adversarial robustness is not well understood. In order to make progress on this, we focus on the problem of understanding generalization in adversarial settings, via the lens of Rademacher complexity. We give upper and lower bounds for the adversarial empirical Rademacher complexity of linear hypotheses with adversarial perturbations measured in $l_r$-norm for an arbitrary $r \geq 1$. We then extend our analysis to provide Rademacher complexity lower and upper bounds for a single ReLU unit. Finally, we give adversarial Rademacher complexity bounds for feed-forward neural networks with one hidden layer.

While there has been a flurry of recent work on designing defenses against such perturbations, the theory of adversarial robustness is not well understood. In order to make progress on this, we focus on the problem of understanding generalization in adversarial settings, via the lens of Rademacher complexity. We give upper and lower bounds for the adversarial empirical Rademacher complexity of linear hypotheses with adversarial perturbations measured in $l_r$-norm for an arbitrary $r \geq 1$. We then extend our analysis to provide Rademacher complexity lower and upper bounds for a single ReLU unit. Finally, we give adversarial Rademacher complexity bounds for feed-forward neural networks with one hidden layer.

paragraphs: A classifier's accuracy on ordinary inputs does not directly describe its behavior when test inputs are deliberately perturbed. This paper studies how learning guarantees change in that adversarial setting. Its focus is generalization: understanding how performance assessed using available data relates to performance beyond those observations when perturbations are allowed.

The analysis uses Rademacher complexity, a measure of the flexibility of a class of predictors. The authors establish upper and lower bounds for its adversarial empirical version for linear hypotheses. Their results cover perturbations measured using any l_r norm with r at least one, providing a framework that spans different definitions of perturbation size.

The paper then extends the analysis to a single ReLU unit, again giving upper and lower complexity bounds. It also derives bounds for feed-forward networks with one hidden layer. Together, these results build a theoretical account of adversarial generalization across increasingly expressive predictor classes, with the architectural scope of the neural-network results explicitly specified.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds adversarial Rademacher complexity for linear predictors, individual ReLU units, and neural networks with one hidden layer.

title: Adversarial Learning Guarantees for Linear Hypotheses and Neural Networks

abstract: The sorting operation is one of the most commonly used building blocks in computer programming. In machine learning, it is often used for robust statistics. However, seen as a function, it is piecewise linear and as a result includes many kinks where it is non-differentiable. More problematic is the related ranking operator, often used for order statistics and ranking metrics. It is a piecewise constant function, meaning that its derivatives are null or undefined. While numerous works have proposed differentiable proxies to sorting and ranking, they do not achieve the $O(n \log n)$ time complexity one would expect from sorting and ranking operations. In this paper, we propose the first differentiable sorting and ranking operators with $O(n \log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space complexity. Our proposal in addition enjoys exact computation and differentiation. We achieve this feat by constructing differentiable operators as projections onto the permutahedron, the convex hull of permutations, and using a reduction to isotonic optimization. Empirically, we confirm that our approach is an order of magnitude faster than existing approaches and showcase two novel applications: differentiable Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient and least trimmed squares.

paragraphs: Sorting and ranking are useful inside machine-learning objectives, but their ordinary forms create problems for gradient-based training. Sorting has points where derivatives are undefined, while ranking is constant between changes in order, leaving derivatives zero or undefined. Existing differentiable substitutes also fall short of the time complexity normally expected for these operations.

This paper constructs differentiable sorting and ranking operators with O(n log n) time and O(n) space complexity. The construction projects onto the permutahedron, the convex shape formed from permutations, and reduces the computation to isotonic optimization. Together, these results make ordering-based quantities more practical within trainable systems: the contribution combines useful gradients with computational costs comparable to familiar sorting procedures, rather than treating differentiability and efficiency as separate goals.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces exactly computable differentiable sorting and ranking operators with O(n log n) time and linear memory.

title: Fast Differentiable Sorting and Ranking

abstract: Coagent policy gradient algorithms (CPGAs) are reinforcement learning algorithms for training a class of stochastic neural networks called coagent networks. In this work, we prove that CPGAs converge to locally optimal policies. Additionally, we extend prior theory to encompass asynchronous and recurrent coagent networks. These extensions facilitate the straightforward design and analysis of hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithms like the option-critic, and eliminate the need for complex derivations of customized learning rules for these algorithms.

In this work, we prove that CPGAs converge to locally optimal policies. Additionally, we extend prior theory to encompass asynchronous and recurrent coagent networks. These extensions facilitate the straightforward design and analysis of hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithms like the option-critic, and eliminate the need for complex derivations of customized learning rules for these algorithms.

paragraphs: Coagent networks are stochastic neural networks trained for reinforcement learning using coagent policy gradient algorithms. The paper strengthens the theoretical foundation of this approach by proving convergence to locally optimal policies. This provides a formal account of where the learning process can lead, with a guarantee specifically about local optimality.

The authors also broaden the theory to cover asynchronous and recurrent coagent networks. Asynchronous operation allows network components to operate without all updating together, while recurrence introduces connections across time. Covering these structures matters because the theory can then address a wider range of reinforcement learning designs within the same general approach.

The extensions support the design and analysis of hierarchical reinforcement learning algorithms, including option-critic. Their practical theoretical benefit is that designers can use the coagent framework instead of developing complicated customized learning rules for each such algorithm. The paper therefore contributes both a convergence result and a more broadly applicable analytical foundation for structured reinforcement learning systems.
summary.tldr: Coagent policy gradient theory gains a local convergence guarantee and extensions supporting asynchronous, recurrent, and hierarchical reinforcement learning.

title: Asynchronous Coagent Networks

abstract: Recently there are a considerable amount of work devoted to the study of the algorithmic stability and generalization for stochastic gradient descent (SGD). However, the existing stability analysis requires to impose restrictive assumptions on the boundedness of gradients, smoothness and convexity of loss functions. In this paper, we provide a fine-grained analysis of stability and generalization for SGD by substantially relaxing these assumptions. Firstly, we establish stability and generalization for SGD by removing the existing bounded gradient assumptions. The key idea is the introduction of a new stability measure called on-average model stability, for which we develop novel bounds controlled by the risks of SGD iterates. This yields generalization bounds depending on the behavior of the best model, and leads to the first-ever-known fast bounds in the low-noise setting using stability approach. Secondly, the smoothness assumption is relaxed by considering loss functions with Holder continuous (sub)gradients for which we show that optimal bounds are still achieved by balancing computation and stability. To our best knowledge, this gives the first-ever-known stability and generalization bounds for SGD with non-smooth loss functions (e.g., hinge loss). Finally, we study learning problems with (strongly) convex objectives but non-convex loss functions.

paragraphs: Stability analysis connects an algorithm's sensitivity to its training data with its ability to generalize. Existing analyses of stochastic gradient descent often require restrictive assumptions about bounded gradients, smooth losses, and convexity. This paper develops a more detailed analysis that relaxes these requirements in several ways.

The authors introduce on-average model stability and derive bounds controlled by the risks of the models encountered during optimization. This removes the bounded-gradient assumption and produces generalization bounds that depend on the behavior of the best model. The analysis also yields fast bounds in a low-noise setting through the stability approach.

The paper further considers losses with Hölder-continuous gradients or subgradients, relaxing smoothness requirements. It shows that balancing computation and stability still gives optimal bounds and provides stability and generalization results for nonsmooth losses such as hinge loss. Finally, it examines problems with convex or strongly convex objectives even when individual loss functions are nonconvex. These extensions broaden the settings covered by the analysis without asserting that all assumptions can be removed simultaneously.
summary.tldr: A new average stability measure broadens SGD generalization guarantees by relaxing bounded-gradient, smoothness, and individual-loss convexity requirements.

title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Stability and Generalization for Stochastic Gradient Descent

abstract: In this paper, we consider multi-agent learning via online gradient descent in a class of games called $\lambda$-cocoercive games, a fairly broad class of games that admits many Nash equilibria and that properly includes unconstrained strongly monotone games. We characterize the finite-time last-iterate convergence rate for joint OGD learning on $\lambda$-cocoercive games; further, building on this result, we develop a fully adaptive OGD learning algorithm that does not require any knowledge of problem parameter (e.g. cocoercive constant $\lambda$) and show, via a novel double-stopping time technique, that this adaptive algorithm achieves same finite-time last-iterate convergence rate as non-adaptive counterpart. Subsequently, we extend OGD learning to the noisy gradient feedback case and establish last-iterate convergence results–first qualitative almost sure convergence, then quantitative finite-time convergence rates– all under non-decreasing step-sizes. To our knowledge, we provide the first set of results that fill in several gaps of the existing multi-agent online learning literature, where three aspects–finite-time convergence rates, non-decreasing step-sizes, and fully adaptive algorithms have been unexplored before.

paragraphs: When several agents learn simultaneously, each agent’s changing behavior affects the others. This paper studies online gradient descent in a particular family called lambda-cocoercive games. That family can accommodate multiple Nash equilibria and includes unconstrained strongly monotone games. The focus is on whether the agents’ current decisions converge, rather than only whether averages of past decisions behave well.

The authors establish finite-time convergence rates for the last iterate of joint online gradient descent. They then design a fully adaptive version that does not need advance knowledge of parameters such as the cocoercivity constant. Using a double-stopping-time argument, they show that this adaptive method achieves the same convergence rate as its non-adaptive counterpart.

The analysis also extends to noisy gradient feedback, providing both almost-sure convergence and quantitative finite-time rates under non-decreasing step sizes. Together, these results address how quickly current behavior settles, how learning can proceed without known problem constants, and how noise affects convergence. The guarantees apply within the studied game class and feedback settings.
summary.tldr: For lambda-cocoercive games, the paper establishes last-iterate convergence rates and a parameter-free adaptive gradient method with matching rates.

title: Finite-Time Last-Iterate Convergence for Multi-Agent Learning in Games

abstract: Anderson acceleration is a well-established and simple technique for speeding up fixed-point computations with countless applications. This work introduces novel methods for adapting Anderson acceleration to proximal gradient algorithms. Under some technical conditions, we extend existing local convergence results of Anderson acceleration for smooth fixed-point mappings to the proposed non-smooth setting. We also prove analytically that it is in general, impossible to guarantee global convergence of native Anderson acceleration. We therefore propose a simple scheme for stabilization that combines the global worst-case guarantees of proximal gradient methods with the local adaptation and practical speed-up of Anderson acceleration. Finally, we provide the first applications of Anderson acceleration to non-Euclidean geometry.

paragraphs: Anderson acceleration is a technique for speeding up computations that repeatedly apply an update until it reaches a fixed point. This paper adapts it to proximal gradient algorithms. The challenge is to retain useful acceleration when the update belongs to a nonsmooth setting, where existing smooth fixed-point results do not directly apply.

Under technical conditions, the authors extend local convergence results to their proposed methods. They also prove that native Anderson acceleration cannot, in general, be guaranteed to converge globally. These findings distinguish behavior near a solution from the broader requirement that an algorithm converge from its starting point.

To address that issue, the paper introduces a simple stabilization scheme. It combines the global worst-case guarantees of proximal gradient methods with Anderson acceleration’s local adaptation and practical speed-up. The work also presents its first applications to non-Euclidean geometry. The resulting contribution is both an extension of acceleration to new settings and a way to preserve convergence safeguards when using it.
summary.tldr: Stabilized Anderson acceleration brings practical speed-ups to proximal gradient methods while retaining their global worst-case guarantees.

title: Anderson Acceleration of Proximal Gradient Methods

abstract: Typical architectures of Generative Adversarial Networks make use of a unimodal latent/input distribution transformed by a continuous generator. Consequently, the modeled distribution always has connected support which is cumbersome when learning a disconnected set of manifolds. We formalize this problem by establishing a "no free lunch" theorem for the disconnected manifold learning stating an upper-bound on the precision of the targeted distribution. This is done by building on the necessary existence of a low-quality region where the generator continuously samples data between two disconnected modes. Finally, we derive a rejection sampling method based on the norm of generator’s Jacobian and show its efficiency on several generators including BigGAN.

paragraphs: A target distribution can contain separate regions of valid data with gaps between them. The paper examines why typical generative adversarial networks struggle with this geometry. In the setup studied, a continuous generator transforms a unimodal input distribution, producing a modeled distribution whose support is connected.

That connectedness creates a problem when the desired output occupies disconnected manifolds. The generator must also sample a low-quality region between separated modes. The authors formalize the resulting restriction through a theorem that places an upper bound on precision when learning such distributions. The claim concerns this specified generator setup and the disconnected structure of the target.

The paper then derives a rejection sampling method based on the norm of the generator's Jacobian, which measures how the output changes with its input. This provides a way to filter generated samples using information from the generator itself. Evaluations on several generators, including BigGAN, demonstrate the method's efficiency and connect the theoretical analysis to a practical sampling procedure.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds precision when continuous GAN generators model disconnected data and proposes Jacobian-based rejection sampling to address low-quality connecting regions.

title: Learning disconnected manifolds: a no GAN’s land

abstract: Recent work demonstrated the benefits of studying continuous-time dynamics governing the GAN training. However, this dynamics is analyzed in the model parameter space, which results in finite-dimensional dynamical systems. We propose a novel perspective where we study the local dynamics of adversarial training in the general functional space and show how it can be represented as a system of partial differential equations. Thus, the convergence properties can be inferred from the eigenvalues of the resulting differential operator. We show that these eigenvalues can be efficiently estimated from the target dataset before training. Our perspective reveals several insights on the practical tricks commonly used to stabilize GANs, such as gradient penalty, data augmentation, and advanced integration schemes. As an immediate practical benefit, we demonstrate how one can a priori select an optimal data augmentation strategy for a particular generation task.

paragraphs: Understanding whether GAN training settles down requires studying the interaction between its competing components. Earlier continuous-time analyses describe this interaction through model parameters, producing finite-dimensional dynamical systems. This paper instead examines local training dynamics in a general space of functions, changing the mathematical objects used to describe convergence.

The authors represent these dynamics as a system of partial differential equations. Convergence properties can then be inferred from eigenvalues of the associated differential operator. They also show that these eigenvalues can be estimated efficiently from the target dataset before training begins, making the analysis potentially useful for choosing how to train a model.

This perspective gives insight into several established stabilization techniques, including gradient penalties, data augmentation, and advanced numerical integration schemes. As a practical application, the authors demonstrate how to select an optimal augmentation strategy for a particular generation task in advance. The scope remains local convergence: the contribution explains behavior through the proposed local dynamics and uses that explanation to guide a concrete training choice.
summary.tldr: A function-space analysis of local GAN dynamics connects convergence to dataset-estimable quantities and guides augmentation selection before training.

title: Functional Space Analysis of Local GAN Convergence

abstract: We study the attribution problem in a graphical model, wherein the objective is to quantify how the effect of changes at the source nodes propagates through the graph. We develop a model-agnostic flow-based attribution method, called recursive Shapley value (RSV). RSV generalizes a number of existing node-based methods and uniquely satisfies a set of flow-based axioms. In addition to admitting a natural characterization for linear models and facilitating mediation analysis for non-linear models, RSV satisfies a mix of desirable properties discussed in the recent literature, including implementation invariance, sensitivity, monotonicity, and affine scale invariance.

paragraphs: Explaining a graphical model can involve more than assigning importance to individual nodes. A change introduced at a source can propagate through the graph, and an attribution method can try to quantify that propagation. This paper develops recursive Shapley value, or RSV, as a model-agnostic approach to this flow-based explanation problem.

RSV generalizes several existing node-based attribution methods while satisfying a set of axioms formulated for flows. The authors establish that RSV is the unique method satisfying that particular set of axioms. This gives the method a precise mathematical justification: its attribution rule follows from specified requirements about how effects should be assigned through the graph.

The method also has a natural characterization for linear models and supports mediation analysis in nonlinear models, connecting attribution to the role of intermediate parts of a graph. It satisfies implementation invariance, sensitivity, monotonicity, and affine scale invariance. Together, these results position RSV as a unified way to reason about propagated contributions while retaining several established desirable properties of explanations.
summary.tldr: Recursive Shapley value attributes how source changes propagate through graphical models and uniquely satisfies a specified set of flow axioms.

title: Flow-based Attribution in Graphical Models: A Recursive Shapley Approach

abstract: Structured nonsmooth convex finite-sum optimization appears in many machine learning applications, including support vector machines and least absolute deviation. For the primal-dual formulation of this problem, we propose a novel algorithm called \emph{Variance Reduction via Primal-Dual Accelerated Dual Averaging (\vrpda)}. In the nonsmooth and general convex setting, \vrpda has the overall complexity $O(nd\log\min \{1/\epsilon, n\} + d/\epsilon )$ in terms of the primal-dual gap, where $n$ denotes the number of samples, $d$ the dimension of the primal variables, and $\epsilon$ the desired accuracy. In the nonsmooth and strongly convex setting, the overall complexity of \vrpda becomes $O(nd\log\min\{1/\epsilon, n\} + d/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ in terms of both the primal-dual gap and the distance between iterate and optimal solution. Both these results for \vrpda improve significantly on state-of-the-art complexity estimates—which are $O(nd\log \min\{1/\epsilon, n\} + \sqrt{n}d/\epsilon)$ for the nonsmooth and general convex setting and $O(nd\log \min\{1/\epsilon, n\} + \sqrt{n}d/\sqrt{\epsilon})$ for the nonsmooth and strongly convex setting—with a simpler and more straightforward algorithm and analysis. Moreover, both complexities are better than \emph{lower} bounds for general convex finite-sum optimization, because our approach makes use of additional, commonly occurring structure. Numerical experiments reveal competitive performance of \vrpda compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

This paper introduces a primal-dual optimization algorithm that combines variance reduction with accelerated dual averaging. Its analysis shows how exploiting that structure improves the computational cost of reaching a desired accuracy.

For n samples, primal dimension d, and target accuracy epsilon, the general convex bound is O(nd log min{1/epsilon, n} + d/epsilon). With strong convexity, the final term becomes d divided by the square root of epsilon. Compared with the stated previous bounds, both results remove a square-root-of-n factor from the accuracy-dependent term. The stronger setting also provides guarantees on distance to the optimal solution.

These complexities improve on lower bounds for general finite-sum convex optimization because the algorithm uses additional structure; the results therefore concern a more specific problem class. Numerical experiments show competitive performance against existing approaches. The contribution combines sharper theoretical scaling with an algorithm and analysis described as simpler and more direct.
summary.tldr: A structured primal-dual algorithm removes a square-root sample-count factor from key complexity terms in nonsmooth convex finite-sum optimization.

title: Variance Reduction via Primal-Dual Accelerated Dual Averaging for Nonsmooth Convex Finite-Sums

abstract: Nondeterminism in neural network optimization produces uncertainty in performance, making small improvements difficult to discern from run-to-run variability. While uncertainty can be reduced by training multiple model copies, doing so is time-consuming, costly, and harms reproducibility. In this work, we establish an experimental protocol for understanding the effect of optimization nondeterminism on model diversity, allowing us to isolate the effects of a variety of sources of nondeterminism. Surprisingly, we find that all sources of nondeterminism have similar effects on measures of model diversity. To explain this intriguing fact, we identify the instability of model training, taken as an end-to-end procedure, as the key determinant. We show that even one-bit changes in initial parameters result in models converging to vastly different values. Last, we propose two approaches for reducing the effects of instability on run-to-run variability.

paragraphs: Repeated neural-network training runs can produce different results, making small performance improvements difficult to distinguish from ordinary variability. Training many copies can help assess that uncertainty, but it adds time and cost. This paper establishes an experimental protocol for separating the effects of different sources of nondeterminism on the diversity of trained models.

Across the sources examined, the authors find surprisingly similar effects on measures of model diversity. They explain this through instability of the full training procedure: a very small initial difference can lead to a substantially different final outcome. Their demonstration shows that changing just one bit in initial parameters can produce models that converge to widely different values.

The paper then proposes two approaches for reducing how this instability affects variation between runs. Its central contribution is to connect observed model diversity to the sensitivity of training as a whole. This helps explain why different sources of nondeterminism can have comparable effects, and why evaluating small claimed gains requires attention to the variability generated during optimization.
summary.tldr: Experiments identify training instability as a key reason different sources of nondeterminism produce similar variation across neural-network runs.

title: Nondeterminism and Instability in Neural Network Optimization

abstract: Humans can learn and reason under substantial uncertainty in a space of infinitely many compositional, productive concepts. For example, if a scene with two blue spheres qualifies as “daxy,” one can reason that the underlying concept may require scenes to have “only blue spheres” or “only spheres” or “only two objects.” In contrast, standard benchmarks for compositional reasoning do not explicitly capture a notion of reasoning under uncertainty or evaluate compositional concept acquisition. We introduce a new benchmark, Compositional Reasoning Under Uncertainty (CURI) that instantiates a series of few-shot, meta-learning tasks in a productive concept space to evaluate different aspects of systematic generalization under uncertainty, including splits that test abstract understandings of disentangling, productive generalization, learning boolean operations, variable binding, etc. Importantly, we also contribute a model-independent “compositionality gap” to evaluate the difficulty of generalizing out-of-distribution along each of these axes, allowing objective comparison of the difficulty of each compositional split. Evaluations across a range of modeling choices and splits reveal substantial room for improvement on the proposed benchmark.

paragraphs: A few examples rarely determine a concept uniquely. A scene might qualify because of its objects' colors, their shapes, their number, or a combination of those properties. CURI turns this ambiguity into a benchmark for learning compositional concepts, asking models to reason when several explanations remain compatible with limited observations.

The benchmark consists of few-shot meta-learning tasks in a concept space that supports constructing new concepts from components. Its evaluation splits test different forms of systematic generalization, including separating factors, combining concepts productively, learning Boolean operations, and binding variables. This makes uncertainty part of concept acquisition itself, rather than evaluating composition only after the relevant rule is established.

The authors also introduce a model-independent compositionality gap for comparing how difficult the different out-of-distribution splits are. That measure helps distinguish the challenge posed by a split from the performance of a particular model. Evaluations across multiple modeling choices reveal substantial remaining room for improvement, positioning CURI as a test of compositional learning under genuinely ambiguous evidence.
summary.tldr: CURI tests whether models can learn and recombine concepts from few examples while accounting for uncertainty about the underlying rule.

title: CURI: A Benchmark for Productive Concept Learning Under Uncertainty

abstract: In policy search methods for reinforcement learning (RL), exploration is often performed by injecting noise either in action space at each step independently or in parameter space over each full trajectory. In prior work, it has been shown that with linear policies, a more balanced trade-off between these two exploration strategies is beneficial. However, that method did not scale to policies using deep neural networks. In this paper, we introduce deep coherent exploration, a general and scalable exploration framework for deep RL algorithms for continuous control, that generalizes step-based and trajectory-based exploration. This framework models the last layer parameters of the policy network as latent variables and uses a recursive inference step within the policy update to handle these latent variables in a scalable manner. We find that deep coherent exploration improves the speed and stability of learning of A2C, PPO, and SAC on several continuous control tasks.
originalAbstract: In policy search methods for reinforcement learning (RL), exploration is often performed by injecting noise either in action space at each step independently or in parameter space over each full trajectory. In prior work, it has been shown that with linear policies, a more balanced trade-off between these two exploration strategies is beneficial. However, that method did not scale to policies using deep neural networks. In this paper, we introduce deep coherent exploration, a general and scalable exploration framework for deep RL algorithms for continuous control, that generalizes step-based and trajectory-based exploration. This framework models the last layer parameters of the policy network as latent variables and uses a recursive inference step within the policy update to handle these latent variables in a scalable manner. We find that deep coherent exploration improves the speed and stability of learning of A2C, PPO, and SAC on several continuous control tasks.

paragraphs: Continuous-control agents often explore by adding independent noise to each action or by perturbing policy parameters for an entire trajectory. These approaches organize randomness over different time spans. Earlier work found benefits from balancing them for linear policies, but that approach did not scale to policies represented by deep neural networks.

Deep coherent exploration provides a scalable framework that generalizes both step-based and trajectory-based exploration. It treats the parameters in the policy network’s last layer as latent variables. A recursive inference step within the policy update handles those variables, allowing the exploration mechanism to be incorporated into deep reinforcement learning.

The approach matters because the temporal structure of exploration becomes part of the learning framework, rather than being restricted to either independent action noise or a trajectory-wide perturbation. Experiments report faster and more stable learning for A2C, PPO, and SAC on several continuous-control tasks. These findings demonstrate benefits across the tested algorithms and tasks while keeping the contribution centered on exploration.
summary.tldr: Deep coherent exploration unifies step-based and trajectory-based exploration and improves learning speed and stability on tested continuous-control tasks.

title: Deep Coherent Exploration for Continuous Control

abstract: It is an important problem in trustworthy machine learning to recognize out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs which are inputs unrelated to the in-distribution task. Many out-of-distribution detection methods have been suggested in recent years. The goal of this paper is to recognize common objectives as well as to identify the implicit scoring functions of different OOD detection methods. We focus on the sub-class of methods that use surrogate OOD data during training in order to learn an OOD detection score that generalizes to new unseen out-distributions at test time. We show that binary discrimination between in- and (different) out-distributions is equivalent to several distinct formulations of the OOD detection problem. When trained in a shared fashion with a standard classifier, this binary discriminator reaches an OOD detection performance similar to that of Outlier Exposure. Moreover, we show that the confidence loss which is used by Outlier Exposure has an implicit scoring function which differs in a non-trivial fashion from the theoretically optimal scoring function in the case where training and test out-distribution are the same, which again is similar to the one used when training an Energy-Based OOD detector or when adding a background class. In practice, when trained in exactly the same way, all these methods perform similarly.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input belongs to the task a model was trained to handle. This paper studies detectors trained with surrogate out-of-distribution examples, which must subsequently recognize unfamiliar out-distributions. It seeks to identify shared objectives and the scoring functions implicit in methods that appear different.

The authors show that binary discrimination between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data is equivalent to several formulations of this detection problem. When trained jointly with a standard classifier, this discriminator performs similarly to Outlier Exposure. This connects a simple discrimination task to approaches presented through other training objectives.

The analysis also identifies a meaningful difference between the score implicit in Outlier Exposure’s confidence loss and the theoretically optimal score when training and test out-distributions coincide. That optimal score resembles those associated with energy-based detection and a background class. Nevertheless, matched training produces similar practical performance across these methods. The findings separate differences in theoretical scoring rules from the empirical effects observed under a shared training procedure.
summary.tldr: Several detectors trained with out-of-distribution examples share underlying objectives and perform similarly when trained under matched conditions.

title: Breaking Down Out-of-Distribution Detection: Many Methods Based on OOD Training Data Estimate a Combination of the Same Core Quantities

abstract: Efficient deep neural network (DNN) models equipped with compact operators (e.g., depthwise convolutions) have shown great potential in reducing DNNs’ theoretical complexity (e.g., the total number of weights/operations) while maintaining a decent model accuracy. However, existing efficient DNNs are still limited in fulfilling their promise in boosting real-hardware efficiency, due to their commonly adopted compact operators’ low hardware utilization. In this work, we open up a new compression paradigm for developing real-hardware efficient DNNs, leading to boosted hardware efficiency while maintaining model accuracy. Interestingly, we observe that while some DNN layers’ activation functions help DNNs’ training optimization and achievable accuracy, they can be properly removed after training without compromising the model accuracy. Inspired by this observation, we propose a framework dubbed DepthShrinker, which develops hardware-friendly compact networks via shrinking the basic building blocks of existing efficient DNNs that feature irregular computation patterns into dense ones with much improved hardware utilization and thus real-hardware efficiency. Excitingly, our DepthShrinker framework delivers hardware-friendly compact networks that outperform both state-of-the-art efficient DNNs and compression techniques, e.g., a 3.06% higher accuracy and 1.53x throughput on Tesla V100 over SOTA channel-wise pruning method MetaPruning. Our codes are available at: https://github.com/facebookresearch/DepthShrinker.

paragraphs: A network with fewer weights or operations does not necessarily use hardware efficiently. Compact operators such as depthwise convolutions can have low hardware utilization, limiting the practical speed benefits of their reduced theoretical complexity. DepthShrinker addresses this mismatch by changing the computation performed by existing efficient networks.

The approach starts from an observation about activation functions. Some help optimization and accuracy during training but can be appropriately removed afterward without harming accuracy. DepthShrinker uses this opportunity to shrink building blocks with irregular computation patterns into dense blocks that make better use of hardware.

The reported networks outperform state-of-the-art efficient architectures and compression techniques while maintaining model accuracy. One comparison reports 3.06% higher accuracy and 1.53 times the throughput of MetaPruning on a Tesla V100. These findings illustrate why the arrangement of computation matters alongside its nominal size. The removable-activation observation concerns some layers and appropriate removal, rather than establishing that nonlinearities can generally be discarded without consequences.
summary.tldr: DepthShrinker removes suitable post-training activations and converts compact network blocks into dense computations that improve real hardware throughput.

title: DepthShrinker: A New Compression Paradigm Towards Boosting Real-Hardware Efficiency of Compact Neural Networks

abstract: Saliency methods are a popular class of feature attribution explanation methods that aim to capture a model’s predictive reasoning by identifying "important" pixels in an input image. However, the development and adoption of these methods are hindered by the lack of access to ground-truth model reasoning, which prevents accurate evaluation. In this work, we design a synthetic benchmarking framework, SMERF, that allows us to perform ground-truth-based evaluation while controlling the complexity of the model’s reasoning. Experimentally, SMERF reveals significant limitations in existing saliency methods and, as a result, represents a useful tool for the development of new saliency methods.

However, the development and adoption of these methods are hindered by the lack of access to ground-truth model reasoning, which prevents accurate evaluation. paragraphs: Saliency methods explain image predictions by highlighting pixels they regard as important to the model. Evaluating those explanations is difficult because researchers usually lack a known account of the model's actual predictive reasoning. Without that reference, judging whether a highlighted region accurately explains a prediction becomes a separate unresolved problem.

The paper introduces SMERF, a synthetic benchmarking framework that makes ground-truth reasoning available for evaluation. It also lets researchers control the complexity of that reasoning. These two capabilities allow saliency methods to be assessed against a defined reference while varying how demanding the explanation problem is. The framework therefore targets the evaluation obstacle directly.

Experiments with SMERF reveal significant limitations in existing saliency methods. The stated finding concerns their performance in this controlled framework, where explanations can be compared with known reasoning. The authors present SMERF as a useful tool for developing new methods because it supplies an explicit target for evaluation and a way to adjust the complexity of the task.
summary.tldr: SMERF evaluates saliency explanations against known reasoning in synthetic settings and exposes significant limitations in existing methods.

title: Sanity Simulations for Saliency Methods

abstract: The effectiveness of knowledge graph embedding (KGE) largely depends on the ability to model intrinsic relation patterns and mapping properties. However, existing approaches can only capture some of them with insufficient modeling capacity. In this work, we propose a more powerful KGE framework named HousE, which involves a novel parameterization based on two kinds of Householder transformations: (1) Householder rotations to achieve superior capacity of modeling relation patterns; (2) Householder projections to handle sophisticated relation mapping properties. Theoretically, HousE is capable of modeling crucial relation patterns and mapping properties simultaneously. Besides, HousE is a generalization of existing rotation-based models while extending the rotations to high-dimensional spaces. Empirically, HousE achieves new state-of-the-art performance on five benchmark datasets. Our code is available at https://github.com/anrep/HousE.

paragraphs: Knowledge graph embeddings represent entities and relations mathematically so that a model can capture the graph’s relational structure. Their effectiveness depends on expressing both patterns among relations and the ways relations map entities to one another. The paper argues that existing approaches have insufficient capacity to capture these properties together.

HousE introduces a parameterization built from two types of Householder transformations. Householder rotations increase the capacity to model relation patterns, while Householder projections address complex relation mappings. These components serve complementary roles within a single embedding framework. HousE also generalizes existing rotation-based models by extending the rotations into higher-dimensional spaces.

The theoretical analysis establishes that HousE can simultaneously represent crucial relation patterns and mapping properties. Experiments report new state-of-the-art performance on five benchmark datasets. The combined findings connect representational capacity with observed benchmark performance: the framework supplies a mathematical way to express multiple aspects of relations together, and the evaluations show practical benefits in the tested knowledge graphs.
summary.tldr: HousE combines Householder rotations and projections to model knowledge-graph relation patterns and mappings simultaneously.

title: HousE: Knowledge Graph Embedding with Householder Parameterization

abstract: The combination of Monte Carlo methods and deep learning has recently led to efficient algorithms for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) in high dimensions. Related learning problems are often stated as variational formulations based on associated stochastic differential equations (SDEs), which allow the minimization of corresponding losses using gradient-based optimization methods. In respective numerical implementations it is therefore crucial to rely on adequate gradient estimators that exhibit low variance in order to reach convergence accurately and swiftly. In this article, we rigorously investigate corresponding numerical aspects that appear in the context of linear Kolmogorov PDEs. In particular, we systematically compare existing deep learning approaches and provide theoretical explanations for their performances. Subsequently, we suggest novel methods that can be shown to be more robust both theoretically and numerically, leading to substantial performance improvements.

Some approaches turn the equation into a loss-minimization problem using an associated stochastic differential equation. Their practical success then depends on whether the gradients used for training can be estimated accurately and with low variance.

This paper investigates those numerical issues for linear Kolmogorov equations. The authors systematically compare existing deep-learning approaches and explain their performance theoretically. Their focus connects the mathematical formulation of the loss with the numerical behavior of the optimization procedure, particularly the quality of the gradient estimates it produces.

Building on that analysis, they propose new methods that are more robust both in theory and in numerical evaluations, with substantial reported performance improvements. The work shows why the formulation of a learning problem matters even when the ultimate goal is the same differential-equation solution. Improving how the objective is estimated and optimized can help the solver converge more accurately and quickly.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes gradient-estimation issues in neural solvers for linear Kolmogorov PDEs and develops theoretically and numerically more robust formulations.

title: Robust SDE-Based Variational Formulations for Solving Linear PDEs via Deep Learning

abstract: When dealing with electro or magnetoencephalography records, many supervised prediction tasks are solved by working with covariance matrices to summarize the signals. Learning with these matrices requires the usage of Riemanian geometry to account for their structure. In this paper, we propose a new method to deal with distributions of covariance matrices, and demonstrate its computational efficiency on M/EEG multivariate time series. More specifically, we define a Sliced-Wasserstein distance between measures of symmetric positive definite matrices that comes with strong theoretical guarantees. Then, we take advantage of its properties and kernel methods to apply this discrepancy to brain-age prediction from MEG data, and compare it to state-of-the-art algorithms based on Riemannian geometry. Finally, we show that it is an efficient surrogate to the Wasserstein distance in domain adaptation for Brain Computer Interface applications.

The authors define a Sliced-Wasserstein distance between probability measures on symmetric positive definite matrices. The distance comes with theoretical guarantees, and the paper demonstrates computational efficiency on multivariate brain-signal time series. This provides a distribution-level comparison that respects the kind of structured objects used to represent the recordings.

Second, it shows that the distance serves as an efficient substitute for Wasserstein distance in domain adaptation for brain-computer interfaces. Together, these applications connect a new mathematical comparison tool to both prediction and adaptation, with computational efficiency central to its practical value.
summary.tldr: A Sliced-Wasserstein distance for distributions of covariance matrices supports efficient brain-signal prediction and domain adaptation.

title: Sliced-Wasserstein on Symmetric Positive Definite Matrices for M/EEG Signals

abstract: We make two contributions in the field of AI fairness over continuous protected attributes. First, we show that the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Renyi (HGR) indicator (the only one currently available for such a case) is valuable but subject to a few crucial limitations regarding semantics, interpretability, and robustness. Second, we introduce a family of indicators that are: 1) complementary to HGR in terms of semantics; 2) fully interpretable and transparent; 3) robust over finite samples; 4) configurable to suit specific applications. Our approach also allows us to define fine-grained constraints to permit certain types of dependence and forbid others selectively. By expanding the available options for continuous protected attributes, our approach represents a significant contribution to the area of fair artificial intelligence.

paragraphs: Fairness assessment becomes more complicated when a protected attribute varies continuously. This paper examines how to measure dependence involving such attributes and how to express the forms of dependence an application should permit. Its starting point is the Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Renyi indicator, or HGR, which the authors find valuable but limited in meaning, interpretability, and robustness.

The authors introduce a family of alternative indicators with semantics that complement HGR. They describe these indicators as transparent, interpretable, robust with finite samples, and configurable for particular applications. The contribution therefore concerns both the numerical measurement of dependence and the ability to understand what a chosen measurement represents.

The framework also supports fine-grained constraints that allow some types of dependence while disallowing others. This matters when an application's fairness requirements cannot be captured by a single undifferentiated restriction on dependence. The paper expands the available ways to specify fairness over continuous protected attributes, giving practitioners more control over which relationships their constraints target rather than presenting one universal fairness definition.
summary.tldr: A configurable family of fairness indicators supports interpretable constraints that selectively permit or forbid dependence on continuous protected attributes.

title: Generalized Disparate Impact for Configurable Fairness Solutions in ML

abstract: Motivated by concerns about making online decisions that incur undue amount of risk at each time step, in this paper, we formulate the probably anytime-safe stochastic combinatorial semi-bandits problem. In this problem, the agent is given the option to select a subset of size at most $K$ from a set of $L$ ground items. Each item is associated to a certain mean reward as well as a variance that represents its risk. To mitigate the risk that the agent incurs, we require that with probability at least $1-\delta$, over the entire horizon of time $T$, each of the choices that the agent makes should contain items whose sum of variances does not exceed a certain variance budget. We call this probably anytime-safe constraint. Under this constraint, we design and analyze an algorithm PASCombUCB that minimizes the regret over the horizon of time $T$. By developing accompanying information-theoretic lower bounds, we show that under both the problem-dependent and problem-independent paradigms, PASCombUCB is almost asymptotically optimal. Experiments are conducted to corroborate our theoretical findings. Our problem setup, the proposed PASCombUCB algorithm, and novel analyses are applicable to domains such as recommendation systems and transportation in which an agent is allowed to choose multiple items at a single time step and wishes to control the risk over the whole time horizon.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decisions in which an agent selects several items at once and must control risk throughout the process. Each item has an expected reward and a variance representing risk. At each step, the agent may choose up to a specified number of items, seeking reward while respecting a budget on their combined variances.

The safety requirement applies jointly across the entire time horizon: with probability at least one minus delta, every selected set must meet the variance budget. This is stronger than checking only an average risk across decisions. The authors develop PASCombUCB to minimize regret while operating under this probabilistic, anytime safety constraint.

Information-theoretic lower bounds establish a comparison with what algorithms can achieve in this problem. Against those bounds, PASCombUCB is almost asymptotically optimal under both problem-dependent and problem-independent analyses, and experiments corroborate the theory. The framework is relevant to settings such as recommendations and transportation where multiple choices are made together and the stated variance-based risk must remain controlled over time.
summary.tldr: PASCombUCB achieves nearly asymptotically optimal regret while enforcing a high-probability variance budget for every decision across the time horizon.

title: Probably Anytime-Safe Stochastic Combinatorial Semi-Bandits

abstract: Gradient regularization (GR) is a method that penalizes the gradient norm of the training loss during training. While some studies have reported that GR can improve generalization performance, little attention has been paid to it from the algorithmic perspective, that is, the algorithms of GR that efficiently improve the performance. In this study, we first reveal that a specific finite-difference computation, composed of both gradient ascent and descent steps, reduces the computational cost of GR. Next, we show that the finite-difference computation also works better in the sense of generalization performance. We theoretically analyze a solvable model, a diagonal linear network, and clarify that GR has a desirable implicit bias to so-called rich regime and finite-difference computation strengthens this bias. Furthermore, finite-difference GR is closely related to some other algorithms based on iterative ascent and descent steps for exploring flat minima. In particular, we reveal that the flooding method can perform finite-difference GR in an implicit way. Thus, this work broadens our understanding of GR for both practice and theory.

paragraphs: Gradient regularization penalizes the size of the training-loss gradient during learning. Earlier work had reported generalization benefits, but the computational procedure for applying the penalty had received less attention. This paper studies how the choice of computation affects both training cost and the behavior encouraged by regularization.

The authors identify a finite-difference procedure combining gradient ascent and descent steps that reduces computational cost and also improves generalization performance. To understand this behavior, they analyze a solvable diagonal linear network. In that model, gradient regularization favors the rich regime, and the finite-difference computation strengthens this desirable implicit bias.

The paper also connects finite-difference gradient regularization to methods that alternate ascent and descent while exploring flat minima. In particular, it shows that flooding can implement this regularization implicitly. These connections explain how apparently different training procedures can share a regularizing mechanism. The theoretical implicit-bias analysis is grounded in the diagonal linear model, while the computational and generalization findings motivate the finite-difference approach in practice.
summary.tldr: A finite-difference implementation makes gradient regularization cheaper and strengthens its beneficial implicit bias in an analyzed linear model.

title: Understanding Gradient Regularization in Deep Learning: Efficient Finite-Difference Computation and Implicit Bias

abstract: We consider the problem of solving large-scale instances of the Max-Cut semidefinite program (SDP), i.e., optimizing a linear function over $n\times n$ positive semidefinite (PSD) matrices with unit diagonal. When the cost matrix is PSD, we show how to exactly reformulate the problem as maximizing a smooth concave function over PSD matrices with unit trace. By applying the Frank-Wolfe method, we obtain a simple algorithm that is compatible with recent sampling-based techniques to solve SDPs using low memory. We demonstrate the practical performance of our method on $10^6\times 10^6$ instances of the max-cut SDP with costs having up to $5 \times 10^6$ non-zero entries. Theoretically, we show that our method solves problems with diagonally dominant costs to relative error $\epsilon$ in $O(n\epsilon^{-1})$ calls to a randomized approximate largest eigenvalue subroutine, each of which succeeds with high probability after $O(\log(n)\epsilon^{-1/2})$ matrix-vector multiplications with the cost matrix.

paragraphs: This paper develops an algorithm for large instances of the Max-Cut semidefinite program. The optimization variable is a positive semidefinite matrix whose diagonal entries must all equal one. At large sizes, working with this matrix creates a substantial computational and memory challenge, motivating a formulation that supports more economical optimization.

When the cost matrix is positive semidefinite, the authors show an exact reformulation: maximize a smooth concave function over positive semidefinite matrices with unit trace. Exactness means this changes the mathematical form without changing the underlying optimization problem. Applying Frank-Wolfe then produces an algorithm compatible with sampling techniques designed to reduce memory use.

The practical demonstration includes matrices with one million rows and columns and up to five million nonzero cost entries. For diagonally dominant costs, the authors also bound the work needed to reach a specified relative error using randomized approximate eigenvalue computations. Those computations succeed with high probability, giving a qualified computational guarantee alongside the large-scale demonstration.
summary.tldr: An exact reformulation enables a memory-compatible Frank-Wolfe algorithm for very large Max-Cut semidefinite programs.

title: A Scalable Frank-Wolfe-Based Algorithm for the Max-Cut SDP

abstract: Foundation models are redefining how AI systems are built. Practitioners now follow a standard procedure to build their machine learning solutions: from a pre-trained foundation model, they fine-tune the weights on the target task of interest. So, the Internet is swarmed by a handful of foundation models fine-tuned on many diverse tasks: these individual fine-tunings exist in isolation without benefiting from each other. In our opinion, this is a missed opportunity, as these specialized models contain rich and diverse features. In this paper, we thus propose model ratatouille, a new strategy to recycle the multiple fine-tunings of the same foundation model on diverse auxiliary tasks. Specifically, we repurpose these auxiliary weights as initializations for multiple parallel fine-tunings on the target task; then, we average all fine-tuned weights to obtain the final model. This recycling strategy aims at maximizing the diversity in weights by leveraging the diversity in auxiliary tasks. Empirically, it improves the state of the art on the reference DomainBed benchmark for out-of-distribution generalization. Looking forward, this work contributes to the emerging paradigm of updatable machine learning where, akin to open-source software development, the community collaborates to reliably update machine learning models.

paragraphs: Many specialized models start from the same foundation model and are then fine-tuned independently on different tasks. This paper proposes reusing those separate adaptations because they contain diverse learned features. Its goal is to turn existing auxiliary-task models into useful starting points for a new target task and improve generalization beyond the target training distribution.

Model ratatouille begins with several auxiliary models derived from the same foundation model. Each supplies the initialization for a separate fine-tuning run on the target task. After those runs finish, their weights are averaged into one final model. The strategy uses diversity among auxiliary tasks to seek diversity in the target-task weights being combined.

Empirically, the approach improves the reported state of the art on DomainBed, a benchmark for out-of-distribution generalization. The result supports recycling specialized models through further training and weight averaging. The authors also position this as a step toward community-driven model updates, where independently developed adaptations can contribute to later models rather than remaining isolated.
summary.tldr: Model ratatouille fine-tunes diverse auxiliary models on one target task and averages their weights to improve out-of-distribution generalization.

title: Model Ratatouille: Recycling Diverse Models for Out-of-Distribution Generalization

abstract: In this paper, we present an effective and efficient structural inference approach by integrating a Reservoir Computing (RC) network into a Variational Auto-encoder-based (VAE-based) structural inference framework. With the help of Bi-level Optimization, the backbone VAE-based method follows the Information Bottleneck principle and infers a general adjacency matrix in its latent space; the RC net substitutes the partial role of the decoder and encourages the whole approach to perform further steps of gradient descent based on limited available data. The experimental results on various datasets including biological networks, simulated fMRI data, and physical simulations show the effectiveness and efficiency of our proposed method for structural inference, either with much fewer trajectories or with much shorter trajectories compared with previous works.

paragraphs: Structural inference seeks to recover connections within a system from its observed behavior. This can be difficult when observations contain only a small number of trajectories or cover short periods. The paper proposes combining reservoir computing with a variational autoencoder framework to make better use of such limited data.

The underlying autoencoder uses bi-level optimization and follows the information bottleneck principle to infer an adjacency matrix in its latent representation. That matrix represents the system’s connections. A reservoir computing network takes over part of the decoder’s role and encourages additional gradient-descent steps with the available data. The contribution therefore changes how the inference framework learns from limited trajectories.

Experiments cover biological networks, simulated brain-imaging data, and physical simulations. The authors report effective and efficient structural inference using substantially fewer trajectories or much shorter trajectories than previous work. These findings suggest that incorporating reservoir computing can improve the data requirements of this structural inference framework across the evaluated types of dynamical systems.
summary.tldr: Adding reservoir computing to a variational structural-inference framework enables effective connection recovery from fewer or shorter trajectories.

title: Effective and Efficient Structural Inference with Reservoir Computing

abstract: Graph augmentation plays a crucial role in achieving good generalization for contrastive graph self-supervised learning. However, mainstream Graph Contrastive Learning (GCL) often favors random graph augmentations, by relying on random node dropout or edge perturbation on graphs. Random augmentations may inevitably lead to semantic information corruption during the training, and force the network to mistakenly focus on semantically irrelevant environmental background structures. To address these limitations and to improve generalization, we propose a novel self-supervised learning framework for GCL, which can adaptively screen the semantic-related substructure in graphs by capitalizing on the proposed gradient-based Graph Contrastive Saliency (GCS). The goal is to identify the most semantically discriminative structures of a graph via contrastive learning, such that we can generate semantically meaningful augmentations by leveraging on saliency. Empirical evidence on 16 benchmark datasets demonstrates the exclusive merits of the GCS-based framework. We also provide rigorous theoretical justification for GCS’s robustness properties. Code is available at https://github.com/GCS2023/GCS .

paragraphs: Graph contrastive learning depends on augmented versions of graphs to learn useful representations without labels. Common augmentations randomly remove nodes or change edges. Those edits can damage meaningful structure and encourage a model to focus on background patterns that are less relevant to what distinguishes the graph.

The proposed framework uses gradient-based Graph Contrastive Saliency to identify graph substructures that matter to the contrastive learning objective. It then uses those saliency signals to create augmentations with more meaningful structural content. The approach makes augmentation adaptive: the learning process helps determine which parts of a graph deserve attention when generating training views.

The authors report empirical support across 16 benchmark datasets and provide theoretical justification for robustness properties of the saliency measure. The findings support treating augmentation design as part of learning, rather than relying entirely on random graph changes. The stated benefit is better generalization through attention to discriminative structure; the experiments demonstrate this benefit in the evaluated benchmark settings.
summary.tldr: Gradient-based graph saliency guides contrastive augmentations toward meaningful substructures, with theoretical robustness support and empirical benefits across 16 datasets.

title: Boosting Graph Contrastive Learning via Graph Contrastive Saliency

abstract: Some extremely low-dimensional yet crucial geometric eigen-lengths often determine the success of some geometric tasks. For example, the height of an object is important to measure to check if it can fit between the shelves of a cabinet, while the width of a couch is crucial when trying to move it through a doorway. Humans have materialized such crucial geometric eigen-lengths in common sense since they are very useful in serving as succinct yet effective, highly interpretable, and universal object representations. However, it remains obscure and underexplored if learning systems can be equipped with similar capabilities of automatically discovering such key geometric quantities from doing tasks. In this work, we therefore for the first time formulate and propose a novel learning problem on this question and set up a benchmark suite including tasks, data, and evaluation metrics for studying the problem. We focus on a family of common fitting tasks as the testbed for the proposed learning problem. We explore potential solutions and demonstrate the feasibility of learning eigen-lengths from simply observing successful and failed fitting trials. We also attempt geometric grounding for more accurate eigen-length measurement and study the reusability of the learned geometric eigen-lengths across multiple tasks. Our work marks the first exploratory step toward learning crucial geometric eigen-lengths and we hope it can inspire future research in tackling this important yet underexplored problem.

paragraphs: Whether an object fits somewhere can depend on just a few dimensions, such as its height beneath a shelf or its width through a doorway. The paper calls these crucial quantities geometric eigen-lengths. It asks whether a learning system can discover such compact, interpretable object descriptions through experience with fitting tasks.

The authors formulate this as a learning problem and build a benchmark suite containing tasks, data, and evaluation metrics. They explore candidate solutions and show that learning eigen-lengths is feasible from observations of successful and unsuccessful fitting trials. This makes task outcomes the evidence from which useful geometric quantities are learned.

Its findings establish an exploratory starting point rather than a complete general solution. The broader contribution is to make the discovery of a few task-relevant geometric measurements an explicit learning objective, with a benchmark for investigating how those measurements emerge and transfer.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and shows the feasibility of learning crucial object dimensions from successful and failed fitting trials.

title: Towards Learning Geometric Eigen-Lengths Crucial for Fitting Tasks

abstract: Finding dense subgraphs is a fundamental algorithmic tool in data mining, community detection, and clustering. In this problem, the aim is to find an induced subgraph whose edge-to-vertex ratio is maximized. We show how to find a $(2+\epsilon)$ approximation of the directed densest subgraph on randomized streams in a single pass while using $O(n \cdot {\rm poly} \log n)$ memory on $n$-vertex graphs. In contrast, the approach by Bahmani et al. (VLDB 2012) uses $O(\log n)$ passes and by Esfandiari et al. (2015) makes one pass but uses $O(n^{3/2})$ memory; both algorithms also apply to arbitrary-ordered streams. Our techniques extend to Massively Parallel Computation (MPC), yielding quadratic improvement over state-of-the-art by Bahmani et al. (VLDB 2012 and WAW 2014). We empirically show that the quality of our output is essentially the same as that of Bahmani et al. (VLDB 2012) while being $2$ times faster on large graphs, even on non-randomly ordered streams.

paragraphs: Finding dense regions of a graph is useful for data mining, community detection, and clustering. The task seeks a subgraph with a high ratio of edges to vertices. For very large graphs, an algorithm must also manage how much data it stores and how many times it reads the stream of edges.

The paper gives a single-pass algorithm for directed graphs whose edges arrive in randomized order. It achieves a (2 + epsilon) approximation while using memory proportional to the number of vertices times a polylogarithmic factor. The cited earlier approaches either require logarithmically many passes or use memory growing as the number of vertices to the power 3/2; those approaches also support arbitrary stream order.

The techniques extend to massively parallel computation, where the authors report a quadratic improvement over prior work. Empirically, output quality is essentially unchanged from the cited comparison method while execution is twice as fast on large graphs. This experimental advantage also appears on nonrandom streams, although the stated single-pass theoretical result assumes randomized order.
summary.tldr: A single-pass algorithm approximates directed dense subgraphs with near-linear memory on randomized streams and runs twice as fast as the comparison method in experiments.

title: Faster Streaming and Scalable Algorithms for Finding Directed Dense Subgraphs in Large Graphs

abstract: We study the algorithmic problem of sparse mean estimation in the presence of adversarial outliers. Specifically, the algorithm observes a corrupted set of samples from $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\mathbf{I}_d)$, where the unknown mean $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is constrained to be $k$-sparse. A series of prior works has developed efficient algorithms for robust sparse mean estimation with sample complexity $\mathrm{poly}(k,\log d, 1/\epsilon)$ and runtime $d^2 \mathrm{poly}(k,\log d,1/\epsilon)$, where $\epsilon$ is the fraction of contamination. In particular, the fastest runtime of existing algorithms is quadratic in the dimension, which can be prohibitive in high dimensions. This quadratic barrier in the runtime stems from the reliance of these algorithms on the sample covariance matrix, which is of size $d^2$. Our main contribution is an algorithm for robust sparse mean estimation which runs in subquadratic time using $\mathrm{poly}(k,\log d,1/\epsilon)$ samples. Our results build on algorithmic advances in detecting weak correlations, a generalized version of the light-bulb problem by Valiant (2015).
