paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a high-dimensional average when some observations have been maliciously corrupted. Its setting has two important structural assumptions: the clean observations follow a Gaussian distribution with identity covariance, and the unknown mean has only k nonzero coordinates. The goal is to use that sparsity while remaining robust to adversarial outliers.

Previous algorithms already needed relatively few samples, with requirements polynomial in sparsity, the logarithm of dimension, and inverse contamination fraction. Their computational cost, however, included a quadratic dependence on dimension. The abstract identifies the sample covariance matrix as the source of this obstacle: it contains a number of entries proportional to the square of the dimension.

The contribution is an algorithm with subquadratic runtime that retains the stated polynomial sample requirement. It builds on advances in detecting weak correlations. This separates the computational burden from explicitly handling a full covariance matrix, addressing a bottleneck that can make robust estimation expensive in high dimensions.
summary.tldr: A new algorithm breaks the quadratic runtime barrier for robust sparse mean estimation under a Gaussian model while retaining polynomial sample requirements.

title: A Subquadratic Time Algorithm for Robust Sparse Mean Estimation

abstract: This study tackles the challenges of adversarial corruption in model-based reinforcement learning (RL), where the transition dynamics can be corrupted by an adversary. Existing studies on corruption-robust RL mostly focus on the setting of model-free RL, where robust least-square regression is often employed for value function estimation. However, these techniques cannot be directly applied to model-based RL. In this paper, we focus on model-based RL and take the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) approach to learn transition model. Our work encompasses both online and offline settings. In the online setting, we introduce an algorithm called corruption-robust optimistic MLE (CR-OMLE), which leverages total-variation (TV)-based information ratios as uncertainty weights for MLE. We prove that CR-OMLE achieves a regret of $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\sqrt{T} + C)$, where $C$ denotes the cumulative corruption level after $T$ episodes. We also prove a lower bound to show that the additive dependence on $C$ is optimal. We extend our weighting technique to the offline setting, and propose an algorithm named corruption-robust pessimistic MLE (CR-PMLE). Under a uniform coverage condition, CR-PMLE exhibits suboptimality worsened by $\mathcal{O}(C/n)$, nearly matching the lower bound. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work on corruption-robust model-based RL algorithms with provable guarantees.

summary.tldr: Uncertainty-weighted maximum likelihood yields corruption-robust model-based reinforcement learning with provable online and conditional offline guarantees.

title: Towards Robust Model-Based Reinforcement Learning Against Adversarial Corruption

abstract: This paper introduces a framework for post-processing machine learning models so that their predictions satisfy multi-group fairness guarantees. Based on the celebrated notion of multicalibration, we introduce $(s,g,\alpha)-$GMC (Generalized Multi-Dimensional Multicalibration) for multi-dimensional mappings $s$, constraints $g$, and a pre-specified threshold level $\alpha$. We propose associated algorithms to achieve this notion in general settings. This framework is then applied to diverse scenarios encompassing different fairness concerns, including false negative rate control in image segmentation, prediction set conditional uncertainty quantification in hierarchical classification, and de-biased text generation in language models. We conduct numerical studies on several datasets and tasks.

paragraphs: Fair Risk Control studies how to modify a trained model's predictions so that they satisfy fairness guarantees across multiple groups. Its starting point is multicalibration, which connects calibration requirements with group-level behavior. The paper broadens that idea into a framework capable of expressing several kinds of fairness-related risk.

The proposed notion, Generalized Multi-Dimensional Multicalibration, is specified through a multidimensional mapping, a collection of constraints, and a chosen threshold. These ingredients define what is measured, what requirements should hold, and the level at which they should be controlled. The authors also develop algorithms for achieving this generalized calibration notion in broad settings.

Applications include controlling false negatives in image segmentation, quantifying uncertainty conditional on prediction sets in hierarchical classification, and reducing bias in language-model text generation. Numerical studies cover several datasets and tasks. The contribution is a common post-processing framework for these different concerns: its guarantees are tied to the selected mappings, constraints, and threshold, allowing the fairness objective to be expressed for the application.
summary.tldr: Fair Risk Control generalizes multicalibration into a post-processing framework for specified fairness risks across multiple groups.

title: Fair Risk Control: A Generalized Framework for Calibrating Multi-group Fairness Risks

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) show potential as computer agents, enhancing productivity and software accessibility in multi-modal tasks. However, measuring agent performance in sufficiently realistic and complex environments becomes increasingly challenging as: (i) most benchmarks are limited to specific modalities/domains (e.g., text-only, web navigation, Q&A) and (ii) full benchmark evaluations are slow (on order of magnitude of multiple hours/days) given the multi-step sequential nature of tasks. To address these challenges, we introduce Windows Agent Arena: a general environment focusing exclusively on the Windows operating system (OS) where agents can operate freely within a real OS to use the same applications and tools available to human users when performing tasks. We create 150+ diverse tasks across representative domains that require agentic abilities in planning, screen understanding, and tool usage. Our benchmark is scalable and can be seamlessly parallelized for a full benchmark evaluation in as little as $20$ minutes. Our work not only speeds up the development and evaluation cycle of multi-modal agents, but also highlights and analyzes existing shortfalls in the agentic abilities of several multimodal LLMs as agents within the Windows computing environment—with the best achieving only a 19.5% success rate compared to a human success rate of 74.5%.

paragraphs: Computer agents need to plan actions, interpret screens, and use applications across many steps. Evaluating these abilities is difficult when benchmarks cover only narrow activities or take hours to complete. Windows Agent Arena provides a real Windows environment where agents can use the applications and tools available to human users.

The benchmark includes more than 150 tasks across representative domains. These tasks exercise planning, screen understanding, and tool use within the operating system. Its evaluation infrastructure supports parallel execution, allowing a complete benchmark run in as little as 20 minutes. This reduces the turnaround time for testing changes to multimodal agents.

The evaluations also reveal a substantial capability gap. The best tested agent achieves a 19.5% success rate, compared with 74.5% for humans. These figures describe performance on this Windows benchmark and show how much room remains for improvement in the assessed abilities. The contribution combines a broader setting for practical computer tasks with faster evaluation, making weaknesses easier to measure during agent development.
summary.tldr: Windows Agent Arena enables fast evaluation on over 150 real Windows tasks and reveals a large success-rate gap between tested agents and humans.

title: Windows Agent Arena: Evaluating Multi-Modal OS Agents at Scale

abstract: We investigate Learning from Label Proportions (LLP), a partial information setting where examples in a training set are grouped into bags, and only aggregate label values in each bag are available. Despite the partial observability, the goal is still to achieve small regret at the level of individual examples. We give results on the sample complexity of LLP under square loss, showing that our sample complexity is essentially optimal. From an algorithmic viewpoint, we rely on carefully designed variants of Empirical Risk Minimization, and Stochastic Gradient Descent algorithms, combined with ad hoc variance reduction techniques. On one hand, our theoretical results improve in important ways on the existing literature on LLP, specifically in the way the sample complexity depends on the bag size. On the other hand, we validate our algorithmic solutions on several datasets, demonstrating improved empirical performance (better accuracy for less samples) against recent baselines.

paragraphs: Learning from label proportions provides supervision for groups of examples rather than individual examples. Training data is divided into bags, and only aggregate label values are observed. The learner must nevertheless make accurate predictions for individual inputs. This paper studies how many samples are needed to achieve small individual-level regret under square loss.

The authors establish essentially optimal sample-complexity results, improving previous understanding of how the required data depends on bag size. Their algorithms use carefully adapted versions of empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient descent. These are combined with specially designed variance-reduction techniques to handle the partial information supplied by aggregate labels.

Experiments on several datasets show better accuracy with fewer samples than recent baselines. The theoretical and empirical contributions address the same practical question: how effectively can group-level supervision support individual predictions? The findings sharpen the data requirements for this learning setting and show that the proposed procedures can turn those improvements into stronger observed performance under the evaluated conditions.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes nearly optimal data requirements for learning individual predictions from aggregate labels and develops empirically stronger algorithms.

title: Nearly Optimal Sample Complexity for Learning with Label Proportions

abstract: Modern science emerged from reasoning over repeatedly-observed planetary motions. We present Gravity-Bench-v1, an environment-based benchmark that challenges AI agents on tasks that parallel this historical development. Gravity-Bench-v1 evaluates agents on the discovery of physics concealed within a dynamic environment, using rigorous gravitational dynamics simulations. Gravity-Bench includes out-of-distribution cases, i.e. with physics that deviates from the real world, to evaluate true scientific generalization capabilities. Agents must plan to collect data within an experimental budget and must perform a dynamic form of data analysis and reasoning to solve tasks efficiently. Our benchmark admits an open-ended space of solutions. Reference solutions for each task are provided to calibrate AI performance against human expertise. Technically at an upper-undergraduate level, our benchmark proves challenging to baseline AI agents. Gravity-Bench-v1 and planned extensions should help map out AI progress towards scientific discovery capabilities.

Its tasks echo the historical process of inferring gravitational physics from observed motion. The relevant physics is concealed within rigorous gravitational simulations, requiring agents to investigate the environment to solve the tasks.

Agents must plan observations within an experimental budget and adapt their analysis and reasoning as data arrives. The benchmark also includes environments whose physics differs from the real world. These cases are intended to probe scientific generalization beyond familiar physical rules, making the ability to infer behavior from evidence central to the evaluation.

Tasks permit an open-ended range of solutions, and reference solutions provide a comparison with human expertise. Although the technical material is described as upper-undergraduate level, baseline AI agents find the benchmark challenging. The resulting environment combines experimental planning, data analysis, and reasoning in one evaluation, offering a way to track progress toward scientific discovery capabilities through agents’ responses to a controlled but initially unknown physical world.
summary.tldr: Gravity-Bench-v1 tests agents’ ability to discover hidden gravitational physics through budgeted experiments, including environments with unfamiliar physical rules.

title: Gravity-Bench-v1: A Benchmark on Gravitational Physics Discovery for Agents

abstract: In the endeavor to make autonomous robots take actions, task planning is a major challenge that requires translating high-level task descriptions to long-horizon action sequences. Despite recent advances in language model agents, they remain prone to planning errors and limited in their ability to plan ahead. To address these limitations in robotic planning, we advocate a self-refining scheme that iteratively refines a draft plan until an equilibrium is reached. Remarkably, this process can be optimized end-to-end from an analytical perspective without the need to curate additional verifiers or reward models, allowing us to train self-refining planners in a simple supervised learning fashion. Meanwhile, a nested equilibrium sequence modeling procedure is devised for efficient closed-loop planning that incorporates useful feedback from the environment (or an internal world model). Our method is evaluated on the VirtualHome-Env benchmark, showing advanced performance with improved scaling w.r.t. inference-time computation. Code is available at https://github.com/anonymous-icml-2025/equilibrium-planner.

paragraphs: Robotic task planning requires turning a high-level instruction into a long sequence of actions. Language model agents can make planning mistakes and struggle to anticipate later steps. This paper proposes a planner that begins with a draft and repeatedly refines it until it reaches an equilibrium, giving the planning process an explicit mechanism for revising its own output.

A central contribution is showing how to optimize this refinement process end-to-end through an analytical formulation. The planner can be trained with supervised learning without separately curating verifiers or reward models. The authors also introduce a nested equilibrium sequence procedure for closed-loop planning, allowing feedback from the environment or an internal world model to inform the plan.

Evaluation on VirtualHome-Env reports strong performance and improved scaling with computation spent during inference. The findings support iterative refinement as a useful way to spend additional planning computation. The closed-loop component also connects that refinement to feedback, addressing the need to update long action sequences as useful information becomes available.
summary.tldr: An equilibrium-based planner learns to refine long action sequences and incorporate feedback without separately trained verifiers or reward models.

title: Closed-Loop Long-Horizon Robotic Planning via Equilibrium Sequence Modeling

abstract: Current robotic planning methods often rely on predicting multi-frame images with full pixel details. While this fine-grained approach can serve as a generic world model, it introduces two significant challenges for downstream policy learning: substantial computational costs that hinder real-time deployment, and accumulated inaccuracies that can mislead action extraction. Planning with coarse-grained subgoals partially alleviates efficiency issues. However, their forward planning schemes can still result in off-task predictions due to accumulation errors, leading to misalignment with long-term goals. This raises a critical question: Can robotic planning be both efficient and accurate enough for real-time control in long-horizon, multi-stage tasks? To address this, we propose a Backward Planning scheme in Latent space (LBP), which begins by grounding the task into final latent goals, followed by recursively predicting intermediate subgoals closer to the current state. The grounded final goal enables backward subgoal planning to always remain aware of task completion, facilitating on-task prediction along the entire planning horizon. The subgoal-conditioned policy incorporates a learnable token to summarize the subgoal sequences and determines how each subgoal guides action extraction. Through extensive simulation and real-robot long-horizon experiments, we show that LBP outperforms existing fine-grained and forward planning methods, achieving SOTA performance. Project Page: https://lbp-authors.github.io.

paragraphs: Robotic planners that predict detailed future images face substantial computation costs and accumulating prediction errors. Using coarser subgoals can reduce the computational burden, but forward predictions may still drift away from the task’s long-term objective. This paper proposes Latent Backward Planning, or LBP, to organize planning around the desired endpoint.

LBP first grounds the task in final goals represented in a latent space, then recursively predicts intermediate subgoals moving closer to the robot’s current state. The final goal gives the backward planning process a persistent reference for task completion. Planning therefore operates on intermediate representations rather than requiring full pixel detail for every future frame.

The action policy is conditioned on the subgoals and uses a learnable token to summarize their sequence. This token helps determine how individual subgoals guide action extraction. In long-horizon experiments involving both simulation and real robots, LBP outperforms the evaluated fine-grained and forward-planning approaches and achieves state-of-the-art performance. The findings support working backward from a grounded endpoint as a useful approach to multi-stage robotic planning.
summary.tldr: LBP plans backward from latent task goals, improving long-horizon robotic policy learning in simulation and real-robot experiments.

title: Efficient Robotic Policy Learning via Latent Space Backward Planning

abstract: Modern physics simulation often involves multiple functions of interests, and traditional numerical approaches are known to be complex and computationally costly. While machine learning-based surrogate models can offer significant cost reductions, most focus on a single task, such as forward prediction, and typically lack uncertainty quantification — an essential component in many applications. To overcome these limitations, we propose Arbitrarily-Conditioned Multi-Functional Diffusion (ACM-FD), a versatile probabilistic surrogate model for multi-physics emulation. ACM-FD can perform a wide range of tasks within a single framework, including forward prediction, various inverse problems, and simulating data for entire systems or subsets of quantities conditioned on others. Specifically, we extend the standard Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM) for multi-functional generation by modeling noise as Gaussian processes (GP). We propose a random-mask based, zero-regularized denoising loss to achieve flexible and robust conditional generation. We induce a Kronecker product structure in the GP covariance matrix, substantially reducing the computational cost and enabling efficient training and sampling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ACM-FD across several fundamental multi-physics systems.

paragraphs: A physics simulation can involve several interacting quantities and several different questions about them. One task predicts outcomes from known inputs; another works backward to infer unknown quantities. Many learned substitutes for numerical simulation specialize in a single task and lack uncertainty quantification. ACM-FD aims to handle these different questions within one probabilistic model.

The method extends a denoising diffusion model to generate multiple functions together, using Gaussian processes to model the noise. Training uses random masks and a zero-regularized denoising loss to support flexible conditioning. This lets the framework generate an entire system or generate selected quantities while treating others as given, supporting forward prediction and various inverse problems.

To make the approach computationally practical, the authors impose a Kronecker product structure on the Gaussian-process covariance matrix. That structure substantially reduces computational cost during training and sampling. Demonstrations across several fundamental multi-physics systems support the approach’s effectiveness. Its central contribution is combining flexible conditional generation with a probabilistic representation, allowing one surrogate to address multiple simulation tasks.
summary.tldr: ACM-FD uses structured Gaussian-process noise to support multiple conditional physics simulation tasks within one efficient probabilistic diffusion model.

title: Arbitrarily-Conditioned Multi-Functional Diffusion for Multi-Physics Emulation

abstract: We address the problem of interactive text-to-image (T2I) generation, designing a reinforcement learning (RL) agent which iteratively improves a set of generated images for a user through a sequence of prompt expansions. Using human raters, we create a novel dataset of sequential preferences, which we leverage, together with large-scale open-source (non-sequential) datasets. We construct user-preference and user-choice models using an EM strategy and identify varying user preference types. We then leverage a large multimodal language model (LMM) and a value-based RL approach to suggest an adaptive and diverse slate of prompt expansions to the user. Our Preference Adaptive and Sequential Text-to-image Agent (PASTA) extends T2I models with adaptive multi-turn capabilities, fostering collaborative co-creation and addressing uncertainty or underspecification in a user’s intent. We evaluate PASTA using human raters, showing significant improvement compared to baseline methods. We also open-source our sequential rater dataset and simulated user-rater interactions to support future research in user-centric multi-turn T2I systems.

paragraphs: PASTA treats text-to-image generation as an ongoing interaction: a user can refine what they want through successive choices. The agent proposes expansions of the prompt to iteratively improve a set of generated images. This approach addresses situations where the user’s initial request leaves parts of their intent uncertain or unspecified.

To support this process, the researchers collected human judgments in a new dataset of sequential preferences and combined it with large existing datasets of preferences collected outside sequences. They used an expectation-maximization strategy to build models of user preferences and choices, identifying different preference types. This gives the agent a basis for adapting its suggestions to varying users.

The system combines a large multimodal language model with value-based reinforcement learning to suggest a diverse set of prompt expansions. The central idea is to make prompt refinement adaptive across multiple turns, allowing the user and system to collaborate as the images develop. The contribution therefore extends the interaction capabilities of text-to-image models.

Human-rater evaluations showed significant improvement over baseline methods. That finding supports the value of PASTA’s approach in the evaluated interactions. The researchers also released their sequential judgment dataset and simulated user-rater interactions, providing resources for studying how image-generation systems can respond to preferences over multiple turns.
summary.tldr: PASTA adapts prompt-expansion suggestions across multiple turns to help users refine generated images, with human evaluations showing significant improvement over baseline methods.

title: Preference Adaptive and Sequential Text-to-Image Generation

abstract: In this paper, we seek to develop a versatile test-time adaptation (TTA) objective for a variety of tasks — classification and regression across image-, object-, and pixel-level predictions. We achieve this through a self-bootstrapping scheme that optimizes prediction consistency between the test image (as target) and its deteriorated view. The key challenge lies in devising effective augmentations/deteriorations that: i) preserve the image’s geometric information, e.g., object sizes and locations, which is crucial for TTA on object/pixel-level tasks, and ii) provide sufficient learning signals for TTA. To this end, we analyze how common distribution shifts affect the image’s information power across spatial frequencies in the Fourier domain, and reveal that low-frequency components carry high power and masking these components supplies more learning signals, while masking high-frequency components can not. In light of this, we randomly mask the low-frequency amplitude of an image in its Fourier domain for augmentation. Meanwhile, we also augment the image with noise injection to compensate for missing learning signals at high frequencies, by enhancing the information power there. Experiments show that, either independently or as a plug-and-play module, our method achieves superior results across classification, segmentation, and 3D monocular detection tasks with both transformer and CNN models.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we seek to develop a versatile test-time adaptation (TTA) objective for a variety of tasks — classification and regression across image-, object-, and pixel-level predictions. We achieve this through a self-bootstrapping scheme that optimizes prediction consistency between the test image (as target) and its deteriorated view. The key challenge lies in devising effective augmentations/deteriorations that: i) preserve the image’s geometric information, e.g., object sizes and locations, which is crucial for TTA on object/pixel-level tasks, and ii) provide sufficient learning signals for TTA. To this end, we analyze how common distribution shifts affect the image’s information power across spatial frequencies in the Fourier domain, and reveal that low-frequency components carry high power and masking these components supplies more learning signals, while masking high-frequency components can not. In light of this, we randomly mask the low-frequency amplitude of an image in its Fourier domain for augmentation. Meanwhile, we also augment the image with noise injection to compensate for missing learning signals at high frequencies, by enhancing the information power there. Experiments show that, either independently or as a plug-and-play module, our method achieves superior results across classification, segmentation, and 3D monocular detection tasks with both transformer and CNN models.

paragraphs: This paper develops a test-time adaptation objective that works across classification and regression at image, object, and pixel levels. The method uses a test image as a prediction target and trains for consistency with a deteriorated version. The challenge is to create a useful learning signal while preserving geometry such as object locations and sizes.

The authors analyze image information power across spatial frequencies under common distribution shifts. They find that low-frequency components carry substantial power, so masking them produces stronger adaptation signals than masking high-frequency components. Their augmentation therefore randomly masks low-frequency amplitudes in the Fourier representation. They also inject noise to increase high-frequency power and compensate for missing learning signals there.

Experiments cover classification, segmentation, and monocular three-dimensional detection using both transformers and convolutional networks. The method achieves superior reported results both independently and as a module added to other approaches. These findings support a shared adaptation principle across tasks: carefully designed image deterioration can provide learning signals without disrupting the geometric information needed for localized predictions.
summary.tldr: Frequency-based image deterioration and noise injection enable a shared test-time adaptation objective across classification, segmentation, and detection.

title: Self-Bootstrapping for Versatile Test-Time Adaptation

abstract: We study the design of iterative combinatorial auctions (ICAs). The main challenge in this domain is that the bundle space grows exponentially in the number of items. To address this, recent work has proposed machine learning (ML)-based preference elicitation algorithms that aim to elicit only the most critical information from bidders to maximize efficiency. However, while the SOTA ML-based algorithms elicit bidders’ preferences via value queries, ICAs that are used in practice elicit information via demand queries. In this paper, we introduce a novel ML algorithm that provably makes use of the full information from both value and demand queries, and we show via experiments that combining both query types results in significantly better learning performance in practice. Building on these insights, we present MLHCA, a new ML-powered auction that uses value and demand queries. MLHCA significantly outperforms the previous SOTA, reducing efficiency loss by up to a factor 10, with up to 58% fewer queries. Thus, MLHCA achieves large efficiency improvements while also reducing bidders’ cognitive load, establishing a new benchmark for both practicability and efficiency. Our code is available at https://github.com/marketdesignresearch/MLHCA.

title: Prices, Bids, Values: One ML-Powered Combinatorial Auction to Rule Them All

abstract: We propose a novel method, namely Gaussian Smoothing with a Power-Transformed Objective (GS-PowerOpt), that solves global optimization problems in two steps: (1) perform a (exponential) power-$N$ transformation to the not necessarily differentiable objective $f:\mathbb{R}^d\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and get $f_N$, and (2) optimize the Gaussian-smoothed $f_N$ with stochastic approximations. Under mild conditions on $f$, for any $\delta>0$, we prove that with a sufficiently large power $N_\delta$, this method converges to a solution in the $\delta$-neighborhood of $f$’s global optimum point, at the iteration complexity of $O(d^4\varepsilon^{-2})$. If we require that $f$ is differentiable and further assume the Lipschitz condition on $f$ and its gradient, the iteration complexity reduces to $O(d^2\varepsilon^{-2})$, which is significantly faster than the standard homotopy method. In most of the experiments performed, our method produces better solutions than other algorithms that also apply the smoothing technique.

paragraphs: GS-PowerOpt tackles global optimization, where the aim is to find the best solution across an objective’s full search space. It allows objectives that are not necessarily differentiable. The method first applies a power transformation to the objective, then optimizes a Gaussian-smoothed version of that transformed function using stochastic approximations.

The theoretical guarantee depends on conditions on the original objective and on choosing a sufficiently large transformation power. Under those conditions, for any positive distance tolerance delta, the method converges to a solution within delta of a global optimum point. The reported iteration complexity is O(d^4 epsilon^-2), where d is the dimension.

When the objective is differentiable and both it and its gradient satisfy Lipschitz conditions, the complexity improves to O(d^2 epsilon^-2). The authors describe this as significantly faster than the standard homotopy method. Empirically, GS-PowerOpt produces better solutions than other smoothing-based algorithms in most of the reported experiments, supporting the value of transforming the objective before smoothing.
summary.tldr: GS-PowerOpt combines a power transformation with Gaussian smoothing to obtain conditional global-optimization guarantees and improved empirical solutions.

title: Global Optimization with a Power-Transformed Objective and Gaussian Smoothing

abstract: Despite recent successes, test-time scaling$-$dynamically expanding the token budget during inference as needed$-$remains brittle for vision-language models (VLMs). Unstructured visual reasoning chains entangle perception and reasoning, leading to long, disorganized contexts where small perceptual mistakes may cascade into completely wrong answers. Reasoning also requires expensive reinforcement learning with hand-crafted rewards. Here, we introduce SPARC (Separating Perception And Reasoning Circuits), a modular framework that explicitly decouples visual perception from reasoning. Inspired by sequential sensory-to-cognitive processing in the brain, SPARC implements a two-stage pipeline where the model first performs explicit visual search to localize question-relevant regions, then conditions its reasoning on those regions to produce the final answer. This separation enables independent test-time scaling with asymmetric compute allocation (e.g., prioritizing perceptual processing under distribution shift), and supports selective optimization (e.g., improving the perceptual stage alone when it is the bottleneck for end-to-end performance). It also accommodates compressed contexts by running global search at lower image resolutions and allocating high-resolution processing only to selected regions, thereby reducing visual token count and compute. SPARC outperforms monolithic baselines and strong visual-grounding approaches across challenging visual reasoning tasks, such as improving Qwen3VL 4B on the $V^*$ VQA benchmark by 6.7 points and surpassing "thinking with images" by 4.6 points in an OOD setting with a 200$\times$ lower token budget.

These findings support structured, separately scalable perception and reasoning as an effective use of inference computation.
summary.tldr: SPARC separates visual search from reasoning so vision-language models can allocate inference computation more efficiently and improve visual-question answering.

title: SPARC: Separating Perception And Reasoning Circuits for Test-time Scaling of VLMs

abstract: Recommender systems (RS) may suffer from feedback-driven exposure concentration, where repeated engagement optimization collapses exposure onto a narrow set of categories, reducing catalog coverage and degrading long-horizon learning. Existing methods are often post hoc and typically lack principled uncertainty-aware risk estimates for regulating exposure under endogenous feedback. We therefore propose CORAL, a model-agnostic, uncertainty-aware framework that formulates exposure regulation as a constrained sequential decision problem. Specifically, we model self-reinforcing interactions to construct an exposure-saturation state, then derive an upper confidence bound on category-conditioned violation risk from observed history and incorporate it through a state-dependent penalty for adaptive intervention near saturation. Moreover, we provide theoretical guarantees for risk bounds, finite-time recovery, and efficient long-term performance. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets and controlled simulations validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, which aligns with our theoretical analysis. Our code is available at: https://github.com/downw/CORAL.

paragraphs: A recommender that repeatedly optimizes engagement can reinforce its own past choices. Exposure may concentrate on a narrow collection of categories, reducing catalog coverage and weakening learning over longer periods. CORAL treats regulation of this concentration as a sequential decision problem with constraints.

The framework models these self-reinforcing interactions through an exposure-saturation state. From the observed interaction history, it constructs an upper confidence bound on category-specific violation risk. That estimate enters a penalty whose strength depends on the current state, allowing intervention to adapt as exposure approaches saturation. Uncertainty therefore contributes directly to how the system regulates exposure.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees covering risk bounds, recovery within finite time, and efficient long-term performance. Experiments on real-world datasets and controlled simulations support the framework’s effectiveness and agree with the theoretical analysis. Because CORAL is model-agnostic, its contribution is a general mechanism for regulating a recommender’s evolving exposure behavior, with attention to both feedback effects and uncertainty in the available history.
summary.tldr: CORAL uses uncertainty-aware risk estimates to adaptively regulate category exposure as recommendation feedback drives concentration.

title: CORAL: Uncertainty-Aware Regulation of Exposure Concentration in Recommender Systems

abstract: Knowledge augmentation has significantly enhanced the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in knowledge-intensive tasks. However, existing methods typically operate on the simplistic premise that model performance equates with internal knowledge, overlooking the knowledge-confidence gaps that lead to overconfident errors or uncertain truths. To bridge this gap, we propose a novel meta-cognitive framework for reliable knowledge augmentation via differentiated intervention and alignment. Our approach leverages internal cognitive signals to partition the knowledge space into mastered, confused, and missing regions, guiding targeted knowledge expansion. Furthermore, we introduce a cognitive consistency mechanism to synchronize subjective certainty with objective accuracy, ensuring calibrated knowledge boundaries. Extensive experiments demonstrate the our framework consistently outperforms strong baselines, validating its rationality in not only enhancing knowledge capabilities but also fostering cognitive behaviors that better distinguish knowns from unknowns. All codes are available at https://github.com/AI9Stars/Know-More-Know-Clearer.

paragraphs: This paper argues that improving a language model's knowledge requires tracking both correctness and confidence. A model can confidently give a wrong answer or express uncertainty about a correct one. Treating task performance as a complete picture of internal knowledge overlooks these mismatches and can make knowledge augmentation poorly targeted.

The proposed framework uses internal cognitive signals to divide knowledge into mastered, confused, and missing regions. These categories guide differentiated interventions, so knowledge expansion responds to the kind of gap the model exhibits. A cognitive consistency mechanism also aligns the model's subjective certainty with its objective accuracy, aiming to make its knowledge boundaries better calibrated.

Experiments report consistent improvements over strong baselines in both knowledge capability and behaviors that distinguish known information from unknown information. The contribution is therefore a joint approach to learning more and assessing that knowledge more accurately. Its central rationale is that augmentation becomes more useful when the system also learns where confidence is justified and where additional knowledge is needed.
summary.tldr: A metacognitive framework targets different knowledge gaps while aligning a language model's confidence with its accuracy.

title: Know More, Know Clearer: A Meta-Cognitive Framework for Knowledge Augmentation in Large Language Models

abstract: While humans develop core visual skills long before acquiring language, contemporary Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) still rely heavily on linguistic priors to compensate for their fragile visual understanding. We uncovered a crucial fact: state-of-the-art MLLMs consistently fail on basic visual tasks that humans, even 3-year-olds, can solve effortlessly. To systematically investigate this gap, we introduce BabyVision, a benchmark designed to assess core visual abilities independent of linguistic knowledge for MLLMs. BabyVision spans a wide range of tasks, with 388 items divided into 22 subclasses across four key categories. Empirical results and human evaluation reveal that leading MLLMs perform significantly below human baselines. Gemini3-Pro-Preview scores 49.7, falling well behind the average adult score of 94.1. These results show despite excelling in knowledge-heavy evaluations, current MLLMs still lack fundamental visual primitives. Progress in BabyVision represents a step toward human-level visual perception and reasoning capabilities. We also explore solving visual reasoning with generation models by proposing BabyVision-Gen and automatic evaluation toolkit. Code and data are released at https://github.com/UniPat-AI/BabyVision.

paragraphs: BabyVision examines whether multimodal language models can solve basic visual problems without depending heavily on linguistic knowledge. The motivation is a striking gap: models that perform well on knowledge-heavy evaluations still fail visual tasks that humans, including young children, can solve readily. Strong language abilities may therefore conceal weaknesses in visual understanding.

The researchers build a benchmark containing 388 items, organized into 22 subclasses within four broad categories. Its purpose is to isolate core visual abilities from linguistic knowledge. They evaluate leading multimodal models and compare their results with human performance, making the benchmark a direct test of the gap between model and human visual reasoning.

The work also introduces BabyVision-Gen and an automatic evaluation toolkit to explore generation models as another approach to visual reasoning.
summary.tldr: BabyVision reveals a large gap between leading multimodal models and humans on basic visual reasoning tasks.

title: BabyVision: Visual Reasoning Beyond Language

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demand substantial computational and memory resources, creating deployment challenges. Quantization-aware training (QAT) addresses these challenges by reducing model precision while maintaining performance. However, the scaling behavior of QAT, especially at 4-bit precision (W4A4), is not well understood. Existing QAT scaling laws often ignore key factors such as the number of training tokens and quantization granularity, which limits their applicability. This paper proposes a unified scaling law for QAT that models quantization error as a function of model size, training data volume, and quantization group size. Through 268 QAT experiments, we show that quantization error decreases as model size increases, but rises with more training tokens and coarser quantization granularity. To identify the sources of W4A4 quantization error, we decompose it into weight and activation components. Both components follow the overall trend of W4A4 quantization error, but with different sensitivities. Specifically, weight quantization error increases more rapidly with more training tokens. Further analysis shows that the activation quantization error in the FC2 layer, caused by outliers, is the primary bottleneck of W4A4 QAT quantization error. By applying mixed-precision quantization to address this bottleneck, we demonstrate that weight and activation quantization errors can converge to similar levels. Additionally, with more training data, weight quantization error eventually exceeds activation quantization error, suggesting that reducing weight quantization error is also important in such scenarios. These findings offer key insights for improving QAT research and development.

summary.tldr: A scaling study links quantization error to model size, training tokens, and group size, identifying shifting weight and activation bottlenecks.

title: Scaling Law for Quantization-Aware Training

abstract: Zeroth-order optimization has emerged as a promising approach for fine-tuning large language models on domain-specific data, particularly under differential privacy (DP) and memory constraints. While first-order methods have been extensively studied from a privacy perspective, the privacy analysis and algorithmic design for zeroth-order methods remain significantly underexplored. A critical open question concerns hidden-state DP analysis: although convergent privacy bounds are known for first-order methods, it has remained unclear whether similar guarantees can be established for zeroth-order methods. In this work, we provide an affirmative answer by proving a convergent DP bound for zeroth-order optimization. Our analysis generalizes the celebrated privacy amplification-by-iteration framework to the setting of smooth loss functions in zeroth-order optimization. Furthermore, it induces better DP zeroth-order algorithmic designs that are previously unknown to the literature.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization is a promising approach to language-model fine-tuning when memory and differential privacy matter. This paper addresses an unresolved theoretical issue in that setting: whether hidden-state privacy analysis can produce convergent privacy bounds for zeroth-order methods, as it already can for first-order methods. The question concerns the privacy behavior of an iterative optimization process.

The authors prove a convergent differential privacy bound for zeroth-order optimization. Their analysis extends the privacy amplification-by-iteration framework to zeroth-order methods with smooth loss functions. Smoothness is therefore part of the stated setting for the result, and the convergence claim concerns the privacy bound rather than a claim about predictive performance.

The analysis also leads to improved designs for differentially private zeroth-order algorithms that the authors identify as previously unknown. The contribution is both analytical and algorithmic: it establishes a privacy guarantee in an underexplored optimization setting and uses that understanding to guide how privacy-preserving optimization methods are constructed.
summary.tldr: The paper proves a convergent hidden-state privacy bound for zeroth-order optimization with smooth losses and derives improved algorithm designs.

title: Privacy Amplification in Differentially Private Zeroth-Order Optimization with Hidden States

abstract: Despite the remarkable practical success of transformer-based language models, recent work has raised concerns about their ability to perform state tracking. In particular, a growing body of literature has shown this limitation primarily through failures in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, such as length extrapolation. In this work, we shift attention to the in-distribution implications of these limitations. We conduct a large-scale experimental study of the data efficiency of transformers and recurrent neural networks (RNNs) across multiple supervision regimes. We find that the amount of training data required by transformers grows much more rapidly with state-space size and sequence length than for RNNs. Furthermore, we analyze the extent to which learned state-tracking mechanisms are shared across different sequence lengths. We show that transformers exhibit negligible or even detrimental weight sharing across lengths, indicating that they learn length-specific solutions in isolation. In contrast, recurrent models exhibit effective amortized learning by sharing weights across lengths, allowing data from one sequence length to improve performance on others. Together, these results demonstrate that state tracking remains a fundamental challenge for transformers, even when training and evaluation distributions match.

paragraphs: State tracking requires a sequence model to maintain the information needed as a sequence unfolds. Earlier concerns about Transformers often centered on generalizing beyond the training distribution, such as processing longer sequences. This paper examines whether difficulties also arise when training and evaluation distributions match.

A large-scale experimental study compares the data efficiency of Transformers and recurrent neural networks under multiple supervision regimes. As state spaces and sequence lengths grow, the training data required by Transformers increases much more rapidly. The authors also examine whether learning at one sequence length supports performance at another, probing how broadly the learned tracking mechanism is reused.

In the evaluated settings, Transformers show negligible or even detrimental sharing across lengths, consistent with learning separate length-specific solutions. Recurrent models show effective shared learning: data at one length can help at others. These findings place the challenge within ordinary in-distribution learning as well as extrapolation. They indicate that matching the evaluation distribution does not remove the observed differences in state-tracking data efficiency.
summary.tldr: Experiments find that Transformers learn state tracking less data-efficiently than recurrent models, even when training and evaluation distributions match.

title: On the "Induction Bias" in Sequence Models

abstract: The rapid advancement of AI-driven video generation has transformed content creation, while simultaneously increasing the risk of misinformation through localized manipulations in long-form videos. Existing video forensic methods predominantly operate on short, independent clips, and thus fail to capture realistic scenarios where AI-generated content is sparsely embedded within otherwise authentic footage. To bridge this gap, we formulate the task of Temporal AI-Generated Segment Localization and Explanation, which targets authenticity detection, temporal localization, and interpretable analysis of manipulated segments in untrimmed long videos. We further introduce TASLE, a large-scale benchmark comprising 12,472 untrimmed videos with diverse manipulation patterns and rich annotation signals, including temporal boundaries, authenticity labels, and segment-level rationales. In addition, we propose MSLoc, a coarse-to-fine forensic baseline that combines a boundary-sensitive proposal generation module for efficient long-video scanning with an MLLM-based refinement module for precise boundary localization and interpretable reasoning. Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed baseline, highlighting the importance of segment-level explainable forensics for long-form AI-generated video analysis. Dataset and code will be made publicly available.

Existing video forensic methods predominantly operate on short, independent clips, and thus fail to capture realistic scenarios where AI-generated content is sparsely embedded within otherwise authentic footage. To bridge this gap, we formulate the task of Temporal AI-Generated Segment Localization and Explanation, which targets authenticity detection, temporal localization, and interpretable analysis of manipulated segments in untrimmed long videos. We further introduce TASLE, a large-scale benchmark comprising 12,472 untrimmed videos with diverse manipulation patterns and rich annotation signals, including temporal boundaries, authenticity labels, and segment-level rationales. In addition, we propose MSLoc, a coarse-to-fine forensic baseline that combines a boundary-sensitive proposal generation module for efficient long-video scanning with an MLLM-based refinement module for precise boundary localization and interpretable reasoning. Experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed baseline, highlighting the importance of segment-level explainable forensics for long-form AI-generated video analysis. Dataset and code will be made publicly available.

paragraphs: A long video can be mostly authentic while containing a small manipulated segment. Analyzing isolated short clips does not fully capture this setting. The paper defines a task that asks a forensic system to determine authenticity, locate manipulated intervals in time, and explain the evidence for those judgments within an untrimmed video.

To support this task, the authors introduce TASLE, a benchmark containing 12,472 long, untrimmed videos with varied manipulation patterns. Its annotations include authenticity labels, temporal boundaries, and explanations for individual segments. This combination supports evaluation of where a manipulation occurs as well as the reasoning attached to its detection.

The proposed baseline, MSLoc, first scans the video with a boundary-sensitive proposal module. A multimodal large language model then refines the proposed boundaries and supplies interpretable reasoning. This coarse-to-fine organization combines efficient scanning with closer inspection of candidate segments. The experiments support the baseline’s effectiveness and the value of evaluating localized, explainable forensics in long videos. The abstract states that the dataset and code will be released.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and coarse-to-fine system for locating and explaining AI-manipulated segments within otherwise authentic long videos.

title: Explainable Forensics of Manipulated Segments in Untrimmed Long Videos

abstract: Generative models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for AI planning, yet their performance remains constrained by the training data distribution. One approach is to improve generated solutions during inference by scaling test-time compute. A more efficient alternative is to optimize the inference process itself. In this paper, we show that a modified version of a classical Open-Closed List (OCL) search provides just such an efficient inference procedure. Our algorithm synergizes two learned components: a generative model that performs fast rollouts from intermediate states and a heuristic model that prioritizes among candidate reasoning paths. Key contributions include novel exploration control mechanisms and integration of learned models within the OCL framework. Across multiple combinatorial planning domains, our approach outperforms both neurosymbolic search baselines and classical solvers in computational efficiency and solution quality.

This paper studies how to organize that computation more effectively through a modified version of classical Open-Closed List search.

A generative model quickly produces continuations from intermediate states, while a heuristic model prioritizes candidate reasoning paths. The search framework coordinates these components, and new exploration controls govern how it investigates alternatives. This gives the learned generator a structured procedure for deciding where further reasoning effort should go.

summary.tldr: A modified Open-Closed List search combines learned rollouts and heuristics to improve generative planning efficiency and solution quality.

title: Efficient Test-time Inference for Generative Planning Models with OCL Search

abstract: We introduce vector diffusion wavelets (VDWs), a novel family of wavelets inspired by the vector diffusion maps algorithm that was introduced to analyze data lying in the tangent bundle of a Riemannian manifold. We show that these wavelets may be effectively incorporated into a family of geometric graph neural networks, which we refer to as VDW-GNNs. We demonstrate that such networks are effective on synthetic point cloud data, as well as on real-world data derived from wind field and neural activity measurements. Theoretically, we prove that these new wavelets have desirable frame theoretic properties, similar to traditional diffusion wavelets. Additionally, we prove that these wavelets have useful symmetries with respect to rotations and translations.

This paper introduces vector diffusion wavelets, inspired by vector diffusion maps, to analyze that kind of information. Wavelets provide representations across scales, and the proposed construction is designed for vector-valued geometric data.

The authors incorporate these wavelets into geometric graph neural networks called VDW-GNNs. They also prove frame-theoretic properties similar to those of traditional diffusion wavelets, providing a mathematical foundation for the representation. Additional results establish useful symmetries under rotations and translations, connecting the construction to transformations of the underlying geometry.

These evaluations connect the wavelet construction to practical learning on different geometric datasets. The contribution therefore combines a new mathematical representation, theoretical properties governing its behavior, and evidence that it can serve as a useful component in graph neural networks.
summary.tldr: Vector diffusion wavelets provide a theoretically grounded representation for geometric graph networks, with applications to point clouds, wind fields, and neural activity.

title: VDW-GNNs: Vector diffusion wavelets for geometric graph neural networks

abstract: Generative modeling provides a powerful framework for learning data distributions. These models initially relied on probabilistic methods such as Gaussian Processes (GP) for uncertainty-aware predictions and shifted towards larger trainable models to learn more complex distributions. In this work, we introduce Random Process (RP) Flow, a Flow Matching-based framework that represents the vector field as a neural implicit function. Unlike modern generative methods, our setting involves a single observed field, from which only sparse measurements are available. RP Flow uses Random Fourier Features to learn an implicit signal representation that can be queried at any arbitrary location from a limited set of observations, while encoding uncertainty through ensemble sampling. We propose constructing a Bayesian posterior by GP regression in the source space to generate high-quality samples. Our empirical results demonstrate that this framework generates realistic samples along with calibrated uncertainty estimates, even under challenging conditions such as high frequency, high sparsity, or high dimensionality. These findings position RP Flow as a milestone towards generative models for reconstruction tasks where data is scarce and uncertainty must remain traceable.

paragraphs: Random Process Flow tackles reconstruction when only sparse measurements of a single observed field are available. The aim is to generate plausible fields while retaining an account of uncertainty. This setting places scarce observations at the center of the modeling problem, rather than relying on many observed fields.

The framework uses flow matching with a vector field represented as a neural implicit function. Random Fourier Features help learn a signal representation that can be queried at arbitrary locations, so the representation is not restricted to the measured points. Ensemble sampling expresses uncertainty, and Gaussian process regression in the source space constructs a Bayesian posterior for generating samples.

Empirical results show realistic samples and calibrated uncertainty estimates under challenging conditions, including high-frequency signals, sparse observations, and high-dimensional settings. These findings support the combination of implicit representations, flow matching, and Gaussian process inference for reconstruction from limited data. The contribution is particularly concerned with making plausible reconstructions and their uncertainty available together from the same sparse observations.
summary.tldr: RP Flow combines flow matching and Gaussian process inference to reconstruct sparsely observed fields with calibrated uncertainty.

title: Random Process Flow Matching: Generative Implicit Representations of Multivariate Random Fields

abstract: E-commerce short videos represent a high-revenue segment of the online video industry characterized by a goal-driven format and dense multi-modal signals. Current models often struggle with these videos because existing benchmarks focus primarily on general-purpose tasks and neglect the reasoning of commercial intent. In this work, we first propose a multi-modal information density assessment framework to quantify the complexity of this domain. Our evaluation reveals that e-commerce content exhibits substantially higher density across visual, audio, and textual modalities compared to mainstream datasets, establishing a more challenging frontier for video understanding. To address this gap, we introduce E-commerce Video Ads Benchmark, which is the first benchmark specifically designed for e-commerce short video understanding. We curated 3,961 high-quality videos from Taobao covering a wide range of product categories and used a multi-agent system to generate 19,785 open-ended Q&A pairs. These questions are organized into Perception and Cognition and Reasoning, which consist of five distinct tasks. Finally, we develop E-VAds-R1, an RL-based reasoning model featuring a multi-grained reward design called MG-GRPO. This strategy provides smooth guidance for early exploration while creating a non-linear incentive for expert-level precision. Experimental results demonstrate that E-VAds-R1 achieves a 109.2% performance gain in commercial intent reasoning with only a few hundred training samples. Data is available at https://github.com/TaobaoTmall-AlgorithmProducts/E-VAds_Benchmark.

summary.tldr: E-VAds introduces a benchmark for dense e-commerce videos and a reinforcement-learning model that improves commercial-intent reasoning with limited training data.

title: E-VAds: An E-commerce Short Videos Understanding Benchmark for MLLMs

abstract: Functional brain network analysis plays an important role in understanding and diagnosing psychiatric disorders. However, current methods struggle with subject variations, impairing the model’s generalization ability to the test set. To address this issue, we propose the Subject Invariance-aware Inverse Graph Contrastive Learning (SI-IGCL) model, which adopts a two-stage paradigm with self-supervised subject-invariant pre-training followed by supervised fine-tuning for identification. During the pre-training phase, we construct an inverse contrastive objective that reshapes the embedding space by repelling intra-subject and attracting inter-subject embeddings to learn subject-invariant representations, with an auxiliary correction term to avoid early optimization plateaus. Meanwhile, we incorporate a structure-preserving reconstruction constraint to preserve discriminative information. Moreover, a Hierarchical Topology Enhanced Transformer (HTET) module is designed to enable multi-level modeling of subject-invariant functional patterns. During the fine-tuning phase, a supervised classifier is integrated to perform psychiatric disorder classification. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms all state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SI-IGCL.

paragraphs: Functional brain networks vary between individuals, and that variation can interfere with learning patterns useful for psychiatric disorder identification. SI-IGCL addresses this with two stages: self-supervised pretraining to reduce dependence on subject identity, followed by supervised fine-tuning for disorder classification.

Its inverse contrastive objective pushes apart embeddings from the same subject and pulls together embeddings from different subjects. This reshapes the representation space toward patterns shared across individuals. An auxiliary correction term helps prevent early optimization plateaus, while a reconstruction constraint preserves network structure and discriminative information. These components balance removing subject-specific variation with retaining useful classification signals.

A Hierarchical Topology Enhanced Transformer models shared functional patterns at multiple structural levels. The final supervised stage adds a classifier to those learned representations. The authors report that the method outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in their experiments. The contribution is a coordinated representation-learning strategy that explicitly addresses subject variation while preserving brain-network information needed for the downstream identification task.
summary.tldr: SI-IGCL learns brain-network representations that reduce subject-specific variation while preserving information useful for psychiatric disorder classification.

title: SI-IGCL: Subject Invariance-aware Inverse Graph Contrastive Learning for Psychiatric Disorder Identification

abstract: We study a setting where the goal is to learn a target function f(x) with respect to a target distribution D(x), but training is done on i.i.d. samples from a different training distribution D’(x), labeled by the true target f(x). Such a distribution shift (here in the form of covariate shift) is usually viewed negatively, as hurting or making learning harder, and the traditional distribution shift literature is mostly concerned with limiting or avoiding this negative effect. In contrast, we argue that with a well-chosen D’(x), the shift can be positive and make learning easier – a perspective called Positive Distribution Shift (PDS). Such a perspective is central to contemporary machine learning, where much of the innovation is in finding good training distributions D’(x), rather than changing the training algorithm. We further argue that the benefit is often computational rather than statistical, and that PDS allows computationally hard problems to become tractable even using standard gradient-based training. We formalize different variants of PDS, show how certain hard classes are easily learnable under PDS, and make connections with membership query learning.

paragraphs: Distribution shift is usually treated as a problem: training examples differ from the population where predictions will be used. This paper studies when choosing a different training distribution can instead make learning easier. Labels still come from the same target function, so the intervention changes which inputs are sampled rather than what counts as correct.

The authors formalize several versions of Positive Distribution Shift and show that selected computationally hard function classes become learnable under suitable training distributions. Standard gradient-based training can benefit from that change. The framework also connects to membership-query learning, where a learner can obtain labels for chosen inputs.

The central claim is that training-data design can improve computational tractability, not merely sample efficiency. This provides a theoretical perspective on progress driven by better training distributions. The contribution does not imply that arbitrary shifts help; the advantage depends on choosing a distribution that exposes useful structure for the particular target-learning problem.
summary.tldr: Positive Distribution Shift formalizes how choosing a different labeled training distribution can make otherwise hard learning problems tractable.

title: Positive Distribution Shift as a Framework for Understanding Tractable Learning

abstract: Feature-importance methods show promise for transforming machine learning (ML) models from predictive engines into tools for scientific discovery. However, expressive models can be unstable due to data sampling and algorithmic stochasticity, leading to inaccurate variable importance estimates, undermining their utility in critical biomedical applications. While ensembling offers a remedy, the choice between explaining a single ensemble model or aggregating individual model explanations is non-trivial due to the non-linearity of importance measures, and remains largely understudied. Our theoretical analysis, developed under assumptions accommodating complex state-of-the-art ML models, reveals that this choice is governed by a trade-off involving the model’s excess risk. In contrast to prior literature, we show that ensembling at the model level provides more accurate variable-importance estimates, particularly for expressive models, by reducing this leading error term. We validate these findings on classical benchmarks and a large-scale proteomic study from the UK Biobank.

paragraphs: Feature importance is often used to turn predictions into scientific insight about which variables matter. But flexible models can change substantially with the sampled data or randomness in training, making their importance estimates unstable. This paper examines how combining multiple models can improve those estimates, with particular motivation from biomedical applications.

There are two natural procedures: combine the models and explain the resulting ensemble, or explain each model separately and combine those explanations. Because importance measures can be nonlinear, these operations need not produce the same answer. The authors analyze the choice under assumptions that accommodate complex models and identify a trade-off involving excess predictive risk.

Their analysis favors combining models before computing importance, especially for expressive models, because this reduces a leading source of estimation error. Experiments on established benchmarks and a large UK Biobank proteomics study support the theoretical findings. The practical message is that the stage at which averaging occurs can affect the accuracy of scientific variable-importance estimates, even when both procedures use an ensemble.
summary.tldr: Combining models before explaining them can improve feature-importance accuracy by reducing a leading error term associated with excess predictive risk.

title: Aggregate Models, Not Explanations: Improving Feature Importance Estimation

abstract: This paper presents STARCaster, an identity-aware spatio-temporal video diffusion model that addresses both speech-driven portrait animation and dynamic viewpoint control, given an identity embedding or reference image, within a unified framework. Existing 2D speech-to-video diffusion models depend heavily on reference guidance, leading to limited motion diversity. At the same time, 3D-aware animation typically relies on inversion through pretrained tri-plane generators, which often leads to imperfect reconstructions and identity drift. We rethink reference- and geometry-based paradigms in two ways. First, we deviate from strict reference conditioning at pretraining by introducing softer identity constraints. Second, we address 3D awareness implicitly within the 2D video domain by leveraging the inherent multi-view nature of video data. STARCaster adopts a compositional approach progressing from ID-aware motion modeling, to audio-visual synchronization via lip reading-based supervision, and finally to novel view animation through temporal-to-spatial adaptation. To overcome the scarcity of 4D audio-visual data, we propose a decoupled learning approach in which view consistency and temporal coherence are trained independently. Comprehensive evaluations demonstrate that STARCaster generalizes effectively across tasks and identities, consistently surpassing prior approaches in different benchmarks.

paragraphs: STARCaster generates talking portraits with speech-driven animation and changing viewpoints, conditioned on an identity embedding or reference image. The paper addresses two obstacles: strong dependence on reference images can restrict motion variety, while reconstruction through pretrained 3D generators can introduce reconstruction errors and changes in identity.

The method uses softer identity constraints during pretraining and learns implicit 3D awareness from the multiple views naturally present in video. Its training approach progresses from identity-aware motion modeling to audio-visual synchronization using lip-reading supervision, then to animation from new viewpoints through temporal-to-spatial adaptation. This combines several capabilities within one video-diffusion framework.

Because suitable 4D audio-visual data are scarce, view consistency and temporal coherence are trained independently. This decoupling addresses the data constraint while supporting both changes across viewpoints and continuity over time. Evaluations report effective generalization across identities and tasks, with consistent improvements over prior approaches on different benchmarks. The contribution is a unified approach to identity, speech synchronization, and viewpoint control that learns these properties through complementary training stages.
summary.tldr: STARCaster combines identity-aware motion, speech synchronization, and viewpoint control in a unified talking-portrait video model.

title: STARCaster: Spatio-Temporal AutoRegressive Video Diffusion for Identity- and View-Aware Talking Portraits

abstract: We introduce SeisMark, a large-scale open benchmark designed to bridge the gap between verifiable ground truth and realistic texture in 3D seismic fault detection. Using a novel pipeline merging procedural geology with diffusion-based synthesis, we produce domain-realistic (survey-specific) textured volumes that expose significant brittleness in existing models masked by simplified physics data. Experiments demonstrate that SeisMark acts as a rigorous discriminator, distinguishing robust modern architecture from legacy model that suffers performance collapse under realistic domain shifts. We release this benchmark to the community to serve as a verifiable standard for developing trustworthy, deployment-ready AI for safety-critical subsurface applications.

paragraphs: Evaluating three-dimensional seismic fault detection requires both trustworthy labels and data that resemble real surveys. SeisMark is an open benchmark designed to bring these properties together. Its motivation is that simplified physics data can conceal weaknesses that become visible when models encounter more realistic seismic textures.

The benchmark is generated through a pipeline combining procedural geology with diffusion-based synthesis. Procedural structure supplies verifiable ground truth, while synthesis produces textured volumes tailored to survey-specific domains. This creates an evaluation setting that connects known geological structure with realistic appearance, allowing robustness to domain changes to be examined more directly.

The reported experiments show that SeisMark distinguishes a robust modern architecture from a legacy model whose performance collapses under realistic domain shifts. The benchmark therefore contributes an evaluation resource that exposes brittleness hidden by simpler data. Its release is intended to support development of trustworthy models for safety-critical subsurface applications, with verifiable labels and realistic texture serving as complementary requirements for assessing progress.
summary.tldr: SeisMark combines verifiable geology with realistic seismic textures to expose fault-detection failures under domain shifts.

title: SeisMark: A Large-Scale Open Benchmark for Robust 3D Seismic Fault Detection

abstract: Learning conditional distributions $\pi^\star(\cdot|x)$ is a central problem in machine learning, which is typically approached via supervised methods with paired data $(x,y) \sim \pi^\star$. However, acquiring paired data samples is often challenging, especially in problems such as domain translation. This necessitates the development of semi-supervised models that utilize both limited paired data and additional unpaired i.i.d. samples $x \sim \pi^\star_x$ and $y \sim \pi^\star_y$ from the marginal distributions. The usage of such combined data is complex and often relies on heuristic approaches. To tackle this issue, we propose a new learning paradigm that integrates both paired and unpaired data seamlessly using data likelihood maximization techniques. We demonstrate that our approach also connects intriguingly with inverse entropic optimal transport (OT). This finding allows us to apply recent advances in computational OT to establish an end-to-end learning algorithm to get $\pi^\star(\cdot|x)$. In addition, we derive the universal approximation property, demonstrating that our approach can theoretically recover true conditional distributions with arbitrarily small error. Finally, we demonstrate through empirical tests that our method effectively learns conditional distributions using paired and unpaired data simultaneously.

paragraphs: Learning a conditional distribution means learning which outputs are plausible for a given input. Paired examples directly reveal those relationships, but they can be difficult to obtain in applications such as domain translation. This paper considers combining limited pairs with additional independent samples from the input and output marginal distributions.

The proposed learning paradigm brings both types of data into a data-likelihood maximization approach. The authors establish a connection to inverse entropic optimal transport, allowing recent computational transport methods to support an end-to-end learning algorithm. The significance is a principled route for combining information about individual input-output relationships with information about the two populations separately.

The paper also derives a universal approximation property: its approach can theoretically represent the true conditional distribution with arbitrarily small error. This is an approximation result, rather than a promise that every finite training run recovers the truth. Empirical tests demonstrate effective simultaneous use of paired and unpaired data. Together, these contributions connect a practical semi-supervised learning problem to both an optimization framework and a representational guarantee.
summary.tldr: A likelihood-based connection to inverse entropic optimal transport enables conditional-distribution learning from paired and unpaired data together.

title: Inverse Entropic Optimal Transport Solves Semi-supervised Learning via Data Likelihood Maximization

abstract: Learning from demonstrations in embodied control is often cast as behavioral cloning, and recent diffusion or flow-matching policies improve this paradigm by modeling multi-modal expert actions. Yet these methods remain offline supervised learners: the policy is trained only on expert states and receives no corrective signal on the states it actually visits. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a natural remedy, but standard OPD assumes a strong fixed teacher, which is unavailable in demonstration-only control. We propose FA-OPD, an adversarial dual on-policy distillation method in which a Flow Matching (FM) teacher is learned from demonstrations and co-trained with a lightweight MLP student. The teacher provides two complementary signals on student rollouts. The reward channel learns an expert-likeness objective over state-action pairs and drives online exploration through long-horizon policy optimization. The action channel supplies dense local targets at student-visited states, stabilizing exploitation. FA-OPD couples them so that reward distillation enables generalization beyond point-wise demonstrations, while action distillation keeps exploration anchored near expert-like behavior.
