originalAbstract: Learning from demonstrations in embodied control is often cast as behavioral cloning, and recent diffusion or flow-matching policies improve this paradigm by modeling multi-modal expert actions. Yet these methods remain offline supervised learners: the policy is trained only on expert states and receives no corrective signal on the states it actually visits. On-policy distillation (OPD) offers a natural remedy, but standard OPD assumes a strong fixed teacher, which is unavailable in demonstration-only control. We propose FA-OPD, an adversarial dual on-policy distillation method in which a Flow Matching (FM) teacher is learned from demonstrations and co-trained with a lightweight MLP student. The teacher provides two complementary signals on student rollouts. The reward channel learns an expert-likeness objective over state-action pairs and drives online exploration through long-horizon policy optimization. The action channel supplies dense local targets at student-visited states, stabilizing exploitation. FA-OPD couples them so that reward distillation enables generalization beyond point-wise demonstrations, while action distillation keeps exploration anchored near expert-like behavior. Across six robot navigation, manipulation, and locomotion benchmarks, FA-OPD beats strong baselines and shows much stronger robustness under noisy or limited demonstrations. Source code: https://github.com/vanzll/FA-OPD.

paragraphs: A control policy trained only on expert demonstrations receives supervision at expert states, even though its own actions may take it elsewhere. Learning from a teacher on those newly visited states could help, but demonstration-only settings do not supply a ready-made strong teacher. FA-OPD addresses this by jointly training a flow-matching teacher and a lightweight student.

The teacher supplies two types of feedback during student rollouts. A reward channel assesses how expert-like state-action pairs are and supports exploration through optimization over longer horizons. An action channel provides local action targets at the states the student actually encounters. These signals connect broader behavioral improvement with immediate corrective guidance.

Their coupling is central: reward feedback supports generalization beyond individual demonstrated actions, while action feedback helps keep exploration close to expert-like behavior. Across six benchmarks covering robot navigation, manipulation, and locomotion, the method outperforms strong baselines and shows substantially better robustness when demonstrations are noisy or limited. The results support learning the teacher and student together as a practical response to missing on-policy supervision.
summary.tldr: FA-OPD jointly trains a teacher and student, combining reward and action feedback on student rollouts to improve embodied control.

title: Adversarial Dual On-Policy Distillation from Expressive Teacher

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can propose natural-language rules, circumventing the reliance on a predefined predicate space in traditional rule learning. However, existing LLM-based methods often neglect the global interactions among rules, and the potential of using fine-grained rule importance scores to calibrate neuro-symbolic reasoning remains underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce RLIE, a framework that integrates LLMs with probabilistic modeling to learn weighted rule sets in four stages: (1) Rule generation: proposing and filtering candidate rules via LLMs; (2) Logistic regression: learning sparse, calibrated weights for global rule selection; (3) Iterative refinement: revising the rule set with error-driven hard examples; and (4) Evaluation: validating the learned system via comparative inference paradigms. Across multiple real-world datasets and LLM backbones, our learned weighted rules achieve superior stability and accuracy, whereas rule-injection prompting yields mixed results and often degrades performance. These results suggest LLMs excel at semantic rule discovery but are less reliable at controlled probabilistic aggregation. Our findings highlight both the promise and the limits of LLMs for inductive reasoning, motivating a principled integration with classic probabilistic rule combination for reliable neuro-symbolic reasoning.

paragraphs: Language models can propose rules in ordinary language, avoiding the need to define every possible predicate beforehand. But a collection of plausible rules still needs a reliable way to combine their effects. RLIE addresses the interactions among rules by pairing language-model rule discovery with a probabilistic model that learns their relative importance.

The framework first generates and filters candidate rules. Logistic regression then learns sparse, calibrated weights for selecting and combining them globally. An iterative refinement stage revisits the rules using difficult examples identified through errors. Finally, the authors compare different inference approaches to evaluate how the learned rules work as a complete reasoning system.

Across multiple real-world datasets and model backbones, the weighted rules deliver better accuracy and stability. Simply inserting rules into prompts produces mixed results and often hurts performance. The authors interpret this as evidence that language models are effective semantic rule discoverers but less reliable probabilistic aggregators, supporting a division of responsibilities between language-based discovery and explicit statistical combination.
summary.tldr: RLIE combines language-model rule discovery with learned probabilistic weights, improving accuracy and stability over less controlled rule use.

title: RLIE: Rule Generation with Logistic Regression, Iterative Refinement, and Evaluation for Large Language Models

abstract: Offline meta reinforcement learning (RL) enables agents to learn a unified policy from multi-task offline data to support generalization in out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. Recent approaches in single-agent RL tackle this by learning an efficient task representation to distinguish between tasks, showing promising adaptation ability. However, when extended to multi-agent settings, these methods struggle with decentralized task identification due to limited global information, and suffer from inefficient knowledge transfer in the absence of role information. To address this, we propose D$^2$TR, a novel context-based meta RL framework with efficient decentralized and disentangled task-role identification. Specifically, D$^2$TR first introduces mutual information knowledge distillation to align decentralized task representations with centralized task representations inferred from global trajectories, enabling efficient decentralized team-centric information identification. Next, D$^2$TR leverages a large language model to assign semantic roles to trajectories in offline data, and achieves effective individual-centric information inference by learning decentralized role representations. Extensive experiments conducted on commonly used multi-agent environments, including CN, SMAC, and SMACv2, demonstrate that D$^2$TR exhibits strong generalization performance to unseen tasks, outperforming prior multi-agent multi-task and context-based meta RL baselines.

paragraphs: Offline meta reinforcement learning uses recorded experience from multiple tasks to train a policy that can generalize to unfamiliar tasks. Extending this idea to teams introduces two difficulties. An individual agent has limited access to global information, making the team’s task harder to identify, and knowledge transfer can suffer when the agent’s role is not represented.

D²TR learns separate representations for the shared task and individual roles. For task identification, mutual-information knowledge distillation aligns representations available to decentralized agents with centralized representations inferred from global trajectories. This provides a training route for transferring team-level information into representations that agents can infer using their more limited observations.

For role identification, a large language model assigns semantic roles to trajectories in the offline dataset. Agents then learn decentralized role representations from that information. Across CN, SMAC, and SMACv2, D²TR generalizes strongly to unseen tasks and outperforms the evaluated multi-task and context-based meta reinforcement learning baselines. The results support treating team context and individual responsibility as distinct sources of information for transfer.
summary.tldr: D²TR separates team-task and individual-role representations to improve decentralized agents’ generalization from offline experience.

title: Decentralized and Disentangled Task–Role Representation Learning for Generalizable Offline Multi-Agent Meta Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Multi-modal image generation, particularly subject-driven customization, has garnered growing attention in recent years. Despite the rapid advancement of generative models, their evaluation remains largely lagging. Existing methods, whether embedding-based or Multi-modal Large Language Model (MLLM)-based, evaluate alignment with each modal condition in isolation, which contradicts the simultaneous condition alignment objective of multi-modal image generation, leading to poor consistency with human judgments. To address this challenge, we propose UFO, the first UniFied framework for Omni-condition alignment simultaneous evaluation. Specifically, UFO introduces a novel Atomized Chain-of-Evaluation paradigm, i.e., it first decomposes omni-condition alignment into a sequential chain of fine-grained, disentangled Atomic Evaluation Units (AEUs), categorizes them into distinct modality-relevance classes, and then employs general or dedicated functional calls for accurate verification of different AEU types. Experimental results demonstrate that UFO achieves the highest correlation with human evaluation preferences, delivering an average improvement of 15.25%. Furthermore, we present UFO-Bench, a dedicated benchmark designed to holistically evaluate the performance of existing customization models under the diverse mutual interactions of textual and visual conditions.

paragraphs: An image customized from text and visual references must satisfy those conditions together. The paper argues that evaluating each condition independently misses their interactions and can disagree with human judgments. UFO addresses this evaluation problem by organizing checks around simultaneous alignment with all relevant conditions.

Its Atomized Chain-of-Evaluation breaks the overall alignment question into a sequence of fine-grained, disentangled units. Each unit is assigned to a modality-relevance category and checked using either a general or a dedicated function. This creates a structured verification process in which different requirements can receive appropriate checks while contributing to the combined assessment.

The authors report the highest correlation with human evaluation preferences in their experiments, with an average improvement of 15.25%. They also introduce UFO-Bench to assess customization models under diverse interactions between textual and visual conditions. Together, the framework and benchmark make joint satisfaction of conditions a central evaluation target. The stated results support decomposed, specialized checking as a way to bring automated judgments closer to human preferences.
summary.tldr: UFO evaluates interacting text and visual conditions through structured atomic checks, improving agreement with human judgments in the reported experiments.

title: UFO: Chain-of-Evaluation for Omni-Condition Alignment in Multi-Modal Image Generation

abstract: Recent advances in reinforcement learning (RL) using numerical rewards have significantly enhanced the complex reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, we identify three fundamental limitations of purely numerical feedback: performance plateaus, ineffective spontaneous self-reflection, and persistent failures. We show that plateaued RL models can successfully refine failed solutions when given natural language critiques. Motivated by this, we propose Critique-GRPO, an online RL framework that integrates both natural language and numerical feedback for policy optimization. This approach enables LLMs to learn simultaneously from initial responses and critique-guided refinements, effectively internalizing the exploration benefits of both stages. Extensive experiments show that Critique-GRPO outperforms all compared supervised and RL-based fine-tuning methods, achieving average Pass@1 improvements of approximately +15.0-21.6% on various Qwen models and +7.3% on Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct across eight challenging reasoning tasks. Notably, Critique-GRPO facilitates effective self-improvement through self-critiquing, achieving substantial gains over GRPO, e.g., a +16.7% Pass@1 improvement on AIME 2024. The code and models are released at: https://github.com/zhangxy-2019/critique-GRPO

paragraphs: Numerical rewards tell a language model how well an answer performed, but they do not explain how to repair it. The authors identify performance plateaus, ineffective spontaneous reflection, and recurring failures in training that relies only on these rewards. They also show that models whose reinforcement learning has plateaued can still improve failed solutions when given critiques in natural language.

Critique-GRPO turns that observation into an online reinforcement learning framework. Training uses both the model’s initial responses and revisions guided by critiques, alongside numerical feedback. This gives the policy opportunities to learn from its first attempt and from a more directed search for a better answer, internalizing benefits from both stages.

Across eight reasoning tasks, the method outperforms all compared supervised and reinforcement learning fine-tuning approaches. Reported average Pass@1 improvements are approximately 15.0–21.6% for various Qwen models and 7.3% for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. The authors also report effective self-critiquing, including a 16.7% Pass@1 improvement over GRPO on AIME 2024. The findings support combining explanatory feedback with reward-based optimization.
summary.tldr: Critique-GRPO combines written critiques with numerical rewards so language models learn from both initial answers and guided revisions.

title: Advancing LLM Reasoning with Natural Language and Numerical Feedback

abstract: Machine learning systems increasingly shape attention, work, education, and social life, yet ML research often treats the question "what is this for?" as external, relying on proxies such as accuracy, engagement, or preference satisfaction. This position paper argues that ML research should be guided by explicit, pluralistic models of human purpose, understood as supporting people’s capacity to pursue meaningful, self-chosen life projects with agency. The paper proposes three community practices: (i) purpose articulation, a structured "Purpose Statement" that specifies intended beneficiaries, mechanisms, and falsifiable failure modes; (ii) purpose evaluation, which measures impacts on agency and meaning alongside task performance and harm; and (iii) purpose governance, which updates purpose frameworks through transparent, participatory processes to reduce unaccountable value-setting. This framing enables concrete technical research directions, including objective design beyond preference satisfaction, benchmarks for agency and meaning, pluralistic system behavior, and institution-aware alignment. The paper provides stakeholder-differentiated recommendations for researchers, benchmark creators, conference organizers, and funders, and addresses credible objections including value neutrality, feasibility and measurement validity, the claim that harm prevention is sufficient, and risks of ideological capture or paternalism.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that machine learning research should explicitly address the human purposes its systems serve. Measures such as accuracy, engagement, and preference satisfaction can leave that question unresolved. The authors define their proposed orientation around helping people pursue meaningful, self-chosen life projects while retaining agency, with room for differing accounts of what matters.

They recommend three practices. A structured Purpose Statement would identify intended beneficiaries, mechanisms, and testable ways the project could fail. Purpose evaluation would examine effects on agency and meaning alongside performance and harm. Purpose governance would revise these frameworks through transparent participation, reducing the scope for unaccountable decisions about values.

The paper connects these practices to technical work on objectives, benchmarks, pluralistic behavior, and alignment attentive to institutions. It offers distinct recommendations for researchers, benchmark creators, conferences, and funders. It also addresses objections involving measurement, feasibility, neutrality, paternalism, and ideological capture. The proposal makes human purpose an explicit and revisable part of research design, including how success and failure are assessed.
summary.tldr: ML research should explicitly state, evaluate, and participatively revise how its systems support human agency and meaningful life projects.

title: Position: Machine Learning Research Should Be Guided by Explicit, Pluralistic Models of Human Purpose

abstract: The ML literature contains many distinct concepts falling under the heading of ‘AI alignment’. After noting three concepts of AI alignment and situating these ideals in the context of their corresponding research programs, we claim that realistic interventions may promote ‘AI alignment’ under one conception while being actively counterproductive from the perspective of others. We suggest that tensions between alignment ideals emerge due to differences in background threat-models, alongside differences in both methodological and normative orientations. In light of our analysis, researchers taking themselves to produce research aimed to further the goal of ‘AI alignment’ should do three things. First, they should distinguish between ‘AI alignment’ as a high-level ideal and the specific ‘alignment proxies’ used in empirical research. Second, they should use more granular concepts to identify the source in addition to the nature of possible AI harms/benefits. Third, they explicitly specify the non-technical background commitments motivating specific conceptions of ‘AI alignment’.

paragraphs: This position paper examines why research described as AI alignment can pursue competing technical priorities. It distinguishes three conceptions of alignment and places them within their associated research programs. Its central claim is that a realistic intervention can advance one conception while working against another, so sharing the same broad label does not establish a shared objective.

The authors trace these tensions to differences in anticipated threats, research methods, and judgments about what ought to matter. These background commitments influence which problems researchers prioritize and what they count as success. Consequently, disagreement about a technical intervention may reflect different underlying goals rather than disagreement about its measured effects.

The paper recommends distinguishing alignment as an overarching ideal from the measurable proxies used in experiments. It also calls for more precise descriptions of both the sources and kinds of potential benefits or harms, alongside explicit statements of motivating nontechnical commitments. These practices would make claims of alignment progress easier to interpret relative to the particular goals they serve.
summary.tldr: Alignment research should state its specific goals and assumptions because progress under one conception can undermine another.

abstract: Recently, instead of selecting a single kernel, multiple kernel learning (MKL) has been proposed which uses a convex combination of kernels, where the weight of each kernel is optimized during training. However, MKL assigns the same weight to a kernel over the whole input space. In this paper, we develop a localized multiple kernel learning (LMKL) algorithm using a gating model for selecting the appropriate kernel function locally. The localizing gating model and the kernel-based classifier are coupled and their optimization is done in a joint manner. Empirical results on ten benchmark and two bioinformatics data sets validate the applicability of our approach. LMKL achieves statistically similar accuracy results compared with MKL by storing fewer support vectors. LMKL can also combine multiple copies of the same kernel function localized in different parts. For example, LMKL with multiple linear kernels gives better accuracy results than using a single linear kernel on bioinformatics data sets.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning combines several kernels and learns their weights during training. The paper identifies a restriction of the standard approach: each kernel receives the same weight throughout the input space. A kernel that is useful for one region therefore cannot receive a different emphasis solely because an example lies elsewhere.

The proposed localized method introduces a gating model that selects appropriate kernels locally. The gate and kernel-based classifier are optimized jointly, so decisions about local kernel use develop alongside the prediction model. The method can also use several copies of the same kernel function, with each copy localized to a different region.

Experiments on ten benchmark datasets and two bioinformatics datasets support the approach's applicability. Compared with ordinary multiple kernel learning, it achieves statistically similar accuracy while storing fewer support vectors. On the bioinformatics datasets, multiple localized linear kernels improve accuracy over a single linear kernel. The findings connect local adaptation both to a more compact classifier representation and, in the stated comparison, to improved predictions.
summary.tldr: Jointly learned local kernel selection achieves comparable MKL accuracy with fewer support vectors and improves some linear-kernel results.

title: Localized multiple kernel learning

abstract: In this paper we show how common speech recognition training criteria such as the Minimum Phone Error criterion or the Maximum Mutual Information criterion can be extended to incorporate a margin term. Different margin-based training algorithms have been proposed to refine existing training algorithms for general machine learning problems. However, for speech recognition, some special problems have to be addressed and all approaches proposed either lack practical applicability or the inclusion of a margin-term enforces significant changes to the underlying model, e.g. the optimization algorithm, the loss functions, or the parameterization of the model. In our approach, the conventional training criteria are modified to incorporate a margin term. This allows us to do large-margin training in speech recognition using the same efficient algorithms for accumulation and optimization and to use the same software as for conventional discriminative training. We show that the proposed criteria are equivalent to Support Vector Machines with suitable smooth loss functions, approximating the non-smooth hinge loss function or the hard error (e.g. phone error). Experimental results are given for two different tasks: the rather simple digit string recognition task Sietill which severely suffers from overfitting and the large vocabulary European Parliament Plenary Sessions English task which is supposed to be dominated by the risk and the generalization does not seem to be such an issue.

Its practical motivation is that earlier margin-based approaches either posed usability problems or required substantial changes to the model, loss, parameterization, or optimization procedure. The authors seek margin-based training that fits existing discriminative training machinery.

They modify the conventional criteria while retaining the efficient accumulation and optimization algorithms and the same training software. They also show equivalence to support vector machines with appropriate smooth losses. Those losses approximate either the nonsmooth hinge loss or a hard error measure such as phone error, connecting the modified speech criteria to large-margin classification.

Experiments cover two contrasting tasks. Sietill digit-string recognition is described as suffering severely from overfitting, while the large-vocabulary European Parliament English task is thought to be dominated by risk, with generalization apparently less problematic. This supplies different contexts for studying the criteria. The abstract presents the evaluation settings without stating a specific performance gain for either one.
summary.tldr: Modified MMI and MPE criteria introduce large-margin speech training while preserving existing optimization algorithms and software.

title: Modified MMI/MPE: a direct evaluation of the margin in speech recognition

abstract: This paper presents a cutting plane algorithm for multiclass maximum margin clustering (MMC). The proposed algorithm constructs a nested sequence of successively tighter relaxations of the original MMC problem, and each optimization problem in this sequence could be efficiently solved using the constrained concave-convex procedure (CCCP). Experimental evaluations on several real world datasets show that our algorithm converges much faster than existing MMC methods with guaranteed accuracy, and can thus handle much larger datasets efficiently.
originalAbstract: This paper presents a cutting plane algorithm for multiclass maximum margin clustering (MMC). The proposed algorithm constructs a nested sequence of successively tighter relaxations of the original MMC problem, and each optimization problem in this sequence could be efficiently solved using the constrained concave-convex procedure (CCCP). Experimental evaluations on several real world datasets show that our algorithm converges much faster than existing MMC methods with guaranteed accuracy, and can thus handle much larger datasets efficiently.

paragraphs: This paper develops a more efficient algorithm for multiclass maximum margin clustering. Its focus is the optimization needed to obtain a clustering under the maximum margin formulation. The practical motivation is scalability: if solving that formulation takes too long, the size of datasets that can be handled becomes restricted.

The proposed cutting plane algorithm works through a nested sequence of relaxed optimization problems. Each successive relaxation more tightly represents the original clustering problem. This creates a progression of intermediate problems rather than requiring the full formulation to be handled at once. Each problem in that sequence can be solved efficiently using the constrained concave-convex procedure, or CCCP.

Evaluations on several real-world datasets show much faster convergence than existing maximum margin clustering methods, with guaranteed accuracy as described in the abstract. The resulting efficiency allows the algorithm to handle substantially larger datasets. The contribution therefore connects an optimization strategy to a practical gain in scale: progressively tightening the problem makes this clustering approach more computationally accessible.
summary.tldr: A cutting plane method makes multiclass maximum margin clustering faster by solving a sequence of progressively tighter relaxations.

title: Efficient multiclass maximum margin clustering

abstract: We describe a new method for learning the conditional probability distribution of a binary-valued variable from labelled training examples. Our proposed Compositional Noisy-Logical Learning (CNLL) approach learns a noisy-logical distribution in a compositional manner. CNLL is an alternative to the well-known AdaBoost algorithm which performs coordinate descent on an alternative error measure. We describe two CNLL algorithms and test their performance compared to AdaBoost on two types of problem: (i) noisy-logical data (such as noisy exclusive-or), and (ii) four standard datasets from the UCI repository. Our results show that we outperform AdaBoost while using significantly fewer weak classifiers, thereby giving a more transparent classifier suitable for knowledge extraction.

paragraphs: This paper learns the conditional probability of a variable with two possible values from labeled examples. Its Compositional Noisy-Logical Learning approach, or CNLL, builds a noisy-logical probability distribution by composing simpler parts. The objective is therefore a probabilistic account of a binary outcome, with logical structure represented in the learned model.

The authors position CNLL as an alternative to AdaBoost and describe two algorithms. The comparison concerns both how learning is organized and which error measure guides it. The compositional approach is especially relevant to the paper's tests involving noisy logical relationships, including noisy exclusive-or, where the relationship between inputs and outputs has an explicitly logical form.

The evaluation covers those noisy-logical problems and four standard UCI datasets. The authors report better performance than AdaBoost while using substantially fewer weak classifiers. That second finding matters for interpretation as well as prediction: a classifier assembled from fewer components can be more transparent. The paper presents this compactness as making the resulting classifier suitable for extracting knowledge from what it has learned.
summary.tldr: CNLL builds noisy-logical probability models that outperform AdaBoost in the reported tests while using fewer weak classifiers.

paragraphs: A matrix can have more than one representation as a product of low-rank factors. Consequently, knowing the product does not uniquely determine the factors that produced it. This paper investigates how that non-identifiability affects Bayesian matrix factorization, focusing on the consequences of the inference method used to fit the model.

The main theoretical finding is that variational Bayesian inference introduces a regularization effect even when the prior is non-informative. A prior that supplies little information therefore does not imply an absence of regularization in the resulting procedure. The authors identify this behavior as intrinsically different from maximum a posteriori estimation.

The analysis also extends to empirical Bayes, where hyperparameters are estimated from the data. This matters for interpreting what controls a fitted factorization: the behavior depends on more than an explicitly informative prior. By connecting non-identifiability with implicit regularization, the paper clarifies a structural difference between Bayesian approximation and point estimation in the matrix-factorization setting.
summary.tldr: Variational Bayesian matrix factorization has an implicit regularization effect even with a non-informative prior, unlike maximum a posteriori estimation.

title: Implicit Regularization in Variational Bayesian Matrix Factorization
